file: 2013/2013-01-31_fear_inventions_machine learning_track customers_machines take over_annihilate all humans.gif
title: Machine Learning Precedes Robot Apocalypse

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Our machine learning technology allows us to track customer preferences and use that knowledge to manipulate them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That seems like the step that happens right before the machines take over the Earth and annihilate all humans.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: There's always one person in every crowd who says that.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Not for much longer, apparently.

situation: A bald presenter explains that his company's machine learning technology tracks customer preferences so they can be manipulated. Dilbert remarks that this sounds like the step right before machines take over and destroy humanity. The presenter dismisses him as the usual naysayer, then ominously adds that he won't be around much longer.
punchline: The presenter's reply implies the machines really will wipe out humans, and the skeptic will be among the first to go.
summary: A pitch for customer-manipulating AI draws a doomsday warning from Dilbert, and the presenter's chilling response confirms the fear.

title: Shaving Head Either Way Charity Pledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we raise $40,000 for charity, I will shave my head!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And if we raise no money at all, I will shave MY head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's messed up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his staff that he will shave his head if they raise $40,000 for charity. Wally, who is already bald, counters that he will shave his own head if no money is raised at all. The Boss calls this messed up, and Wally calmly questions that.
punchline: Wally is already bald, so his pledge costs him nothing, which makes his 'sacrifice' meaningless while he blithely brushes off the Boss's complaint.
summary: A manager's showy charity pledge gets undercut by a bald employee offering an empty counter-pledge.

title: Managers Are In The Top 110%

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A study says 74% of managers think they are above average.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That means 36% of managers aren't aware that they are above average too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The way I look at it, you're all in the top 110%.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly. Thank you.

situation: The Boss, holding a tablet, reports that a study found 74% of managers think they are above average. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, does some quick arithmetic and concludes that the remaining 36% must be unaware of their own above-average status. He then says all managers are in the top 110%, which the Boss takes as a compliment.
punchline: Dilbert's math is nonsensical (74% plus 36% adds up to 110%), and his sarcastic 'top 110%' remark is lost on the Boss, who accepts it as genuine praise.
summary: A boss cites a statistic about managers rating themselves highly, and an employee's absurd arithmetic flatters him without him noticing the insult.

title: Meaningless Job, Better Coping

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd feel more loyalty to the company if management would acknowledge my contributions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If my job were as meaningless as yours, I wouldn't want management to notice me at all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You and I have the same job.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I seem to be handling it better.

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert holds a coffee mug and complains to a bald, bespectacled coworker that management never acknowledges his contributions. The coworker replies that if his job were as meaningless as Dilbert's, he would prefer to go unnoticed. Dilbert points out they have the same job, and the coworker smugly says he is handling it better.
punchline: The coworker insults Dilbert's job as meaningless, then unwittingly admits his own is equally pointless, claiming only to cope better by staying invisible.
summary: A colleague mocks Dilbert's craving for recognition by calling his work pointless, only to be reminded that his own work is identical.

title: Bring Me Solutions, Not Problems

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our mission, vision, strategy, road map, and core values are not aligned.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So instead of flailing around with no clear direction, I plan to spend my days looking at inappropriate websites.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yesterday, when you said, "Bring me solutions, not problems," I hope you meant it.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the seated Boss that the company's mission, vision, strategy, road map and core values are misaligned. He announces that his solution is to spend his days browsing inappropriate websites instead of flailing around. He then reminds the Boss that he had demanded solutions rather than problems.
punchline: Wally treats the Boss's demand for solutions as a loophole, offering his own lazy idleness as the 'solution' to the company's lack of direction.
summary: An idle employee uses his manager's own catchphrase to justify surfing questionable websites rather than working in a directionless company.

title: Reflexive Disagreement Backfires on Programmer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you make the software changes I suggested?

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: No, because I reflexively disagree with every suggestion that anyone ever makes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're very reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: No, I'm a total jerk... Wait, what did you just do there?

situation: Dilbert asks a bearded coworker whether he implemented the software changes Dilbert suggested. The coworker admits he automatically disagrees with every suggestion anyone makes. Dilbert then calls him very reasonable, and the coworker reflexively disagrees with that too, contradicting his own self-image before realizing he's been manipulated.
punchline: Dilbert uses reverse psychology on a habitual contrarian, so the man's reflex to disagree makes him deny being unreasonable and admit he's a jerk.
summary: A knee-jerk naysayer gets outmaneuvered when a compliment triggers his compulsion to contradict anything said to him.

title: Boss Blocks Promotion He Caused

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I can't promote you because the other managers don't know you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's because you shut me out of meetings and take credit for my work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds unsolvable.

situation: The Boss tells Asok he can't be promoted because the other managers don't know him. Asok points out that this is the Boss's own doing, since he excludes Asok from meetings and claims credit for his work. The Boss shrugs and declares the problem unsolvable.
punchline: The Boss treats a problem he personally created as an unfixable fact of life, using it as an excuse to keep Asok down while ignoring the obvious solution of changing his own behavior.
summary: A manager refuses an employee's promotion over a visibility problem that the manager himself engineered, then dismisses any fix as impossible.

title: Time Machine For Mailing Signatures

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You'll need to mail me the original signature page after everyone signs it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I'll use my time machine to go back to an era in which mailing original signatures made some kind of sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if there will ever be a way to send images over the telegraph system.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to physically mail the original signed signature page. Dilbert sarcastically says he'll use a time machine to travel to an era when that made sense. He then stands up, apparently having gone back in time, and muses about whether images could ever be sent over the telegraph.
punchline: Insisting on mailed original signatures is so outdated that Dilbert jokes he must travel back to the telegraph era to find it sensible.
summary: Dilbert mocks a demand for paper signatures by pretending to time travel to a bygone age of telegraphs.

title: Intuition Is Just Guessing, Allegedly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if I should rely more on my intuition to make decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You mean guessing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. Guessing is totally different from intuition because of the... um...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These things make sense in my head!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is there room in there with all of the intuition?

setting: Outdoor grassy field with a tree stump
situation: Dilbert muses aloud about trusting his intuition more when making decisions, and Dogbert, sitting on a tree stump, bluntly calls that guessing. Dilbert tries to explain the difference but cannot articulate it, then insists his reasoning makes sense in his head. Dogbert snarks that there may not be space in there for it.
punchline: Dilbert cannot explain how intuition differs from guessing, and Dogbert implies his head is too empty or cluttered with bad ideas to hold any real intuition.
summary: A man tries to defend gut-feeling decision making against the charge that it is mere guessing, and his dog mocks him for it.

title: Dilbert Overwhelmed by First Compliment

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Customer meeting

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: The secret of our company's success is that we hire good people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying I'm good? I've never heard a compliment at work. What is that feeling inside me? Is it the thing called self-esteem?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Awkward.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Just ignore him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Behold my goodness!

setting: Conference room during a customer meeting
situation: A coworker tells a customer that the company succeeds because it hires good people. Dilbert, who has never received a compliment at work, takes it personally and marvels at the unfamiliar feeling of self-esteem. He then throws his arms up and boasts in front of the embarrassed customer while his coworker tells her to ignore him.
punchline: Dilbert is so starved of workplace praise that a generic company boast sends him into an embarrassing display of self-esteem.
summary: A passing remark about hiring good people sends a praise-starved engineer into a gloating spectacle in front of a client.

file: 2013/2013-02-05_deception_fake websites_gullibility_idiopathy epidemic_internet & world wide web_search engine_slap the victim.gif
title: Fake Websites Cause Idiopathy Epidemic

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've learned to control reality by creating fake websites and doing search engine optimization.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you hear about the idiopathy epidemic? The symptoms include pointy hair and gullibility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only treatment is for someone else to slap the victim.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ask for it like you mean it.

situation: Alice, holding a coffee mug, boasts to Dilbert that she controls reality by building fake websites and gaming search engine optimization. The Boss walks up reading from a paper about an 'idiopathy epidemic' whose symptoms are pointy hair and gullibility, which describes himself. When he says the only cure is for someone else to slap the victim, Alice invites him to ask for it properly.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly reads out a description of his own condition, and Alice, who exploits gullible people with fake websites, eagerly offers to administer the slap cure.
summary: A bragging coworker manipulating the web gets an unwitting audience when her boss reads aloud about a gullibility disease he clearly has, and she volunteers to deliver the remedy.

title: Clown Car Office Plan

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Productivity went down when we moved the engineers from private offices to cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Productivity went down again when we tried the open office plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have we tried putting all of them in one clown car?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: No, but I don't see why that wouldn't work.

situation: A manager reports to The Boss that productivity fell after engineers were moved from private offices to cubicles, and fell again with an open office plan. The Boss, seated at his desk, suggests cramming everyone into a single clown car, and the manager agrees it might work.
punchline: Each cost-cutting move that crowds employees closer together has hurt productivity, yet the two managers absurdly propose an even more cramped arrangement, showing they never connect the cause to the effect.
summary: Two managers puzzle over falling output after shrinking workspace and then cheerfully propose an even tighter squeeze.

title: Boss Accidentally Teaches Mentoring Lesson

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Would you be my mentor?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better for me if none of my underlings are qualified to take my job.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I think you just taught me something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I hate it when I do that!

situation: A subordinate stands before the boss's desk and asks him to be his mentor. The boss declines by openly admitting he prefers his underlings to be unqualified so none can take his job. The employee points out that this honest answer was itself a lesson, which horrifies the boss.
punchline: The boss refuses to mentor out of self-preservation, but his explanation is itself a valuable lesson, so he ends up mentoring the employee anyway against his wishes.
summary: A manager who wants his staff to stay unqualified is dismayed to discover that explaining why has just educated the very person he meant to keep in the dark.

title: Dilbert Asks Boss for Fake Encouragement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My motivation is low today. I understand it's your job to fix that situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: An insincere attaboy or a fake interest in my life would be enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Drop dead and let the flies eat you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I set the bar too high again.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert standing in front of his desk
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his motivation is low and says it is the boss's job to fix that. He lowers his request to just a fake compliment or feigned interest in his life. The boss responds with a brutally hostile remark instead.
punchline: Dilbert asks for only insincere encouragement, yet the boss can't even manage that and wishes him dead, so Dilbert wryly admits he expected too much.
summary: An employee begs his manager for even a phony pep talk and gets a vicious insult instead.

title: Miracle Request: Diet Coke Into Wine

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We bought a start-up just so we could get the engineers, including you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do something that's worth a million dollars. I want to see what that looks like.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: You don't sound entirely sincere.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Can you turn my Diet Coke into wine?

situation: A manager with big hair tells an engineer that the company acquired his start-up purely to obtain its engineers. She then demands he do something worth a million dollars so she can see what that looks like. When he points out she doesn't sound sincere, she responds by asking him to perform a miracle and turn her Diet Coke into wine.
punchline: Management's vague demand for million-dollar results is so unrealistic that she might as well be asking for a miracle, and her flippant request shows she isn't serious about the work or the engineers.
summary: After buying a company just for its talent, a manager issues a vague order to produce something priceless, then mocks the engineer with a request for a miracle.

title: Software Vendor Blames Third-Party Library

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The software you sold us stopped working after a week. What's up with that?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We use a third-party library, and it isn't compatible with the new version of Windows.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And . . . ?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We appreciate your business?

situation: Dilbert confronts a software salesman because the product he bought stopped working after one week. The salesman explains that a third-party library is incompatible with the new version of Windows. When Dilbert waits for a fix or remedy, the salesman offers only a thank-you for the purchase.
punchline: The vendor offers an excuse and no solution, tacking on a hollow expression of gratitude as if that were an adequate response to selling broken software.
summary: A customer demands answers about a product that died within days, and the vendor shrugs off responsibility with a technical excuse and a polite thank-you.

file: 2013/2013-07-07_obliviousness_work ethic_lawyer_60 page contract_amendements_900 contracts_tax law_17 managers_good leaders_standards_legal.gif
title: Impossible Contract Review Due Tomorrow

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our lawyer sent over a sixty-page contract renewal that I need you to review.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure you compare it to the original contract and all six or seven amendments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are there six or... seven?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one really knows.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Check out our other nine hundred contracts to make sure this one doesn't violate any of those.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep in mind our five-year strategic plan and all likely changes to tax law.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then get buy-in from the seventeen managers who hate my guts and will take it out on you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good leaders set high standards.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a sixty-page contract renewal and keeps piling on requirements: compare it to the original and its amendments, check it against nine hundred other contracts, factor in the strategic plan and tax law, and win approval from seventeen hostile managers. He then demands it all be done by tomorrow. Walking away, he congratulates himself in a thought bubble for setting high standards.
punchline: The Boss mistakes assigning an absurd, impossible workload with an overnight deadline for good leadership, showing his complete obliviousness.
summary: A manager loads a subordinate with an ever-growing pile of impossible review tasks due by tomorrow, then privately praises his own demanding leadership style.

title: PhD Holder Admits Total Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have no real-world experience and I am incompetent at everything.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But unlike any of you, I have a Ph.D., and that means you have to take me seriously.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is pretending allowed?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Totally. It all looks the same to me.

situation: At a meeting table, a bearded coworker with a Ph.D. cheerfully admits he has no real-world experience and is incompetent at everything, yet insists his degree means everyone must take him seriously. Dilbert asks whether pretending to be competent is acceptable, and the Ph.D. holder says it is, because he can't tell the difference between real and fake expertise.
punchline: The credentialed expert cannot distinguish genuine competence from bluffing, which implies that degrees and confident pretending are indistinguishable and that his authority is meaningless.
summary: A boastful academic confesses he is useless at everything but demands respect for his degree, then admits he cannot tell faking it from the real thing.

title: Follow Your Passion: Eating Bread

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, the secret to success is to do what you love and stick to it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I like eating bread.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly! Follow your passion.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six months later

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe I should try something else.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quitter.

setting: Office hallway, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss walks with Asok and tells him that success comes from doing what you love and sticking with it. Asok says he likes eating bread, and the Boss enthusiastically tells him to follow that passion. Six months later, Asok holding a coffee mug says he should try something else, and the Boss, seated at his desk, calls him a quitter.
punchline: The Boss's glib 'follow your passion' advice sets Asok up to fail, and then the Boss blames him for quitting rather than owning the bad advice.
summary: A manager's cheerful career advice leads an employee into a hopeless pursuit, and the manager then scolds him for giving up.

title: Mentoring Feels Great Inside

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: Dilbert and two coworkers sit at a table with coffee mugs.)

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: The two coworkers sip from their mugs while Dilbert looks on.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The mentor thing isn't for everyone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't know how this looks, but it feels great on the inside.

setting: A conference table in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert sits silently with two coworkers who sip from coffee mugs. Dilbert then remarks that mentoring isn't for everyone, and one of the coworkers replies that it feels great on the inside, while looking blank and unengaged. The coworkers' expressions show no sign of the enthusiasm they claim.
punchline: The coworker claims to be enjoying the mentoring experience, but his deadpan, expressionless face shows no outward sign of it, undercutting his claim of feeling great inside.
summary: A man insists he is deeply enjoying a mentoring session even though nothing in his blank face suggests it.

title: Blame the Firewall Guy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to install the new firewall.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Noooo!!!! Why me? Why me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The firewall guy gets blamed for every problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People will say, "Everything worked until you changed the firewall."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There will be no rest for me. I will have to defend myself against a continuous barrage of accusations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's always the firewall! Everyone blames the stinkin' firewall!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I surrender to the inevitable! Villagers, grab your pitchforks and torches!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did he get that way?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I blame the firewall.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to install the new firewall, and Dilbert panics, predicting he will be blamed for every future problem. He spirals into despair, ranting about constant accusations and finally calling for villagers with pitchforks and torches. The Boss asks a coworker how Dilbert got so upset.
punchline: The coworker's answer, "I blame the firewall," proves Dilbert's point that the firewall gets blamed for everything, even his own breakdown.
summary: A technician dreads being the scapegoat for a network change, and his meltdown is promptly pinned on the very thing he feared.

title: Outsourcing Both Jobs To Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard a rumor that you have two jobs and you outsource both of them to Elbonia and keep the difference.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's crazy. I assure you I do NOT have two jobs outsourced to Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it more than two?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's a different conversation.

situation: The Boss confronts a seated employee about a rumor that he holds two jobs, outsources both to Elbonia, and pockets the pay difference. The employee sips his coffee and denies having exactly two outsourced jobs. When the Boss asks if it is more than two, the employee dodges, saying that is a different conversation.
punchline: The employee's carefully worded denial of only 'two' jobs implicitly admits he is outsourcing even more than that.
summary: A worker slyly sidesteps accusations of secretly farming out his jobs overseas while pocketing the savings, accidentally confessing to an even bigger scheme.

title: Standing Be Good Consulting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert ergonomic consulting company to tell us about the health benefits of standing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Standing be good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The topic isn't as complicated as you might think.

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that he hired Dogbert's ergonomic consulting company to explain the health benefits of standing. Dogbert, seated at the table, delivers his entire finding in three words. When the Boss asks if that's all, Dogbert says the topic is simple.
punchline: Dogbert collects a consulting fee for a trivially obvious three-word answer, then justifies the minimal effort by saying the subject is simple.
summary: A consultant dog boils his whole ergonomic study down to a three-word verdict and defends its brevity.

title: Scheduled Time to Glare

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's next on my schedule?

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: For the next five minutes you're scheduled to glare at me like an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: Four minutes to go.

setting: Office cubicle area, beside the assistant's desk
situation: The Boss walks up to his assistant's cubicle and asks what is next on his schedule. She deadpans that he is booked to glare at her like an idiot for five minutes. He does exactly that, and she checks her watch and announces how many minutes remain.
punchline: The assistant insults her boss by turning his idiotic staring into a scheduled calendar item, and he is too dim to notice and obediently follows it.
summary: A manager asks his assistant what he has planned next and she dryly assigns him an appointment to stare stupidly at her, which he dutifully carries out.

file: 2013/2013-04-26_rich people_thinking_fool proof_plan for success_think about shoes_easy tasks.gif
title: Rich People Think About Shoes

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I have a fool-proof plan for success.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I will read a book on how rich people think. Then I will start thinking that way.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Rich people think about their shoes a lot.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can do that!

setting: Office break area, then Asok's desk
situation: Asok tells Dilbert and Wally, who are holding coffee mugs, that his foolproof plan for success is to read a book about how rich people think and then copy their thinking. Later, at his desk with a smartphone, he learns that rich people think about their shoes a lot and happily decides he can do that.
punchline: Asok's self-help plan to become rich boils down to the trivially easy habit of thinking about shoes, mistaking a superficial trait of wealthy people for the cause of their success.
summary: A young employee plans to get wealthy by adopting rich people's mindset and is delighted to find the secret is just thinking about footwear.

title: Wally Glasses Make Reality Unappealing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I invented "Wally Glasses" to compete with Google's glasses.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Google's glasses enhance reality, whereas Wally Glasses make reality look like it isn't worth the effort.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me know if they kill you.

situation: Wally pitches his invention, "Wally Glasses," to the Boss as a rival to Google's glasses. He explains that they make reality seem not worth the effort, and the Boss puts them on. Wally then casually asks to be told if the glasses end up killing him.
punchline: Wally's gadget is designed to promote apathy, and he shows no concern that his untested product might kill the person trying it.
summary: A lazy inventor pitches a high-tech eyewear rival whose selling point is draining all motivation, and he is unbothered by the risk of lethal side effects.

title: Meeting Time Theft Claims Servant

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, your meeting stole an hour of my life.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: According to international law, I may now claim you as my indentured servant.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow. That... actually is a law.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Or I'm really good at SEO.

situation: Alice complains to Asok that his meeting wasted an hour of her life, then declares that international law lets her claim him as her indentured servant. Asok checks on his phone and is amazed to find such a law really exists. Alice privately thinks that she may just be good at search engine optimization.
punchline: Alice's invented legal claim shows up as real in a web search, so either the law exists or she has gamed search results to make her bluff look true.
summary: A annoyed engineer threatens to enslave a colleague over a wasted hour, and an online search appears to back her up.

file: 2013/2013-06-09_frustration_bias for action_enemy of good_folksy_spray defective stuff.gif
title: Bias for Action Meets Carpenter

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to have a bias for action.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't let perfect be the enemy of good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So . . . a carpenter should saw the board first and measure it later?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your use of that folksy saying makes my strategy sound dumb.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do you care if your strategy is perfect or not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just said it's more important to spray your defective stuff on the universe than it is to get things right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Spray my defective stuff"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should I have waited for a perfect way to say that?

situation: The Boss tells the team to have a bias for action and not let perfect be the enemy of good. Dilbert applies a folksy carpenter analogy that exposes the flaw in the strategy, and Alice points out that the Boss's own reasoning implies that shipping defective work matters more than getting it right. The Boss ends up unintentionally mocking his own phrasing.
punchline: The Boss's rush-to-act philosophy is undercut when he's forced to admit that his hastily chosen words, like his strategy, were imperfect and sloppy.
summary: A manager pushing speed over quality gets his own folksy wisdom turned against him, ending with him defending his clumsy phrasing as proof of his point.
keywords: perfect is the enemy of good

title: Motivational Coach Offers Existential Dread

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's my motivation today?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Robot
transcript.text: You're a temporary arrangement of matter sliding toward oblivion in a cold, uncaring universe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Robot
transcript.text: Did I already say "needy"?

situation: Dilbert, dressed for work with his bag over his shoulder, asks his small egg-shaped robot what his motivation is for the day. The robot responds with a bleak description of human existence as matter drifting toward oblivion. Dilbert is unimpressed, and the robot adds that he might also have said Dilbert is needy.
punchline: The robot's idea of motivation is a deeply nihilistic description of mortality, and it treats calling Dilbert "needy" as the only useful detail it might have left out.
summary: A man asks his household robot for a pep talk and gets a grim cosmic reality check instead.

file: 2013/2013-04-11_ignorance (knowledge)_managers & supervisors_work ethic_wifi enabled_bus_commute from san fransico_business.gif
title: Be More Like a Bus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Google provides a Wi-Fi-enabled bus for its employees to commute from San Francisco.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't we be more like that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want to be more like a bus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found the problem.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss in a meeting that Google provides a Wi-Fi-enabled bus for employees commuting from San Francisco. The boss responds that the company should be more like that, and Dilbert takes the remark literally, asking if he wants the company to be more like a bus.
punchline: The boss's vague desire to emulate Google gets taken literally, and the final line shows he completely misses the point, with the exaggerated stupidity of his reply showing the problem is the boss himself.
summary: After hearing about a tech giant's commuter perk, a clueless manager wants his company to imitate it, and his employee mocks the absurd literal interpretation.

file: 2013/2013-01-17_business shake_etiquette & ethics_handshake_macaroni and cheese_moist and squishy.gif
title: Wet Sock Handshake Insult

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Allen, from Sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your handshake feels like a wet sock full of macaroni and cheese. It makes me wish we never met.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: Please let go of my hand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's moist and squishy.

situation: Allen from Sales introduces himself to Dilbert and they shake hands. Dilbert bluntly insults the quality of Allen's handshake, comparing it to a wet sock full of macaroni and cheese. Allen asks to be released, but Dilbert keeps holding on because the grip is so moist and squishy.
punchline: Dilbert rudely criticizes Allen's limp, clammy handshake yet keeps holding on, so the thing he finds repulsive is the very thing he won't let go of.
summary: A new acquaintance from Sales gets a brutally honest review of his clammy handshake from a colleague who then refuses to let go.

file: 2013/2013-04-17_deception_stock market_hedge fund compnay_investment fund_misleading claims_3 week period_money.gif
title: Hedge Fund's One Lucky Streak

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best way to evaluate an investment fund is to look at its misleading claims of past performance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Hedge Fund beat the market average for a three-week period . . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That one time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you do that again?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It depends on what you mean by "that."

situation: The Boss sits at a desk opposite Dogbert, who runs a hedge fund. The Boss says the way to evaluate a fund is to look at its misleading past performance claims, and Dogbert cites a single three-week stretch where the fund beat the market. When the Boss asks if he can repeat it, Dogbert dodges with a weaselly answer.
punchline: Hedge fund performance claims rely on cherry-picked lucky streaks, and Dogbert evades the question of repeatability by quibbling over what "that" means.
summary: A cynical fund manager touts one fleeting winning stretch as proof of skill, then wriggles out of promising a repeat.

title: Raised By A Thermos Of Coffee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think success is mostly a function of your genetic makeup or your upbringing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My mom raised me by putting a warm thermos of coffee in my crib and going out for the day. And I turned out great.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have no follow-up questions, in case you wondered.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not the curious type.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally whether success comes from genes or upbringing. Wally, holding his ever-present coffee mug, says his mother raised him by leaving a warm thermos of coffee in his crib and going out for the day, and claims he turned out great. He then announces he has no follow-up questions because he is not curious.
punchline: Wally treats a neglectful, coffee-dependent childhood as proof of a great upbringing, and his total lack of curiosity shows he is content to do as little as possible.
summary: Asked about nature versus nurture, a coffee-clutching coworker credits his neglected infancy for his success and refuses to be curious about anything further.

file: 2013/2013-03-31_frustration_questioning_navigation button_top of page_idea people_difficult_people not answering.gif
title: Move the Button, But Whose Idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would it be better with the navigation button at the top of the page?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: I can make that change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know you can make the change. I'm asking if you agree it would be a good idea.

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: It's no problem to move buttons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But is it a good idea?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: I can have it done in ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But should we do it at all?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: Whatever you want.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is not an answer! Forget it!

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: I'm going to tell your boss you're difficult to work with.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When will you move the button?

transcript.speaker: Programmer
transcript.text: As soon as it's my idea.

situation: Dilbert asks a programmer whether moving a website's navigation button to the top of the page would be a good idea. The programmer keeps answering only that he is able to make the change, never giving an opinion, until Dilbert loses patience and storms off. The programmer then threatens to complain that Dilbert is difficult, and reveals he will only act once the idea is his own.
punchline: The programmer refuses to offer any opinion or take direction, and will only implement the change once he can claim the idea as his own.
summary: A coworker dodges every request for his opinion on a design tweak, then confesses he'll only act when he gets the credit.

title: Break Eggs If Network Fails

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The upgrade could make our network unstable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't make an omelet without breaking some eggs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I interpret your folksy response to mean I should upgrade the network despite the risks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'm saying I'll break your eggs if the network goes down.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: Dilbert warns his boss that a network upgrade could cause instability. The boss replies with the folksy proverb about omelets and eggs, which Dilbert takes as approval to proceed. The boss then clarifies that he actually meant a threat: he will physically hurt Dilbert if the network goes down.
punchline: The boss's cheerful proverb about breaking eggs turns out to be a veiled threat of violence against Dilbert, not permission to take the risk.
summary: A manager's cliché about making omelets is revealed to be a menacing warning aimed at the employee who proposed a risky system change.

file: 2013/2013-04-30_comic ends early_embedded punchline_follow passion_joking_made fat_set up_blank frame_sight gag.gif
title: Comic Ends Early: Punchline In Setup

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I tried to follow my passion but it only made me fat.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Message to readers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This comic ends early because some idiot embedded the punch line in the setup.

setting: Office break area, then a desk
situation: In the first panel a heavyset coworker holding a coffee mug tells Dilbert that following his passion only made him fat. The second panel is a 'Message to Readers' from a figure at a desk, explaining that the comic ends early because the punchline was already delivered in the setup. The third panel is left completely blank.
punchline: The strip admits the joke was delivered too soon, so the remaining panel is intentionally left empty, mocking the cartoonist's own poor joke structure.
summary: A one-liner about passion and weight gain is followed by a cartoonist's notice that the joke ran out of room, leaving an empty final frame.

title: Dilbert Matches Pay With Effort

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best I can give you is a 2% raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I'll just lower the quality of my work until my pay feels fair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't do that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm taking side bets that say I can.

setting: The Boss's office, during a salary discussion
situation: The Boss offers Dilbert a meager 2% raise in a one-on-one meeting. Dilbert calmly responds that he will simply reduce the quality of his work until it matches what he feels he is being paid. When the Boss insists he can't do that, Dilbert says he is taking bets that he can.
punchline: Dilbert turns the underpaid employee's quiet resentment into open policy, treating deliberately lowering his work quality as a sure bet the Boss can't prevent.
summary: Offered a stingy raise, an engineer announces he will scale his effort down to match his pay and wagers that his manager cannot stop him.

title: Gullible Reveals Natural Leader

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Studies show that you can identify a natural leader by the way he says the word "gullible."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gullible! Gullible! Gullible!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gullible! Gullible! Gullible!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Some-times I love my job.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert and the Boss that a study says natural leaders can be identified by how they say the word "gullible." The Boss falls for it and starts shouting "Gullible!" repeatedly, while Dilbert looks on silently. Wally sips his coffee and says he sometimes loves his job.
punchline: Wally invents a fake study to trick the Boss into shouting "gullible," which proves the Boss is exactly that, and Wally enjoys the prank.
summary: A coworker fools his clueless supervisor into loudly performing a silly word test, delighting in how easily he is manipulated.

title: Circular Reasoning Is The Key

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What is the key to success?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Hire the right employees!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How do you know you hired the right ones?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: You know because the business is successful.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So the key to success is circular reasoning?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Yes, because circular reasoning is the key.

situation: Dogbert, seated across a table from a bald executive, asks him for the key to business success. The executive says to hire the right employees, and when pressed on how he knows they were right, he says the company's success proves it. Dogbert points out the circular logic and the executive cheerfully confirms it, again using circular reasoning.
punchline: The executive is so unaware of his flawed logic that he justifies circular reasoning with more circular reasoning.
summary: A businessman's advice on success collapses into a loop when his explanation for good hiring depends on the very success he is trying to explain.

title: Confidence Called Poor Teamwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I want you to collaborate with Larry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And by collaborate you mean water down my brilliance with this dullard's brain flatulence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She doesn't play well with others.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I were a man, you'd call it confidence.

situation: The Boss tells Alice to collaborate with a coworker named Larry. Alice bluntly says this just means diluting her brilliant work with his dull ideas. The Boss tells Larry she doesn't play well with others, and Alice retorts that a man behaving this way would be praised as confident.
punchline: Alice points out the workplace double standard: the same assertive, self-assured behavior is labeled a flaw in a woman but a strength in a man.
summary: A manager pairs a sharp-tongued engineer with a weaker colleague, then criticizes her attitude, prompting her to call out the gender bias in how he judges her.

title: CEO Bullied Over Cannibalizing Products

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new product is cannibalizing our old product.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Either we have a brilliant strategy for staving off competition, or our CEO is the victim of a bully.

transcript.speaker: Bully
transcript.text: Ha ha! Why don't you stop cannibalizing yourself?

setting: Conference room presentation, then the CEO's office
situation: Dilbert presents a slide showing a new product eating an old product, explaining that it is cannibalizing sales. A coworker at the table remarks that either the company has a clever competitive strategy or the CEO is being bullied. The final panel shows a bully holding the CEO in a headlock and taunting him with the same cannibalizing language.
punchline: The coworker's guess that the CEO is being bullied turns out to be literally true, as a bully mocks him with a schoolyard-style taunt while holding him in a headlock.
summary: A product strategy that undermines its own earlier offering is explained away as either genius or the CEO being picked on, and the second option is shown to be real.

title: Parents Told Him Anything Was Possible

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My parents taught me that if I worked hard, I could be anything I wanted.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And you chose . . . this?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: His parents sound like morons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe he didn't work hard.

setting: Office break area, coworkers holding coffee mugs
situation: A coworker with horn-like hair says his parents taught him that hard work could make him anything he wanted. Alice skeptically asks if he really chose his current office job, then insults his parents. Dilbert offers a different explanation: that the coworker simply didn't work hard.
punchline: Both Alice and Dilbert insult the coworker's career outcome, one by blaming his parents' advice and the other by blaming his lack of effort, implying his job is nothing to aspire to.
summary: A man credits his parents' pep talk for his career, and his colleagues respond by mocking both the advice and his effort.

title: Boss Squeezes Engineer Like Sponge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I adjusted your time estimate on the proposal from two years to one so we could win the bid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I plan to make up the time by squeezing you like a wet sponge that insulted me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then that wet sponge insulted me.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has cut the project estimate in half from two years to one so the company can win a bid. He explains he'll recover the lost time by squeezing Dilbert like a wet sponge that insulted him. In the last panel he stands holding a coffee mug near Catbert and repeats that the sponge insulted him.
punchline: The Boss's threat to wring extra work out of Dilbert is both menacing and absurd, since his stated motive is petty grievance, and the repetition in the last panel shows he is oddly fixated on the insult.
summary: A manager slashes a project schedule to win a contract and threatens to make his employee work harder to compensate, using a bizarre sponge metaphor.

title: Unblocking a Website Through Bureaucracy

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: This website has been blocked by your company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mordac, I need access to a blocked site for business reasons.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I can only unblock the site if the Director of Human Resources sends me a written approval.

transcript.speaker: Director of Human Resources
transcript.text: I can only make recommendations. Our CIO still has to approve it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Chief Information Officer

transcript.speaker: CIO
transcript.text: How dare you bother me with your trivial website problem!

transcript.speaker: CIO
transcript.text: Crawl back into your hole and think about the career mistake you just made!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we skip the part where you ask me what I accomplished this week?

setting: Corporate office, cubicle, and executive offices
situation: Dilbert hits a blocked website and asks Mordac to unblock it for business reasons. Mordac demands written approval from the HR director, who says the CIO must approve it. The CIO angrily berates Dilbert for the trivial request, and Dilbert later sits in a meeting having accomplished nothing.
punchline: After being bounced through layers of bureaucracy for nothing, Dilbert sarcastically asks to skip the weekly accomplishments review since his whole week was wasted on the approval runaround.
summary: Chasing permission to open one restricted web page sends an employee up the chain of command until an angry executive scolds him, leaving him with nothing to report.

title: Boss Admires His Own Voice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Underlings, listen to the charismatic tone of my deep, confident voice!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Should we listen to the content, too, or will that just confuse us?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll have to do some research and get back to you.

situation: The Boss addresses his staff at a meeting and tells them to focus on how impressive his voice sounds. Alice asks whether they should also pay attention to what he is actually saying, or whether that would only confuse them. The Boss admits he does not know and says he will have to research it.
punchline: The Boss is so focused on sounding confident that he has no idea whether his words contain anything meaningful, and Alice's sarcastic question exposes that his content is empty.
summary: A manager urges his team to admire his commanding delivery, and when asked if his actual words matter too, he has to look into it.

title: The Vanishing Middle Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say hello to the ephemeral middle manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But hurry because he won't last long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, I'm...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you just look stupid.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a new middle manager, warning that he is ephemeral and won't last long. While Dilbert begins to introduce himself, the middle manager fades into a dotted outline and then disappears entirely. Dilbert is left holding out his hand to nobody, and the Boss says he now looks stupid.
punchline: Middle managers are so short-lived in the company that one can vanish mid-introduction, leaving the employee looking foolish for even trying to greet him.
summary: A newly introduced manager evaporates before a handshake can happen, leaving an employee reaching out to empty air.

title: Schrödinger's Cat Escapes as Zombie

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This is Wulf. He used to work for a famous physicist named Schrödinger.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: He escaped before the experiment was finished and now he's both alive and dead at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like a zombie?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Wulf
transcript.text: Wow. I have half a mind to be offended by that.

situation: Catbert introduces an orange cat named Wulf, who used to belong to the physicist Schrödinger and escaped before the famous experiment ended. Wulf is therefore both alive and dead. Dilbert asks if that makes him like a zombie, and Wulf takes offense.
punchline: Wulf the Schrödinger's cat is only half alive, so when Dilbert calls him a zombie he says he has 'half a mind' to be offended, a pun suggesting he's literally half brain-dead.
summary: A cat who fled a quantum physics experiment is compared to the undead and responds with a pun about being half-minded.

file: 2013/2013-05-27_animal costumes_big game hunting_costumes_furry lifestyle_go on safari_take a trip_like animals.gif
title: Carol's Furry Lifestyle Safari Plot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, why did you send me a link about people who like to dress in animal costumes?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's called the furry lifestyle. I thought you might want to try it out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll take a look.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your end game?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If the furry thing sticks I'll try to get him to go on a safari.

situation: The Boss asks Carol why she sent him a link about people who dress in animal costumes. Carol explains it's the furry lifestyle and suggests he try it, and he agrees to look. Dilbert then asks her true motive, and she reveals she hopes to get him to go on a safari.
punchline: Carol is manipulating the Boss into wearing an animal costume so that she can get him to go on a safari, implying he would be mistaken for game and hunted.
summary: An assistant slyly nudges her clueless manager toward a hobby that would make him look like prey in the wild.

title: Employee Needs Micromanagement to Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't wait to see the changes I asked you to make on the interface.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our last meeting was two months ago. You must be finished by now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I haven't started yet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had a few questions. I figured I'd ask you about them the next time we talked.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In the meantime I only did work for people who yelled at me every day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Micromanagement has a bad reputation, but I'm not too proud to say I need it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... well, I'm optimistic that you can make those changes for me by next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably should have asked my questions.

setting: Office, in Dilbert's cubicle or office
situation: The Boss expects Dilbert to have finished interface changes after two months, but Dilbert reveals he has not even started because he had questions and was waiting for the next meeting. Dilbert explains he only worked for people who yelled at him daily, admits he needs micromanagement, and the Boss responds by assigning the work back to Dilbert for next week.
punchline: The Boss, who is the one who actually assigned the work and needed to answer the questions, ends up taking Dilbert's failure as his own cue to blame himself only in his thoughts, showing he misunderstood who was supposed to ask the questions and who was responsible for the delay.
summary: A manager waiting for results learns his subordinate stalled for months over unasked questions and confesses to needing constant pressure, leaving the manager to realize he botched the exchange himself.

title: Distracting Staff With Worse Policies

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Employees are in a furor over our new policy of banning telecommuting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? You mean we found a way to make them stop obsessing over my pay package?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try canceling all maternity leave and see if it makes them stop talking about telecommuting.

situation: An employee tells the boss that staff are furious about the new ban on telecommuting. The boss is pleased because the outrage has pulled attention away from his own pay package. He then suggests cancelling maternity leave to distract everyone from the telecommuting ban.
punchline: The boss treats employee outrage as a cheap distraction tool, planning to pile on ever more cruel policies so that nobody scrutinizes his compensation.
summary: A manager delights that a hated new rule has diverted attention from his salary and proposes an even harsher one to repeat the trick.

file: 2013/2013-01-13_air travel_extra legroom_aisle seat_no baby section_extra bag_priority boarding_in flight entertainment_flight insurance_wi-fi_airplane etxras.gif

summary: A manager agrees to every optional upgrade a booking agent offers, ending up with an astronomically priced multi-stop ticket and cheerfully asking to repeat it for the way back.

file: 2013/2013-04-12_anger_employees_violence_contradcited_meeting_fist of death_robots_no legal rights_cardio_oiled my pan_business.gif
title: Alice Punches Robot for Cardio

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You contradicted me in a meeting today and I didn't appreciate it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to use my Fist of Death on humans, but you robots have no legal rights.

transcript.text: Squirt!

transcript.speaker: Alice

She says she can't use her Fist of Death on humans, but robots have no legal rights, so she can hit it. The robot nervously squirts oil from its mug and says it just oiled its pan, as Alice prepares to punch it as part of her exercise routine.
punchline: Alice treats beating up a legally unprotected robot coworker as a convenient workout, while the robot's nervous remark about oiling its pan suggests it expects to be used as a cooking-pan-like punching target.
summary: An irritated Alice announces she will take out her workplace grievance on a robot colleague, since the law doesn't protect machines, and calls the beating her exercise.

title: Jurors Divide Damages By Zero

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: A small company is suing us for patent infringement.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: We'll be fine unless the court somehow finds twelve citizens who aren't smart enough to get out of jury duty yet are inexplicably able to do math.

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: We recommend an award of whatever the square root of 22 over zero is.

situation: The company's lawyer tells The Boss that a small company is suing them for patent infringement. He says they'll be fine unless the jury is made up of people who can do math. In the courtroom, a juror reads the verdict: an award equal to the square root of 22 over zero, an undefined amount.
punchline: The lawyer's confident assumption that jurors can't do math is undercut by a jury that can, and its verdict of a number divided by zero is mathematically undefined, so the award has no valid value.
summary: A lawyer banks on a mathematically clueless jury, but the jurors turn out to be numerate enough to deliver a verdict that is literally undefined.

file: 2013/2013-04-28_frustration_wages_bounuses_usual formula_pure luck_performance_huge consumer demand_bad job_marketing_engineers_bonus_hard wrok_business_money.gif
title: Bonus Formula Based on Luck

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your bonuses this year will be based on the usual formula.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: 50% is based on pure luck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And 50% is based on the performance of people you have never even met.

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Some guy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This year, the luck factor was good. Our industry experienced huge consumer demand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Unfortunately, people who you have never met did a bad job of marketing and sales are terrible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And for that, you engineers must be punished.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No bonuses for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily for me, my bonus is based on how well I can convince you idiots to work hard while getting no bonuses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like to brag, but I'm fairly sure I'm nailing it.

situation: The Boss tells the engineers their bonuses are half luck and half the performance of unseen colleagues in other departments. Although luck was good, poor marketing and sales results mean the engineers get no bonus. The Boss then reveals his own bonus depends on persuading them to keep working hard without pay.
punchline: The Boss's bonus rewards him for convincing employees to work hard for nothing, and he smugly believes he is succeeding.
summary: Management cancels the engineers' payouts because of other people's failures, then gloats that his own reward comes from keeping them motivated anyway.

title: Wally's Procrastination Is a System

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, are you almost done with your part of the project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I work best under pressure, so I wait until the deadline is almost here.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What if something more important comes up and you don't have time?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's the cornerstone of my system.

situation: Alice asks Wally whether he has nearly finished his share of a team project. Wally, holding his coffee mug, explains he deliberately waits until the deadline is close because he works best under pressure. When Alice points out the risk that something more important could come up, Wally says that possibility is the foundation of his approach.
punchline: Wally's excuse for procrastinating is that he's counting on a more important task appearing so he never has to do the work at all.
summary: A coworker quizzes a habitual slacker about his deadline strategy and discovers his plan depends on getting out of the work entirely.

title: Boss Removes Last Shred of Meaning

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: Ignore the page revisions I sent out ten minutes ago. Your boss revised them again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I ignore the new revisions, too? I'm only asking because that was my plan.

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: Thank you for removing the last shred of meaning from my work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's what I do.

situation: A coworker at her desk tells Dilbert to disregard the page revisions she sent out ten minutes earlier because his boss revised them again. Dilbert asks if he can also ignore the new revisions, since that was already his plan. She thanks him for draining the last bit of meaning from her work, and he replies that this is what he does.
punchline: Dilbert's habit of ignoring everything makes him the perfect, apathetic recipient of constantly changing revisions, and his deadpan reply that crushing her sense of purpose is his job is sarcastic self-awareness.
summary: A colleague's endlessly revised documents get dismissed by an indifferent Dilbert, who cheerfully admits to sucking the purpose out of her efforts.

title: Honest Feedback on Corporate Culture

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for ideas on how we can improve our corporate culture.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You could start by being less of a micromanaging D-bag who hides like a Higgs-boson whenever we need a decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That didn't help.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Will honesty still be taboo in the new culture?

situation: The Boss asks his team for ideas to improve the corporate culture. Alice bluntly tells him to stop micromanaging and to stop hiding when decisions are needed. He scowls and says that didn't help, and she asks if honesty will still be off-limits in the new culture.
punchline: The Boss solicits suggestions for a better culture but punishes candid feedback, showing that the company's real culture of suppressing honesty will not change.
summary: When a manager invites ideas to fix the company's culture, a blunt employee criticizes his own behavior and then points out that he plainly doesn't welcome the truth.

title: Evaluating Wally's Dubious Quarterly Accomplishments

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, this is my brother, Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked him to interpret your accomplishments for this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You have 25 alleged accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Eight of these accomplishments involved simply being on a project team that did something.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Nine accomplishments involved fixing problems you created.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Five of these are just buzzwords that don't mean anything.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And three are duplicates that you reworded to appear different.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I'd recommend harvesting his organs, but those probably don't work either.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's just mean.

setting: Conference room during a performance review meeting
situation: The Boss introduces his brother Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light, to review Wally's quarterly accomplishments. Phil breaks the 25 claimed accomplishments down into team participation, self-inflicted problems, buzzwords and duplicates, leaving nothing of real value. He ends by suggesting Wally's organs be harvested before conceding they would be useless too.
punchline: After showing that every one of Wally's accomplishments is bogus, Phil insults him further by saying even his organs would be worthless, and Wally can only call it mean.
summary: A demonic reviewer dismantles a lazy employee's list of achievements category by category, then tops it off with a morbid insult.

title: Punished Either Way: Maintenance Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we buy the maintenance plan or just take our chances? What do you prefer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I prefer to punish you for buying the maintenance plan and going over budget. But I also don't mind firing you for not buying it if we later need it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which one of us has a better job?

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether the company should buy a maintenance plan or gamble without one. The Boss cheerfully explains that he will punish Dilbert whichever way it turns out: for overspending if he buys it, or by firing him if it's needed and wasn't bought. Dilbert responds by asking which of them has the better job.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the boss has the enviable position of being able to blame his subordinate no matter what, while carrying none of the risk himself.
summary: A manager reveals that any decision his employee makes about a service contract will end in blame, prompting a sarcastic question about who really has it better.

title: Monster Rewriting Tax Code Frustratingly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for a monster named Stanky Bathurd.

transcript.speaker: Green Monster
transcript.text: He's kind of busy rewriting the tax code to be more frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I know. He hired me to help.

setting: Outdoors in a forest clearing near a stone cave entrance, with a hollow tree and mountains behind
situation: Dogbert walks happily past a hollow tree and arrives at a stone-arched monster cave, where he asks a green, tentacled monster for another monster named Stanky Bathurd. The monster says Stanky is busy rewriting the tax code to make it more frustrating. Dogbert replies that he already knows because Stanky hired him to help.
punchline: Dogbert is cheerfully a collaborator in making the tax code more frustrating, which implies the notorious complexity of taxes is deliberate, monster-made, and helped along by a consultant.
summary: A cheerful Dogbert visits a cave of monsters and reveals he has been hired to help make the tax code even more maddening.

title: Wearable Computing Shock Collar Prank

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wearable computing is the next big thing. This is my prototype of a necklace computer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Prepare to be shocked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just talk him into wearing a remotely controlled shock collar?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People think I have no goals.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

situation: Wally shows the Boss a curved device he calls a prototype necklace computer, and the Boss puts it around his neck. Wally warns him to prepare to be shocked. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks if Wally tricked him into wearing a remote-controlled shock collar, and Wally clicks a remote in his hand.
punchline: Wally presents a shock collar as trendy wearable tech to trick his boss, proving he does have a goal: zapping the boss for fun.
summary: Wally dupes his gullible manager into putting on a zapping gadget disguised as the future of fashionable technology.

title: Fired If You Do, Fired If Don't

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm on a deadline, so don't let anyone disturb me for at least an hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If anyone gets past you, you're fired.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Tell your boss to come to my office now.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: He'll fire me if I disturb him.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'm your CEO! Disturb your boss now or I'll fire you!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard that. And if you disturb me, you're fired!

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: You're fired if you don't!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're fired if you do!

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Whoa! Hold on! I'm getting a sudden wave of euphoria.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Me too!

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Is it because we're overpaid?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It... it feels... wonderful!

situation: The Boss tells his assistant to keep everyone away while he works on a deadline, threatening to fire her if anyone gets through. The CEO arrives and threatens to fire her if she doesn't disturb the Boss, and the Boss threatens to fire her if she does. She is caught in the middle, and the two executives are suddenly overcome with euphoria as they stand over her, ending up thrilled with their own power and pay.
punchline: Two overpaid executives get a blissful rush from tormenting a powerless employee with contradictory firing threats, and the strip hints that their euphoria comes from their unearned pay and power.
summary: An assistant is squeezed between two bosses issuing opposite dismissal threats, while the pair revel in the thrill of their own privilege.

title: Son Replaceable By A Hammer

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My 12-year-old wants to know what career would prevent him from being replaced by a robot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've met your son, and I'm pretty sure he could be replaced by a hammer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This took an ugly turn.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe the robots can use him as furniture.

situation: A coworker in her cubicle tells Dilbert that her 12-year-old son wants to know which career is safe from robot automation. Dilbert responds by insulting the boy, saying a hammer could replace him. When she objects, he doubles down, suggesting robots could use the boy as furniture.
punchline: Asked for sincere career advice, Dilbert answers with escalating insults about the child's uselessness, implying the boy is so unskilled he is worthless even to robots.
summary: A worried parent seeks robot-proof career tips for her kid and instead gets a blunt, escalating put-down of the boy's usefulness.

title: Giant Robot Flea Drains Company

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our ex-CEO negotiated an unusually generous severance package.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We had to build a giant robotic flea to suck the assets out of the company.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The weird part is that it seemed reasonable at the time.

setting: Conference room, with an office building exterior in the last panel
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains to Dilbert and a coworker how the company paid out its former CEO's huge severance package. He says the company built a giant robotic flea to drain the assets out of the company. The final panel shows the flea sucking money from an office building with its long proboscis.
punchline: The ex-CEO's severance package was so absurdly large that it amounted to a giant parasite draining the company, yet it seemed like a reasonable deal when it was agreed.
summary: A departing executive's lavish payout is depicted as a colossal mechanical parasite bleeding the firm dry, and the company admits it all made sense when it signed off.

title: Wally Dodges Work With Tech Excuses

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd love to help you, but I'm in the middle of defragging my disk drive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When that's done, my computer will be compiling code for a few hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hear bad things about it.

setting: Office cubicle area and the break room coffee station
situation: A female coworker asks Wally for help, and he refuses by claiming his computer is busy defragging its disk drive, then compiling code for hours. Later, while pouring coffee in the break room, Dilbert asks how work is going and Wally says he has only heard bad things about it, as if work were something he has no direct experience with.
punchline: Wally's technical-sounding excuses are just cover for avoiding work entirely, and he admits as much by talking about work as an unfamiliar thing he only knows by bad reputation.
summary: A lazy employee fobs off a request with computer jargon, then jokes about work as though it were a rumored place he has never visited.

title: Legal Review Circular Dependency Loop

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you approve the purchase of this software?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to run the software license past Legal first.

transcript.speaker: Legal Employee
transcript.text: You need to fill out a Legal Services Request form. I'll email it to you.

transcript.speaker: Legal Employee
transcript.text: Make sure you specify whether the software is open source or not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would I know if it meets your definition of open source?

transcript.speaker: Legal Employee
transcript.text: It depends how the license is written. You'll need to ask Legal to review it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never mind. I'll just forge your signature on the form.

transcript.speaker: Legal Employee
transcript.text: Maybe this is why I've never seen a software license.

setting: Office cubicle area and the legal department office
situation: Dilbert asks his boss to approve a software purchase and is sent to Legal. The legal employee requires a request form that asks whether the software is open source, but Dilbert can't answer that without Legal reviewing the license, which is the very thing the form is meant to start. Dilbert gives up and says he will forge the signature.
punchline: The legal department's process is a circular dependency that only works if nobody ever submits a request, which explains why the legal employee has never actually seen a software license.
summary: A simple software purchase gets stuck in a bureaucratic loop where the paperwork requires information that only the department behind the paperwork can provide.

title: Awkward Handshake With Drug Sample

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I'd like you to meet the CEO of the company that is our biggest customer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd shake but I have coffee in one hand, my random drug test sample in the other, and I don't want either one to get cold.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, I'm not the one who made this awkward.

situation: The Boss introduces Wally to the CEO of the company's biggest customer. Wally declines to shake hands because he is holding coffee in one hand and a random drug test sample in the other. The Boss, clearly uncomfortable, disclaims responsibility for the awkwardness.
punchline: Wally casually reveals he is holding a urine sample while meeting a key client, and the Boss deflects blame for the embarrassing moment.
summary: A routine executive introduction goes sideways when Wally's hands are full of a hot drink and a specimen cup.

file: 2013/2013-06-18_ignorance (knowledge)_work ethic_too many smart people_boost perfromance_strategy_not paying attention.gif
