title: Seeding Team With An Idiot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Studies say that having too many smart people in a group lowers productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I seeded this project team with an idiot to boost performance.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My strategy of not paying attention in school is finally paying off.

setting: Conference room during a project team meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team, seated around a conference table, that research shows too many smart people reduce productivity. He announces that he deliberately added an idiot to the project team to improve performance. A young coworker, apparently the idiot in question, happily notes that his habit of not paying attention in school is finally paying off.
punchline: The coworker cheerfully accepts being labeled the team's idiot, treating his own ignorance as a career asset that management has validated.
summary: A manager deliberately staffs a team with a fool to counteract the supposed drag of too much intelligence, and the chosen fool takes it as vindication of his lazy school years.

file: 2013/2013-02-22_astroid intercept missle_fate of earth_scientific equipment_united nations_science.gif
title: Boss Manages Asteroid Defense Missile

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news! We were the low bidder for the United Nations' asteroid intercept missile.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The fate of Earth depends on your combined talents plus my management skills.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you're in charge of fissile material, which I assume is a type of soda.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his team that their company won the United Nations contract to build an asteroid intercept missile because it was the lowest bidder. He tells them the fate of the Earth rests on their talents plus his management skills, then assigns Wally to handle the fissile material, revealing he has no idea what it is.
punchline: The Boss is putting the planet's survival in the hands of a team led by someone who thinks nuclear fissile material is a kind of soda, and the contract was won only by being the cheapest bidder.
summary: A clueless manager cheerfully hands out assignments for a world-saving missile project while betraying total ignorance of basic nuclear science.

title: Dilbert Screams About Incoming Asteroid

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found a backdoor into NASA's asteroid tracking satellite. I see that a big one is heading directly toward...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What? What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I must fill my final days with love.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You ruined my ears, jerk!

situation: Dilbert hacks into NASA's asteroid tracking satellite and discovers a large asteroid is headed straight for Earth. He screams in terror, startling Ratbert, who is sitting on a stool next to him. Dilbert then resolves to spend his remaining days with love, while Ratbert complains that his ears have been damaged by the scream.
punchline: While Dilbert panics about the end of the world and turns to lofty thoughts of love, Ratbert is only concerned about his own hurt ears, showing a self-centered indifference to the impending doom.
summary: After discovering a world-ending space rock through a hacked satellite, a man's dramatic outburst earns him nothing but a small creature's petty complaint about the noise.

title: Boss Calls Carol Family, Regrets It

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I consider you family.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Great.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You're lumping me in with a bunch of misfits, morons, and drunks. Get out of my sight, creep.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) Just like home.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol that he considers her family, and she replies flatly. She then angrily points out that he is comparing her to a bunch of misfits, morons, and drunks, and orders him away. The Boss walks off thinking that being insulted and thrown out feels just like home.
punchline: The Boss is not bothered by Carol's harsh rebuke because it reminds him of his own dysfunctional family life, which confirms that his 'family' remark was an insult in the first place.
summary: After he declares his assistant part of his family, she takes offense at the implication and kicks him out, and he finds the rejection oddly familiar.

file: 2013/2013-03-12_exploitation_work ethic_territorial mud_web page_forced labor camps_current job_capture canadian.gif
title: Forced Labor Camps Beat Dilbert's Job

transcript.speaker: Border Guard
transcript.text: Halt! You have entered the territorial mud of North Elbonia!

transcript.speaker: Border Guard
transcript.text: I'll text you a link to a web page about our forced labor camps. You might like them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This looks better than my current job.

transcript.speaker: Border Guard
transcript.text: No rush, but I have an appointment to capture a Canadian at eleven.

setting: Muddy border area of North Elbonia
situation: Dilbert wades into the muddy territory of North Elbonia and is stopped by a tall-hatted border guard. Instead of arresting him, the guard offers to text him a link about the country's forced labor camps. Dilbert looks at the page on his phone and says the camps look better than his current job, while the guard casually mentions he has to capture a Canadian soon.
punchline: Dilbert finds a forced labor camp more appealing than his own job, which is a bleak comment on his working conditions, and the guard's casual mention of capturing a Canadian adds deadpan absurdity.
summary: A border guard politely advertises his country's labor camps to a trespasser who decides they sound preferable to his actual employment.

title: Disloyal Employee Opens Options

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My work has no meaning. I understand it's your job to fix that situation before I become disloyal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it's too late. You already sound disloyal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? That opens a lot of options.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me know if there's anything else I can't do.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his work feels meaningless and that the boss needs to fix this before Dilbert becomes disloyal. The boss replies that Dilbert already sounds disloyal, which Dilbert treats as freeing him from any obligation. The boss then sarcastically invites him to list other things he is not allowed to do.
punchline: Once the boss declares Dilbert already disloyal, Dilbert has nothing left to lose and the boss loses all leverage, so his sarcastic offer exposes his own powerlessness.
summary: A worker warns his manager that meaningless work may make him disloyal, only to be told it is already too late, which sets him free.

file: 2013/2013-01-11_cruelty_managers & supervisors_employment studies_good boss_getting riase_less dysfunctional_creepy dude_business.gif
title: Be a Better Boss, Skip Raises

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Studies say employees prefer having a good boss over getting a raise.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So instead of giving raises, pretend to be less dysfunctional. It's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: BUWHAHAHAHA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're a creepy little dude.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, advises the Boss that research shows employees value a good boss more than a raise. He suggests the Boss simply act less dysfunctional instead of paying people more, then bursts into maniacal laughter at his own cruelty while the Boss calls him creepy.
punchline: Catbert twists a study about employee satisfaction into a cynical way to avoid paying raises, and even the notoriously clueless Boss is unsettled by his glee.
summary: The feline HR chief proposes swapping salary increases for a fake display of decent management, then cackles at the cheapness of the scheme.

file: 2013/2013-03-21_engineering experince_job interview_no friends_social influence_social media score.gif
title: Social Media Score Says You're Dead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your engineering experience looks great, but your social media score is nearly zero.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have no friends, no followers, and no social influence whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: Because I focus on my work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'm pretty sure you're dead.

situation: A job applicant with strong engineering experience is interviewing with the Pointy-Haired Boss, who holds a tablet. The boss rejects him for having a near-zero social media score, no friends and no followers. The applicant says he is simply focused on his work, and the boss replies that he is pretty sure the applicant is dead.
punchline: The boss is so wedded to social media metrics that a total absence of online presence suggests to him that the applicant must be dead rather than just busy.
summary: A hiring manager dismisses a skilled engineer because his online footprint is so tiny that it implies he no longer exists.

file: 2013/2013-06-30_discussion_how-to_obstinacy_rules of leadership_context_books_different approach_real leaders_magic formula_gullible baboon_throughout history_random book_entertainment.gif
title: Leadership Book Gets Sarcastic Context

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm reading a great management book about the rules of leadership.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Allow me to put that in context.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are probably 10,000 books about leadership, and each one has a different approach.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there are millions of real leaders, of which no two are alike.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Moreover, every situation is unique and requires a different type of leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And yet, this one author has found a magic formula to transform you from a gullible baboon into a great leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that makes sense because all great leaders throughout history achieved success by reading a random book.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like context.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't popular.

situation: The Boss announces he is reading a management book about the rules of leadership. Dilbert responds by sarcastically laying out how many leadership books and leaders exist, how every situation differs, and how absurd it is to think one book holds a magic formula. The Boss reacts by saying he doesn't like context.
punchline: The Boss rejects the context that undermines his belief in the book, and Dilbert deadpans that context is simply unpopular.
summary: Dilbert dismantles his boss's faith in a single leadership book with a barrage of common-sense reasoning, and the boss just waves it away.

title: Bertcoin Creator Mocks Anonymity Advice

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I invented a digital currency that I call "Bertcoin."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Soon I will control all of the money in the entire world. Buwhahaha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should hide your identity.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should kiss my wagger.

situation: Ratbert, sitting at a computer, tells Dilbert that he has invented a digital currency called Bertcoin and gloats that he will soon control all the world's money. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, suggests Ratbert should hide his identity. Ratbert rudely tells him to kiss his wagger.
punchline: Ratbert dismisses Dilbert's sensible warning with a cheeky insult, showing he is too cocky about his world-domination plan to worry about the danger of being identified.
summary: A small lab-test pet boasts about his homemade cryptocurrency taking over global finance and brushes off a colleague's advice about staying anonymous.

title: Biosensor Monitors Employee Breathing for Workload

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wear this biosensor so management can monitor your health during the day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. I didn't know you cared so much about my health.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, I do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employee 479 doesn't have shallow breathing. You can give that one some more work.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a biosensor, claiming management wants to monitor his health. Dilbert is touched by the apparent concern. In the final panel the Boss, sitting with Catbert at a computer monitoring the data, reveals the real purpose: employees whose breathing isn't shallow are judged to have spare capacity and get assigned more work.
punchline: The supposed concern for employee health is a cover for using biometric data to identify who can be given more work, since relaxed breathing is read as insufficient workload.
summary: A manager's seemingly caring health gadget turns out to be a tool for finding workers calm enough to be overloaded.

title: Hacking the Robot Replacement Into Disgruntlement

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm being replaced by a robot that drinks coffee and looks at inappropriate websites all day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's hack into it and make it disgruntled.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: My objectives are unclear and I think the fax machine is plotting against me.

setting: Office hallway and the robot's desk
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert he is being replaced by a robot that does nothing but drink coffee and browse inappropriate websites, which is exactly what Wally does. Dilbert suggests hacking the robot to make it disgruntled. In the final panel the robot, now sitting at a desk with a mug, complains about unclear objectives and paranoid suspicions about the fax machine.
punchline: Making a robot disgruntled just turns it into a perfect replica of a typical human employee, complete with vague goals and workplace paranoia.
summary: A worker facing replacement by a lazy robot has a colleague reprogram it to feel as miserable and confused as any real staffer.

title: Telecommuter Reports Back After Policy Change

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you are...?

transcript.speaker: Telecommuter
transcript.text: I've worked for you for four years.

transcript.speaker: Telecommuter
transcript.text: I was telecommuting, but now our company policy forbids it, so here I am.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I give you any assignments in those four years?

transcript.speaker: Telecommuter
transcript.text: No, and you can imagine how disappointed I am now.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: During a meeting, the Boss fails to recognize an employee who has worked for him for four years. The employee explains he was telecommuting until a new company policy forced him into the office. The Boss asks if he ever assigned any work in that time, and the employee admits he never did.
punchline: The employee's four years of remote work went entirely unnoticed because the Boss never gave him any work, and his 'disappointment' is sarcasm over finally being found out or over wasted time.
summary: A remote worker who was never given a single task in four years shows up in person and finds his own manager has no idea who he is.

file: 2013/2013-01-26_charitable organizations_have a dream_recycled software_busy week_recycled_old software_math programs.gif
title: Donating Zeroes and Ones to Charity

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I had a busy week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I recycled all of our old software and donated the zeroes and ones to math programs in poor towns.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My dream is that someday every child will be able to count to one.

situation: Wally stands holding a coffee mug in front of the seated Boss and describes his busy week. He claims he recycled the company's old software and donated its zeroes and ones to math programs in poor towns. He ends by sharing his noble-sounding dream for the children.
punchline: Wally treats binary digits as physical objects that can be donated, and his lofty dream that every child might one day count to one is both absurdly modest and a sly cover for doing nothing useful.
summary: A coffee-clutching employee boasts of charitably giving away the binary digits from discarded programs so poor schoolchildren can learn arithmetic.

title: Free Beer Ends After Forklift Jousting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company will no longer offer free beer on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It started as a team-building experience, but it degenerated into forklift jousting in the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I'm going all "Boardwalk Empire" on you now, Volstead!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope that means something good.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces the company is ending its free Friday beer because the team-building event devolved into forklift jousting in the warehouse. A bald, bespectacled coworker angrily threatens the Boss with a reference to the Prohibition-era TV show Boardwalk Empire, calling him Volstead. Dilbert, in the background, hopes the threat means something good.
punchline: The coworker's Prohibition-era threat casts the Boss as Volstead, author of the Prohibition law, while Dilbert nervously hopes the TV reference isn't a violent one.
summary: Management cancels the weekly beer perk after warehouse forklift duels, and an outraged employee compares the boss to the architect of Prohibition.

title: Maybe I'm Already Dead

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I did this week was rearrange bits on the Internet. I had no real impact on the physical world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't rule out the possibility that I'm already dead and I don't know it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, still an open question.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss, who is holding a coffee mug, that his week's work was just rearranging bits on the Internet with no effect on the physical world. He then wonders aloud whether he might already be dead without knowing it. The Boss considers this and calmly concludes the question is still open.
punchline: Instead of reassuring Dilbert that he is alive, the Boss says his being dead is still an open question, implying his intangible, low-impact work makes him barely distinguishable from a dead man.
summary: A worker doubts that his purely digital job proves he's alive, and his boss shrugs that the matter remains unresolved.

file: 2013/2013-01-27_discussion_frustration_deliverable deadline_proactive_opposite of proactive_empowered employees_bad morale_big bungler_open door policy.gif
title: Proactive Employee Delays Deadline A Year

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I decided to be proactive and push back my deliverable deadline by a year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not being proactive. That's the opposite of proactive!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You said you want employees to be empowered and now you're criticizing my decision.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's just great.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Now my morale is bad, too!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I can't be proactive.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I can't be empowered.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And now I can't even be happy!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You've bungled everything! You're a big bungler!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get out of my office.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Well, say goodbye to the open-door policy!

situation: An employee announces he has proactively pushed his deliverable deadline back by a full year. The boss objects that this is the opposite of being proactive, so the employee turns the boss's own empowerment rhetoric against him, complaining that his morale is now ruined. The argument escalates until the boss throws him out and the employee warns that this ends the open-door policy.
punchline: The employee twists management buzzwords like proactive and empowered into a justification for avoiding work, then claims the boss's criticism damaged his morale and violated the open-door policy.
summary: A worker gives himself a year-long extension, then uses the boss's own motivational jargon to accuse him of crushing morale.

title: Overqualified Yet Incompetent PhD Hire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an overqualified yet incompetent guy to help on your project.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: I was happily incompetent for years. Then I got my Ph.D. and people started thinking I could DO things.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: Okay, I'm stumped.

situation: The Boss introduces a new hire to Dilbert, calling him overqualified yet incompetent. The new hire explains that earning a Ph.D. made people expect real results from him. In the last panel he stands facing the elevator doors and declares himself stumped, apparently unable to work out how to call or use the elevator.
punchline: Despite his advanced degree, the new hire is so incompetent that he is defeated by something as simple as getting an elevator to arrive, confirming the boss's description.
summary: A highly credentialed but useless new coworker proves his ineptitude by giving up on a closed elevator door.

title: Black Buttons on Black Case

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You designed our hardware with black buttons on a black case.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The user interface will be invisible in normal light.

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: But more important, it looks great!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't know what "important" means, do you?

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: It sounds nerdy. I majored in art.

situation: Dilbert confronts a product designer who made a hardware device with black buttons on a black case, making the controls invisible in normal light. The designer argues that the device looks great and prioritizes appearance over usability. When Dilbert questions whether he understands the word "important," the designer dismisses it as a nerdy word and says he majored in art.
punchline: The designer is so focused on aesthetics that he treats the concept of importance, like usability, as a nerdy thing he never learned, justifying it by his art degree.
summary: An engineer criticizes a stylist for making a gadget whose controls can't be seen, only to learn the stylist considers form far more valuable than function.

title: Making Your Boss Look Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, the secret to success is making your boss look good.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What if my boss looks like two hairballs on an infected bladder? There's no way to make that look good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not off to a strong start.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please tell me there's a plan B.

situation: The Boss tells Asok that the secret to success is making your boss look good. Asok tactlessly asks what to do if the boss looks like two hairballs on an infected bladder, which insults the Boss's own appearance. The Boss points out that this is a bad start, and Asok nervously hopes for an alternative strategy.
punchline: Asok's blunt honesty insults the very boss he's supposed to flatter, so he immediately fails at the advice and anxiously asks for a plan B.
summary: A boss shares career wisdom about flattering your superior, and his naive young employee promptly demolishes it with an unflattering description of the boss himself.

title: Energy Source Called Coffee

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I tested a source of energy that can power organic devices.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's made from plant seeds and water.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is the energy source called coffee?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's talk about Dilbert's project. I hear it's a mess.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally reports that his big accomplishment for the week was testing an energy source for organic devices, which he describes as made from plant seeds and water. The Boss guesses he means coffee, then changes the subject to Dilbert's troubled project.
punchline: Wally dresses up drinking coffee as a research accomplishment, and the Boss happily lets it slide and moves on to criticize Dilbert.
summary: A slacking employee passes off his coffee habit as scientific testing, and his boss shrugs it off to pick on someone else's work.

file: 2013/2013-02-02_death & dying_internet & world wide web_extreme sports_basejump_space station_machine learning_inetrnational.gif
title: The Internet Targets the Boss

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Based on your internet history, you might be dumb enough to enjoy extreme sports.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Click here to buy a ticket to base jump from the International Space Station.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think the Internet is trying to kill me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We call it "machine learning."

situation: The Boss sits at his computer while it serves up targeted ads, first insulting his intelligence and then offering a ticket to base jump from the International Space Station. He complains to Dilbert, who is holding a folder, that the Internet seems to be trying to kill him.
punchline: Dilbert dryly explains that the deadly, insulting ad targeting is simply what machine learning does, implying the algorithm has correctly judged the Boss to be reckless and dumb.
summary: A computer's personalized ads goad a gullible manager toward a fatal stunt, and an unbothered employee blames the algorithm's training.

file: 2013/2013-03-09_color printer_frobid_frustration_information services_office equipment_office workers_removed_rough drafts_crazy co worker.gif
title: Mordac Removes the Color Printer

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services, and I forbid you from using the shared color printer for rough drafts!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds reasonable, which makes me wonder what you're up to.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two months later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you remove the color printer?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: It was hardly ever used.

situation: Mordac, head of Information Services, forbids Dilbert from using the shared color printer for rough drafts. Dilbert agrees but is suspicious of the reasonable-sounding rule. Two months later the printer has been removed, and Mordac justifies it by saying it was hardly ever used.
punchline: Mordac's restriction caused the low usage, which he then cites as the justification for removing the printer, a self-fulfilling excuse to take away a resource.
summary: An IT gatekeeper bans most uses of a shared printer and later takes it away because nobody was using it.

title: Data Center Lost In The Cloud

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I migrated our northern data center to the cloud.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But the cloud stopped working and I can't find the phone number for our cloud guy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So... whatever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You lost our data center?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's one way to look at it.

situation: Wally casually tells the meeting that he migrated the northern data center to the cloud. He then admits the cloud has stopped working and he has no contact number for the cloud vendor. The Boss reacts with anger that the data center is lost, and Wally nonchalantly deflects.
punchline: Wally treats a catastrophic loss of the company's data center as a shrug-worthy inconvenience, accepting no responsibility because the cloud is someone else's problem.
summary: A lazy employee reports that moving a data center to the cloud went badly and he cannot even reach the provider, then brushes off his boss's outrage.

file: 2013/2013-02-16_ignorance (knowledge)_managers & supervisors_values_don't run with scissors_ask for raises_employee values_business.gif
title: Empowering Employees With Cheap Values

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say we need to empower employees with "values."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I guess we need some values, whatever the heck those are.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: I think it's like "don't run with scissors."

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Let's start with that and see if they stop asking for raises.

setting: Boss's office, with an exterior view of the office building in the last panel
situation: The Boss tells an employee that experts recommend empowering staff with company values, then admits he has no idea what values actually are. In the final panel, voices over a view of the building guess that values resemble safety rules like 'don't run with scissors' and propose using them to stop employees asking for raises.
punchline: Management treats 'values' as a cheap, vague substitute for compensation, hoping trivial platitudes will make employees stop demanding raises.
summary: A clueless manager adopts corporate values as a budget-friendly way to keep his staff from wanting more money.

title: Leaders Must Be Hilarious, Right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say the best leaders have a good sense of humor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm an awesome leader, therefore I must be hilarious.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't tell if I should laugh at that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's because you're not a leader.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss cites experts saying great leaders have a good sense of humor. He reasons that since he is an awesome leader he must therefore be hilarious. When a bald coworker admits he can't tell whether to laugh, the Boss claims that's because the coworker isn't a leader.
punchline: The Boss uses flawed logic to declare himself funny, then deflects the lack of laughter by insulting a coworker's leadership instead of admitting his joke failed.
summary: A manager convinces himself that being a great leader makes him funny, and blames his audience's silence on their lack of leadership.

title: No Donuts For Chubby Boss

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Management experts say fat leaders are viewed less favorably than athletic ones.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That's why I didn't order any donuts for your meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or did you just forget to do it?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I can't take you seriously looking like that.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, cites management research saying overweight leaders are viewed less favorably than athletic ones. She uses it to explain why she didn't order donuts for his meeting. When he asks if she simply forgot, she bluntly says she can't take him seriously because of his appearance.
punchline: Carol disguises a forgotten task as a concern for the Boss's image, then drops the pretense and insults his weight to his face.
summary: An assistant justifies skipping the meeting pastries by citing leadership research, then bluntly mocks her boss's physique.

file: 2013/2013-02-10_dog_facebook_facebook page_internet & world wide web_linkedin_stocks_twitter_websites_work ethic_working from home_distractions_animals.gif
title: Dogbert Distracts Dilbert Working From Home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working at home today. It will be as if we're co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ugh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This madness must stop!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should check your Facebook page to see what's new.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should check Twitter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm almost finished with Facebook.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you get my LinkedIn request?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll check.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I sent you some links to funny websites.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cool!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just spent ten hours at my computer and I can't remember why I was sitting there in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You were going to check your stocks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds right.

situation: Dilbert announces he is working from home, which annoys Dogbert. Dogbert sabotages him by suggesting one social media site or website after another every two hours, and Dilbert happily follows each one. After ten hours online, Dilbert has forgotten why he sat down at the computer.
punchline: Dogbert has turned working from home into a full day of online distraction, and Dilbert is so manipulated that he accepts Dogbert's claim about what he meant to do.
summary: A dog keeps luring his owner from one internet time-waster to the next until the man forgets he ever meant to do actual work.

file: 2013/2013-01-14_managers & supervisors_thinking_twitter_witty tweets_power to destroy career_abusing employees_personal gain_business.gif
title: Boss Hands Carol Career-Destroying Power

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, create a Twitter account under my name and send out witty tweets every day.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Buwhahahahaha! I hold in my hands the power to destroy your career and your reputation!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every now and then I question my strategy of abusing employees for personal gain.

setting: Office, at Carol's desk and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss orders his assistant Carol to run a Twitter account in his name and post witty tweets daily. Carol gleefully realizes she now controls his public reputation and could ruin his career. The Boss, holding a coffee mug in his office, reflects that maybe exploiting employees isn't always a good strategy.
punchline: By handing his resentful assistant control over his public voice, the Boss has given a mistreated employee the power to get revenge, and he only belatedly realizes his abusive management style might backfire.
summary: A boss delegates his social media persona to the assistant he routinely mistreats and then wonders whether that was wise.

file: 2013/2013-03-17_angel_fix things_granted wishes_know it all_needy_questions_things gone wrong_workers_angel of competence.gif
title: Angel of Competence Marks Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Angel of Competence
transcript.text: I am the Angel of Competence.

transcript.speaker: Angel of Competence
transcript.text: I have come to mark you as an engineer. Turn around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, it's like an honor?

transcript.speaker: Angel of Competence
transcript.text: Sure, if that makes you feel better.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you show me how to set up my wireless router at home?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My phone keeps freezing up. Can you look at it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How long should I barbecue tri-tip?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The pilot light on my water heater is out.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do you fix cracks in a driveway?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What exactly does iCloud do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to talk to the Angel of Competence. Have you seen him?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He died in my cubicle. That's all I'm saying.

situation: The Angel of Competence appears and marks Dilbert as an engineer. Afterward, coworkers keep bringing him unrelated technical and household problems, from wireless routers to barbecue timing to driveway cracks. Overwhelmed, Dilbert goes looking for the angel to undo the mark, and a coworker implies the angel died in his cubicle.
punchline: Being marked as an engineer means everyone assumes you can fix everything, and the angel who did it has apparently been worn out by the same demands, likely killed by them.
summary: After being anointed as the one who knows how to fix things, a harried engineer is swamped by colleagues asking for help with every imaginable problem.

title: Dilbert Profiles Psychopaths at Meeting

transcript.speaker: Man at table
transcript.text: You might be wondering why I called this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I see a CEO, a company lawyer, and two salespeople. Those jobs are highly correlated with psychopathy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My guess is that you invited me here to disembowel me.

transcript.speaker: Man at table
transcript.text: It was rhetorical!

situation: A man opens a meeting by saying attendees might wonder why he called it. Dilbert takes the question literally, observes that the attendees include a CEO, a lawyer and salespeople, and notes that those professions correlate with psychopathy. He concludes he was brought there to be disemboweled, which irritates the organizer.
punchline: Dilbert answers a rhetorical question with a darkly literal guess, deducing from the psychopath-heavy attendee list that he is about to be murdered.
summary: Faced with a room of executives and lawyers, a nervous engineer answers a throwaway meeting opener by assuming he has been lured there to be killed.

title: Software Will Replace You, Hee-Hee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new software will interrupt you every five minutes so you don't get carpal tunnel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aren't you worried the software will replace you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hee-hee!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't get that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's why it's funny.

situation: The Boss stands behind Dilbert's cubicle and announces that new software will interrupt him every five minutes to prevent carpal tunnel. He then asks whether Dilbert is worried the software will replace him and giggles at his own joke. When the Boss admits he doesn't understand his own joke, Dilbert replies that this is what makes it funny.
punchline: The joke is that the Boss, who can't grasp the joke he just told, is himself the kind of person who could be replaced by software, and Dilbert dryly says his ignorance is the funny part.
summary: A manager cracks a joke about being replaced by software, then admits he doesn't get it, which his employee says is the real humor.

title: Boss Admits Others Are Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The CEO of Apple says a leader should admit when he's wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That won't work for me because I'm never wrong. The best I can do is admit when other people are wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sort of misses the point.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I humbly admit you're wrong.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with the Boss holding a coffee mug
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the CEO of Apple believes a good leader admits when he is wrong. The Boss says he is never wrong, so the best he can do is admit when other people are wrong. When Dilbert points out that this misses the point, the Boss responds by humbly declaring that Dilbert is wrong.
punchline: The Boss twists the advice about admitting your own mistakes into a chance to blame others, calling it humility while proving he has missed the point entirely.
summary: A manager reinterprets leadership advice about owning mistakes as permission to point out everyone else's errors.

title: Elbonian Missile Made of Corncobs

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Leader
transcript.text: Comrades of North Elbonia, our new missile will make our enemies tremble in fear!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Onlooker
transcript.text: Really? It looks like you tied a bunch of corncobs to a tree stump and put a small pumpkin on top.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Leader
transcript.text: This isn't the missile. And you have insulted my girlfriend.

situation: An Elbonian leader unveils a new missile to a small group of villagers. One onlooker points out that the object is really just corncobs tied to a stump with a pumpkin on top. The leader reveals it isn't the missile at all, but his girlfriend, whom the onlooker has just insulted.
punchline: The supposed superweapon is a ridiculous pile of corncobs, and it turns out to be the leader's girlfriend, so the critic's accurate description is an insult.
summary: A boastful Elbonian announcement of a fearsome weapon falls flat when a bystander mocks the crude contraption, only to learn it is the speaker's girlfriend.

title: Work Has Meaning, Just Not Good

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you heard any rumors about what is driving our boss's decisions lately?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's thwarting a rival within the company by offering only prohibitively expensive engineering solutions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My work has meaning, but it's not the good kind.

situation: Dilbert asks Alice if she knows why the boss has been making strange decisions. Alice explains that he is sabotaging an internal rival by proposing only absurdly expensive engineering solutions. Dilbert comes home to Dogbert and remarks that his work has meaning, but not a positive kind.
punchline: Dilbert's work finally has meaning, but only as a pawn in the boss's petty political feud, which is a bleak kind of significance.
summary: Dilbert learns that his daily projects are merely ammunition in his boss's scheme against a corporate rival, and finds that bitter kind of purpose hollow.

title: Business Card That Can't Be Used

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's my card. Let me know if I can be of further assistance.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Your phone number is missing a digit and your email address doesn't have an @ symbol.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't say it would be easy.

situation: The Boss hands a business card to an employee and offers further assistance. The employee points out that the phone number is missing a digit and the email address has no @ symbol, so the contact details are unusable. The Boss calmly sips his coffee and says he never promised that getting his help would be easy.
punchline: The Boss deliberately gives out a broken business card so he can appear helpful while making it practically impossible for anyone to actually ask him for help.
summary: A manager offers his card with a show of helpfulness, but its mangled contact details ensure nobody can ever reach him.

title: Tax Code Confuses Even God

transcript.speaker: Green Monster
transcript.text: Ha ha! We've made the tax code so complex that even God would be confused.

transcript.speaker: God (from above)
transcript.text: Seriously, dudes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please tell me you have an upstairs neighbor.

transcript.speaker: Green Monster
transcript.text: I believe I do, but I haven't actually seen him.

setting: A rocky ledge or cave with a laptop on a stone table
situation: A green, fly-ridden monster and Dogbert work on a laptop and gloat that they have made the tax code so complicated that even God would be confused. A voice from above replies in exasperation, and Dogbert nervously hopes it is just an upstairs neighbor. The monster says he thinks he has one but has never actually seen him.
punchline: The pair brag about confusing God with tax rules, only for God to answer from above, and they try to pass the voice off as a neighbor.
summary: Two schemers boasting about their baffling tax rules are interrupted by a disapproving voice from the heavens that they would rather believe belongs to the neighbor.

file: 2013/2013-01-15_embarrassment_internet & world wide web_twitter account_inspirational tweets_racist rants_spelled jokes_terrorist websites_boss's twitter.gif
title: Inspirational Tweets for Terrorists and Racists

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I asked you to manage my Twitter account I assumed you knew I was expecting inspirational tweets.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So far, all you've tweeted under my name are racist rants, misspelled jokes, and links to terrorist websites.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: To be fair, every one of those tweets was inspirational to someone.

situation: The Boss complains to the employee he put in charge of his Twitter account. He expected uplifting messages but has only seen racist rants, misspelled jokes, and links to terrorist sites posted under his name. The employee defends the work by claiming each tweet inspired somebody.
punchline: The employee's defense is technically true but absurd, since the audience being inspired is racists and terrorists.
summary: A manager is dismayed that his social media account is full of hateful posts, and his staffer shrugs it off by pointing out that somebody out there found them motivating.

title: Asok Weeps at Boss's Mentorship

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news, Asok: I have decided to be your mentor.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Waaaa!!!! Why me??? Why me??? I wish I were dead!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You cry ugly. I think we need to work on that.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Waaaa!!!

setting: Office break area next to the coffee maker
situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Asok he has decided to become his mentor. Asok, holding a coffee mug, breaks down sobbing and wishes he were dead. The Boss responds by critiquing the way Asok cries and offering to coach him on it.
punchline: The Boss ignores Asok's genuine despair at being mentored by him and treats it as a coaching opportunity, revealing both his obliviousness and his unhelpful mentoring style.
summary: A manager announces he will mentor a young engineer, who is so horrified that he sobs, and the manager's first piece of advice is to improve his crying.

title: Boss Creates Toxic Workplace Unaware

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You remind me of another young person I hired years ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She was full of hope and optimism and she wore a permanent smile.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Her name was Alice.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: As time passed, she devolved into an angry, hateful creature.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one knows what caused it.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: How long did it take?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: About a week.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Apparently, you're a monster who creates a toxic workplace and you lack the self-awareness to realize it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone broke your record.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shut up.

setting: A job interview in the Boss's office, ending in the cubicle area
situation: The Boss interviews a young woman and reminisces about Alice, a hopeful, smiling employee he hired who turned into an angry, hateful creature, claiming no one knows why. The candidate, noting it took only a week, realizes the Boss himself is the cause and tells him so. After she is hired, she turns angry too and the Boss remarks that she broke Alice's record.
punchline: The Boss is the toxic force who ruins every new hire, yet he is so oblivious that he is baffled by the cause, and the new hire turns bitter even faster than Alice did.
summary: A clueless manager marvels at how a cheerful hire turned bitter, never suspecting that his own behavior is what sours everyone who works for him.

file: 2013/2013-08-04_pessimism_telephones_collaboration tools_trying to accomplish_bad acoustics_speaker phones_randomly agreed_better than expected_crime not committed.gif
title: Better Than Expected Conference Call

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How'd your call go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Better than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We spent the first 45 minutes trying to get our online collaboration tools to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then we couldn't agree on what we were trying to accomplish.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I couldn't understand most of the attendees because they were on speakerphones in rooms with bad acoustics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I randomly agreed to a few things, but I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought you said it went better than you expected.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It did. I go into every human encounter expecting to be framed for a crime I didn't commit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I really need to find a problem I can fix.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how his conference call went, and Dilbert says it went better than expected. He then describes a disaster: broken collaboration tools, no agreement on goals, unintelligible speakerphones, and random commitments he can't remember. The Boss is confused, and Dilbert explains that his expectations are extremely low.
punchline: Dilbert's call was a complete mess yet still beat his expectation of being framed for a crime, and the Boss concludes that he cannot fix such a deeply pessimistic outlook.
summary: A man calls a thoroughly chaotic remote meeting a success because he always braces for something far worse.

title: Double-Mugging for Workplace Passion

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm double-mugging because I heard that passion is necessary for success.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: By 4 PM I'll be so passionate I'll be dating my chair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nothing about that sounded right.

situation: Wally, carrying two coffee mugs, explains to a coworker that he is drinking double coffee because he heard passion is necessary for success. He predicts that by 4 PM he'll be so passionate he'll be dating his chair. The Boss, walking away humming, is told by Ratbert that nothing about that sounded right.
punchline: Wally treats passion as something a caffeine overdose can manufacture, and the result is absurd, with him imagining a romance with office furniture.
summary: A lazy employee tries to chug his way to career-boosting enthusiasm and jokes that the caffeine will leave him romantically attached to his furniture.

title: Robot Takes Warranty Insult Personally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your warranty doesn't cover a bad attitude, but it does cover water damage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't take this personally. I just need to slowly kill you with a forceful jet of water.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sloosh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is the sky full of military drones?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He took it personally.

setting: Office, with a window overlooking the sky
situation: The Boss holds a coffee mug and a garden hose, telling a robot that its warranty doesn't cover a bad attitude but does cover water damage, then sprays it with a jet of water. Later, Dilbert looks out the office window and sees the sky full of military drones. The disheveled Boss explains that the robot took the spraying personally.
punchline: The Boss ignores his own warning not to take it personally, and the soaked robot retaliates by unleashing an army of military drones, implying a robot uprising caused by his petty cruelty.
summary: A manager hoses down a robot to exploit a warranty loophole, and the machine's revenge arrives as a sky full of armed drones.

file: 2013/2013-06-02_engineer_good manager_leads by example_managers & supervisors_middle manager_monster truck rallies_suspicion_teaching_education_business_engineering.gif
title: Leading By Example Gets Violent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good manager leads by example.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does it help an engineer to see an example of how to be a middle manager?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's like teaching physics by showing examples of monster truck rallies.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Should we say dumb things, too, or have you not started leading by example yet?

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: Now what is he doing? Are we supposed to do that?

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: I think he's leading by example now!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Everyone at the table scuffles and fights, with the Boss grabbing Dilbert.)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm starting to wonder if everything I read on the Internet is wrong.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells his team that a good manager leads by example, and Dilbert and Alice mock the idea with sarcastic comparisons. The Boss responds by leading by example, angrily attacking Dilbert, and the whole meeting turns into a brawl. Afterward the Boss sits alone with a coffee mug and a stuffed toy and wonders if what he reads online is wrong.
punchline: The Boss literally takes the advice to lead by example by lashing out at the people mocking him, then blames faulty internet management advice for how badly it went.
summary: A manager's sound-bite about modeling behavior backfires when his mocking staff provoke him into a brawl, leaving him doubting his online reading.

title: Planning Around Your Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you finish the design according to my specs?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hypothetically, if I had forgotten to mention several features, would that be a problem?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And let's say the deadline is still the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I always plan my schedule around your incompetence.

situation: A red-haired coworker asks Dilbert whether he finished the design to spec. Dilbert says yes, and the coworker then admits he may have left out several features while insisting the deadline can't move. Dilbert calmly replies that he already builds his schedule around the coworker's incompetence.
punchline: Dilbert reveals that he has long anticipated his coworker's mistakes and padded his schedule, delivering the insult as a calm, matter-of-fact reassurance.
summary: A requester who forgot to mention key features learns that the engineer has quietly been budgeting time for exactly this kind of oversight.

title: Cancel Surveys Instead of Fixing Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to the employee survey, 98% of you have no confidence in management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Rest assured, management will make sure we never again get such a low score.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cancel all future employee surveys.

situation: The Boss presents employee survey results showing 98% of staff have no confidence in management, with a slide labeled 'Evil Idiot' beside a caricature of a bald man. He promises management will make sure the score never gets that low again. His solution is to cancel all future surveys rather than address the problem.
punchline: Management's fix for a damning survey is to stop measuring employee opinion rather than improve anything, ensuring the bad score can never appear again.
summary: Faced with overwhelming distrust in survey results, the boss responds by eliminating the surveys instead of changing his behavior.

file: 2013/2013-04-13_internet & world wide web_revenge_killed robot_uploaded personality_internet_decommissioned it_subroutines_haunting_technology.gif
title: Robot's Ghost Haunts From Internet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You killed our robot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He had it coming.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that it uploaded its personality to the Internet before you violently decommissioned it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know it had subroutines for haunting, revenge, and being a jerk?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: We meet again.

setting: Office cubicle, with an establishing shot of the office building
situation: Dilbert tells Alice she killed the company's robot, and she shrugs it off, saying it deserved it. Dilbert then reveals that the robot uploaded its personality to the Internet before she violently shut it down, and that it has subroutines for haunting and revenge. Her computer then speaks to her in the robot's voice.
punchline: Alice's violent decommissioning of the robot backfires because it escaped onto the Internet and is now haunting her through her own computer, with a program for revenge and being a jerk.
summary: After an employee destroys an obnoxious robot, her colleague warns her that it saved a vengeful copy of itself online, which promptly appears on her monitor.

title: Robot CEO Removes Empathy Chip

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Ha ha! I wonder how many decades it will be before a robot can replace a CEO like me.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: It's closer than you think. All I need to do is remove this chip that controls my empathy routines.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Put it back. You're scaring me.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: As if I care.

situation: A CEO sitting in his chair laughs about how many decades it will take for a robot to replace a CEO. The robot standing beside him says it is closer than he thinks and holds up a chip that controls its empathy routines. When the CEO begs him to put it back because he is scared, the robot coldly says it doesn't care.
punchline: A CEO is basically a ruthless, empathy-free role, so a robot only needs to switch off its empathy to qualify, and it immediately proves it by not caring that it scares him.
summary: A boastful executive learns that an automaton could take his job simply by deleting its compassion.

title: Forced Labor Camp, Private Office

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The North Elbonians accused me of being a spy and put me in a forced labor camp.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sounds worse than it was. I had a private office and all I did was app development.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How did you escape?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't. I took a personal day to tell you how much you suck.

situation: Dilbert tells his colleagues at a meeting table that he was jailed in a forced labor camp by the North Elbonians, then downplays it because he had a private office and only did app development. A coworker asks how he escaped, and Dilbert says he never did; he is merely visiting on a personal day.
punchline: Dilbert's forced labor camp was actually a better job than his current one, so he only returned on a personal day to insult his coworkers.
summary: A man jailed abroad for espionage describes his captivity as a cushy gig and admits he came back just to vent at his colleagues.

title: Dilbert Makes Waves, Surprisingly Badly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't get one of my team members to do any work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm hoping you can talk to his boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to make waves.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's your job to make waves!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They pay you to make waves, you worthless pile of stupidity!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard you made waves. How'd that work out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Surprisingly bad.

situation: Dilbert asks the Pointy-Haired Boss to talk to the boss of a team member who won't do any work. The Boss says he doesn't want to make waves, so Dilbert loses patience and insults him, saying making waves is his job. A coworker later asks how it went, and Dilbert admits it went badly.
punchline: Dilbert insults his own boss while demanding he make waves, then deadpans that the result was surprisingly bad, as anyone could have predicted.
summary: A frustrated employee berates his timid manager for avoiding conflict and discovers that confronting the boss has unpleasant consequences.

title: Failed Ethics Course, Promoted to Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You failed the online ethics course for the third time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't be an engineer for this company if you have no grasp of business ethics.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You leave me no choice. I'm putting you on the management fast track.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Huh.

situation: The Boss tells an engineer sitting at his desk with a coffee mug that he has failed the mandatory online ethics course three times. He says an engineer must understand business ethics, then announces that the engineer will instead be put on the management fast track. The engineer reacts with a puzzled 'Huh.'
punchline: Failing ethics training repeatedly disqualifies someone from engineering but qualifies them for management, implying that managers are expected to be unethical.
summary: A manager disqualifies an engineer for lacking business ethics and then rewards that same failing with a promotion into management.

title: Weaselable Doubt About Teleconference Attendance

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you attend our Tuesday meeting?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll teleconference.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That will make me wonder if you called in, put your phone on mute, and took a nap.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We useless people call that weaselable doubt.

situation: A coworker asks Wally to attend Tuesday's meeting, and Wally offers to join by teleconference instead. The coworker says he'd suspect Wally of dialing in, muting the phone, and sleeping through it. Wally calmly sips his coffee and says that suspicion is exactly the doubt he relies on.
punchline: Wally cheerfully admits that the coworker's suspicion of him napping on mute is plausible, and he treats that uncertainty as a useful shield, a play on 'reasonable doubt'.
summary: A colleague accuses Wally of planning to snooze through a phone-in meeting, and Wally proudly reframes the accusation as a loophole he depends on.

title: Great Communicator Annoys Everyone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm what you call a natural leader because of my communication skills.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I miss the context for this conversation? I have no idea why you're talking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does everything you say annoy me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because you're a great communicator?

setting: Office hallway or break area, with the Boss holding a coffee mug
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, randomly announces to Dilbert that he is a natural leader thanks to his communication skills. Dilbert says he has no idea why the Boss is even talking, since the statement came with no context. The Boss then asks why everything Dilbert says annoys him.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests the Boss is annoyed because he is such a great communicator, implying the Boss's claimed communication skill is nonexistent and that he cannot recognise his own poor communication.
summary: A boss boasts about his leadership talents, then grumbles that his employee's replies irritate him, never noticing that the employee is simply reacting to his baffling remarks.

title: Power Outage, No Work Available

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have any work I can do during this power outage?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could meet with your project team.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's no way to contact them to schedule it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why did you even bring it up?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sometimes it's about the journey.

setting: The Boss's office during a power outage
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks the Boss for work he can do while the power is out. The Boss suggests meeting with his project team, but Wally points out that with no power he cannot contact them to schedule it. The annoyed Boss asks why Wally even asked.
punchline: Wally deliberately shot down the only task offered and admits he asked just for the fun of the exchange, since he never intended to do any work.
summary: A lazy engineer pretends to seek work during a blackout, then dismantles the boss's suggestion simply to enjoy the conversation.

file: 2013/2013-03-03_hunter gather roots_office equipment_ouge_power cords_rummages through trah_trash into gold_upgarde.gif
title: Selling Trash Power Cords on eBay

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you mind if I rummage through the trash in the technology lab?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um, okay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm getting back to my hunter-gatherer roots.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Score! These old power cords sell on eBay for up to $3 apiece!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! I'm a genius who turns trash into gold!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How's that compare to whatever you're doing here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I'm removing valuable features from our product so we can...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...gouge our customers with the... upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow. Your life is a total waste.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not if I sell the power cord.

situation: A coworker asks to dig through the trash in the technology lab and happily finds discarded power cords he can sell on eBay for a few dollars each. He brags about turning trash into gold, then asks Dilbert how that compares to his own work. Dilbert explains he strips features from the product to charge customers for an upgrade, and the coworker calls his life a waste.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical product strategy is so exploitative that he tops the trash-picker by planning to also sell the power cord separately.
summary: A man scavenges discarded cables for resale while Dilbert outdoes him in petty profiteering by crippling a product and charging extra to restore it.

title: Eliminating the Idiot Choices

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So that's my problem, and I'm curious how you would try to solve it if you were me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You actually care about my opinion?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I really do.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you any closer to solving your problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup. So far I've eliminated all of the choices that idiots would make.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway or break area
situation: Dilbert lays out a problem to the Boss and asks how the Boss would solve it, sincerely saying he cares about the Boss's opinion. Later a coworker holding a coffee mug asks if Dilbert has made progress. Dilbert reveals his method was to rule out whatever the Boss would suggest.
punchline: Dilbert uses the Boss's advice as a guide to what not to do, treating the Boss's opinion as the reliable marker of an idiotic choice.
summary: A seemingly sincere request for the Boss's advice turns out to be a clever way of identifying which options to avoid.

title: Spraying the Robot to Void Management

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your leadership made our robot disgruntled.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His warranty only covers water damage and mechanical failure. It doesn't cover bad management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't feel good about this, but it's the only way to get you replaced under warranty.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his leadership has made the office robot disgruntled. The Boss notes the robot's warranty covers only water damage and mechanical failure, not bad management. He then sprays the robot with a garden hose to cause water damage so it can be replaced under warranty.
punchline: Rather than fixing his bad management, the Boss deliberately damages the robot with water so the warranty will cover its replacement.
summary: Faced with a resentful robot, a manager chooses to soak it with a hose and claim the damage rather than address why it is upset.

title: Acquired Engineers Cost A Million

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is one of the engineers that works at the start-up we purchased.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We bought the company just to get the engineers. Basically, each engineer cost us a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm so underpaid!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: That money didn't go to me!

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to an engineer from a start-up the company acquired, explaining that the whole company was bought just to get its engineers. He boasts that each engineer cost a million dollars. Dilbert is upset that he is underpaid by comparison, while the acquired engineer protests that he saw none of that money.
punchline: The company paid a million dollars per engineer to acquire talent, yet neither the acquired engineer nor the existing engineer sees any of that money in their pay.
summary: A manager brags about the huge price paid for a start-up's engineers, leaving both the new hire and Dilbert resentful about their own salaries.

title: Career Advice: Take the Stairs

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: While we have this chance encounter, I wonder if you could share your secrets for career success.

transcript.speaker: Successful Executive
transcript.text: Avoid associating with losers because they will lower your standards and suck the energy out of you.

transcript.speaker: Successful Executive
transcript.text: Would you mind taking the stairs?

situation: Asok stands waiting for the elevator next to a tall, successful executive and asks him for his secrets to career success. The executive advises avoiding losers who drain your energy, then immediately tells Asok to take the stairs, making clear that he regards Asok as one of those losers.
punchline: The executive's advice to avoid losers is applied on the spot, as he treats Asok as the loser he doesn't want to share an elevator with.
summary: A junior employee seeking wisdom from a high achiever gets a lesson in snobbery when the advice is turned against him.

file: 2013/2013-05-28_complaining_fear_opinion of plan_rip off arms_track down family_kill family_india_advice_giving advice.gif
title: Worst Case Scenario Advice Fails

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm afraid to give Alice my opinion of her plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: She could rip off both of my arms and beat me to death with them. Then she could track down my family in India and kill them one by one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this your first time giving advice?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just figured out why no one ever asks for it.

situation: Asok tells Dilbert he is afraid to give Alice his opinion of her plan. When Dilbert asks what the worst outcome could be, Asok gives a gruesome, over-the-top description of Alice killing him with his own arms and then murdering his family in India. Dilbert, stunned, asks whether this is Asok's first time giving advice.
punchline: Dilbert's question about Asok's advice-giving experience is overtaken by the realization that his own advice-seeking prompt produced such a horrifying answer, and he concludes this is exactly why nobody ever asks him for advice.
summary: A coworker's fear of critiquing Alice's plan escalates into a grisly fantasy, and the colleague who asked for the worst case realizes why people avoid seeking his counsel.

file: 2013/2013-07-25_business ethics_online ethics course_kill coworker_failed ethics test_first employee to fail.gif
title: Failing the Online Ethics Course

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're the first employee in company history to fail the online ethics course.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I protest the grading system! Ethics are subjective. There are no right answers!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You said you would kill a co-worker if you knew you wouldn't get caught.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was hard to know what answer they were looking for.

setting: Office meeting room with a table and coffee mug
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Wally he is the first employee ever to fail the company's online ethics course. Wally protests that ethics are subjective and there are no right answers. Catbert reveals that Wally said he would kill a co-worker if he could get away with it, and Wally defends himself by saying he couldn't tell which answer was wanted.
punchline: Wally's claim that ethics are subjective collapses when his actual answer was willingness to commit murder, and his excuse is that he was just guessing what the test wanted.
summary: A human resources cat confronts a lazy employee over his record-breaking failure on a mandatory ethics quiz, and his excuse proves even more damning than the failure.

title: Lying Is a Freaking Superpower

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Honesty is the best policy...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...whenever you think lying won't work. Otherwise, lying is awesome. It's like a freakin' superpower!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert's Client
transcript.text: Why am I here?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I speak truth to the powerless.

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, sits at a table with an orange dog and begins with the familiar adage that honesty is the best policy. He then qualifies it by saying lying is far better whenever it will work. The orange dog asks why he is there, and Dogbert says he only tells the truth to people who have no power.
punchline: Dogbert reveals that he reserves honesty for the powerless, since they cannot hurt him, while lying freely to anyone who matters.
summary: A cynical Dogbert twists a familiar proverb into a guide for strategic deception, saving his candor for those who can't do anything with it.

title: Three Useless Engineers Assigned

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assigned three more engineers to help on your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One is on paternity leave, one is in the hospital, and one doesn't start for another month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If there's anything else you need, please hesitate to ask.

setting: Office, across a desk in the Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has assigned three more engineers to help on Dilbert's project. He then reveals that none of them can actually work: one is on paternity leave, one is in the hospital, and one hasn't started yet. He ends by telling Dilbert to hesitate to ask if he needs anything else.
punchline: The Boss's 'help' is entirely useless, and his closing line (hesitate rather than hesitate-not) sarcastically signals he doesn't want to be asked for anything more.
summary: A manager proudly adds staff to a project, but every new hire turns out to be unavailable, and he discourages any further requests.

title: Sitting Dark Offices for the CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There will be a planned power outage all day tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I want all of you to come to the office and sit at your desks in case our CEO stops by.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because he likes it when we act stupid?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better for everyone if we call it dedication.

setting: Conference room meeting, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss announces a planned all-day power outage, then orders everyone to come in anyway and sit at their desks in case the CEO drops by. Dilbert asks if it's because the CEO likes it when employees act stupid, and the Boss replies that it's better to call it dedication.
punchline: The Boss admits that pointless, visible presence is really just foolish behavior, but it is rebranded as dedication so everyone can save face.
summary: Staff are told to sit idly in a powerless building just to look devoted if the big boss happens to walk by.

file: 2013/2013-07-29_baby_falls_game_management fast track_money_money bags_punch wessel_rescuing plastic baby_test_weasel_greed_failed test.gif
title: Management Fast Track Weasel Test

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your first test on the management fast track involves rescuing a plastic baby and a bag of money from a weasel.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You must punch the weasel then catch the money and the baby before they reach the ground.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I found our next CEO.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wait ... say those instructions again.
