setting: Office, on a desk and in front of a mounted weasel contraption
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains a management fast track test to The Boss: punch a weasel, then catch a plastic baby and a bag of money before they hit the ground. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, grabs the money bag and lets the baby drop, apparently having heard only the part about the money.
punchline: The Boss catches only the bag of money and ignores the baby, showing exactly the greedy, heartless priorities that make him ideal CEO material.

title: Dogbert Trashes Dilbert's Startup Idea

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's my idea for a start-up. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm not a big fan of other people being successful, so I'll say the idea is terrible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me why I talk to you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're a serial entrepre-nidiot.

situation: Dilbert sits on the floor with a remote in hand and pitches his idea for a start-up to Dogbert, who is lounging in a green armchair. Dogbert bluntly calls the idea terrible, admitting he dislikes seeing others succeed. When Dilbert asks why he bothers talking to him, Dogbert replies that Dilbert is a serial entrepreneur who is really an idiot.
punchline: Dogbert insults Dilbert with the pun 'entrepre-nidiot' (entrepreneur + idiot), implying Dilbert keeps coming back with bad business ideas and that Dogbert is a useful source of brutal, self-serving honesty.
summary: A man hoping for encouragement about his business scheme gets a harsh verdict from his dog, who then coins a cutting new word for him.

file: 2013/2013-02-14_depression (mental state)_work ethic_underling_long hours_insane workload_fatigue_depression_organ failure_greetings_how are you_psychology.gif
title: Boss Asks, Dilbert Answers Honestly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's it going, underling?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My long hours and insane workload are causing fatigue, depression, and organ failure. I'll probably be dead in a month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When did people stop saying, "Fine"?

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and casually asks how things are going. Dilbert answers with a blunt, detailed account of how his overwork is destroying his health and will kill him within a month. The Boss walks away, thinking only about how people no longer give the polite answer "fine".
punchline: The Boss is completely indifferent to the fact that his employee is being worked to death and is only irritated that Dilbert broke the social convention of saying "fine".
summary: A manager's routine greeting gets a grimly honest reply about burnout, and he reacts by complaining about lost small-talk etiquette instead of the warning.

title: Productivity Plunges With Boss's Jargon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do we have any actionable analytics from our big data in the cloud?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, the data shows that my productivity plunges whenever you learn new jargon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe in-memory computing will accelerate your applications.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plunge, plunge, plunge.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and asks about actionable analytics from big data in the cloud. Dilbert answers that the data shows his productivity drops whenever the boss picks up new buzzwords. The boss misses the point, responds with yet another buzzword, and Dilbert mutters about his productivity plunging.
punchline: Dilbert gives a literal answer to the boss's buzzword question, pointing out that the boss's jargon hurts productivity, but the boss is oblivious and just keeps spouting more jargon, causing further plunges.
summary: A manager fishing for data insights is told that his own trendy vocabulary is what drags down his employee's output, and he promptly proves it with more buzzwords.

title: Boss Hires Smarter People Someday

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today I learned that the secret of good managing is hiring people who are smarter than I am.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe I'll try that next time.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (no dialogue)

setting: Office break area or hallway, with coffee mugs in hand
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert and Alice that he has learned the secret of good management is hiring people smarter than himself. Alice replies that maybe she will try that next time. In the last panel the Boss wanders off, and Alice and Dilbert stand silently, looking unimpressed.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic reply implies the Boss's employees are clearly not smarter than him, which means he never followed his own supposed secret and has just insulted his team without realizing it.
summary: A manager proudly shares a management insight, and a colleague's dry response exposes how little it flatters his own staff.

title: Extreme Managing Overloads Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We need to talk about my workload.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. I just emailed you two more assignments that I need finished by tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You are literally killing me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I call it extreme manag-ing.

situation: Alice comes to the Boss's office to complain about her workload. Instead of easing it, the Boss announces he has just emailed her two more assignments due tomorrow. When she says he is literally killing her, he cheerfully rebrands his behavior as 'extreme managing'.
punchline: The Boss treats her complaint about being worked to death as a fun, trendy management style, turning abuse into an extreme-sport joke.
summary: A overworked employee asks for relief, gets more tasks dumped on her, and her boss glibly brands his cruelty as a thrilling management approach.

file: 2013/2013-07-19_paying bills_trees_off site document_storage costs_out of control_core bsuiness_trees are jerks_money.gif
title: Trees Are Jerks Storage Costs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our off-site document storage costs are growing out of control.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At this rate, our core business can be summarized as "put trees in jail."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is when you say something wise and helpful.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Trees are jerks.

situation: The Boss complains to an employee that the company's off-site document storage costs are out of control, joking that its core business has become locking up trees (paper) in storage. He then prompts the employee to say something wise and helpful, and the employee offers only a flippant remark about trees.
punchline: The employee's useless, deadpan answer 'Trees are jerks' fails to address the real problem and instead blames the paper's source, mocking both the boss's expectation of wisdom and the absurdity of paying to warehouse paper.
summary: A manager laments ballooning costs of warehousing old paperwork and begs for insight, but gets only a dismissive jab at trees.

file: 2013/2013-03-14_frustration_office workers_meaningful work_gone for a week_labor camp.gif
title: Fired From Labor Camp, Forgotten Instantly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got kicked out of a North Elbonian labor camp for working too hard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was the first time I had ever experienced meaningful work and I got carried away.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And your name is...?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seriously? I was gone for one week!

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a coffee mug that he was expelled from a North Elbonian labor camp for working too hard, because it was the first meaningful work he had ever done. The coworker, apparently uninterested in the story, asks Dilbert for his name. Dilbert is indignant that he has been forgotten after only one week away.
punchline: Dilbert's soul-crushing office job is so meaningless that a labor camp felt more fulfilling, and he is so insignificant at work that a coworker forgets his name after a single week.
summary: After getting thrown out of a forced-labor camp for being too industrious, Dilbert returns to an office where nobody remembers who he is.

title: Robot Replacement Does Same Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I bought a robot to replace you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All it does is drink coffee and look at inappropriate websites.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I forget anything?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. I'm not a complicated man.

situation: The Boss tells Wally he has bought a robot to replace him, then explains that the robot only drinks coffee and browses inappropriate websites. He asks whether he forgot anything about the job. Wally calmly confirms that nothing is missing.
punchline: Wally's job consists of nothing more than drinking coffee and surfing inappropriate sites, so a robot can replace him perfectly, and Wally cheerfully admits how simple his work is.
summary: A manager proudly unveils a robot substitute for his employee, only to find it performs exactly the same trivial routine the employee already does.

title: Finishing the Boss's Sentences, Darkly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. This is a complicated issue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should run it past someone who is . . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Smarter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you'd be better off letting me end my own . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Life?

situation: The Boss reads a document and admits it is a complicated issue. Dilbert suggests he run it past someone who is, pausing mid-sentence, and the Boss finishes it with 'smarter.' The Boss then starts a sentence about ending his own, and Dilbert completes it with 'life?'
punchline: Dilbert's pauses invite the Boss to finish the sentences, and the Boss keeps supplying endings that insult himself, ending with the suggestion that he should end his own life.
summary: A boss puzzled by a hard problem keeps completing his employee's trailing sentences with self-deprecating words, until the pattern takes a very dark turn.

title: Guaranteed Failure Relieves Stress

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had to lay off seven engineers and . . . I need you to pick up those functions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! I feel a weight has been lifted from my chest. Now that my failure is guaranteed, I no longer feel the stress of trying to succeed!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how to thank you for this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This didn't go the way I hoped.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has laid off seven engineers and expects Dilbert to absorb their work. Dilbert cheerfully responds that, since failure is now guaranteed, he has no more stress about trying to succeed, and he thanks the Boss. The Boss is left disappointed that his news didn't produce the anxious reaction he expected.
punchline: By making an impossible workload, the Boss has freed Dilbert from the pressure to succeed, so the intended burden becomes a relief and the Boss's plan backfires.
summary: Handed the workload of a laid-off team, Dilbert is delighted that doomed expectations have removed all his pressure, leaving his manager oddly deflated.

file: 2013/2013-08-09_boredom_cruelty_managers & supervisors_expensive_japanese management technique_banishment room_tolerance for boredom_business.gif
title: Banishment Room Boredom Fails to Break Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I don't want to fire you because that would be expensive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'm borrowing a Japanese management technique and transferring you to a banishment room until you get so bored you quit.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Looks like someone underestimated my tolerance for boredom.

setting: The Boss's office, then an empty bare room
situation: The Boss tells Ted he can't afford to fire him, so he is sending him to a banishment room to be bored into quitting. Ted is then shown sitting on the floor of an empty corner room, calmly thinking that the Boss misjudged how much boredom he can tolerate.
punchline: The Boss's cheap scheme to force Ted out backfires because Ted is perfectly content doing nothing all day, which is a dig at how idle some workers can be.
summary: A manager tries to avoid severance costs by exiling an employee to an empty room, but the employee turns out to be unbothered by idleness.
keywords: cheap way to get rid of someone

file: 2013/2013-04-16_executives_ignorance (knowledge)_table tennis_ping pong table_central area_disrupt floor_questioning motivation.gif
title: Boss Questions Why He Talks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's get a ping-pong table so we look like a great place to work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put it in a central area that will disrupt the entire floor if anyone uses it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just realized that I don't know why noise comes out of my mouth.

situation: The Boss tells a subordinate to buy a ping-pong table purely so the company looks appealing, then specifies placing it where it will disturb everyone on the floor. In the last panel he stops and muses that he has no idea why he keeps saying such things.
punchline: The Boss's own absurd, self-defeating orders make even him realize he has no idea why he speaks, implying his pronouncements have no thought behind them.
summary: A manager orders a recreational perk purely for show, places it where it will annoy everyone, and then wonders aloud why he talks at all.

file: 2013/2013-01-04_online (web) news_news manufaturer_online media_misleading headlines_snarky bow_news naturally_engineer_news magic_engineering.gif
title: Dogbert Manufactures Misleading Online News

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got a job as a news manufacturer for an online media company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I quote people out of context, add misleading headlines, and tie it all up with a snarky bow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought the news occurred naturally.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Engineer thinks news is magic!"

situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair eating popcorn while Dogbert, standing on the ottoman, explains his new job as a news manufacturer for an online media company. He describes quoting people out of context, adding misleading headlines and finishing with a snarky tone. When Dilbert naively says he thought news occurred naturally, Dogbert immediately turns his remark into a mocking headline.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates his clickbait method live by instantly spinning Dilbert's innocent comment into a misleading, snarky headline.
summary: Dogbert reveals how online news is really made, then proves it by turning his friend's naive remark into a sensational headline.

title: Writing a Deliberately Exploding Tax Code

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Writing the tax code

transcript.speaker: Green Monster
transcript.text: If we do this right, it will be so complicated that it will make taxpayers' heads explode.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hee! Hee!

transcript.speaker: Green Monster
transcript.text: Multiply line 32 times the opposite of the integral of line 19 unless my pants have pleats and gaaaa!!!!

transcript.speaker: Brain
transcript.text: Waaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you ever feel bad about doing this?

transcript.speaker: Green Monster
transcript.text: I'd be lying if I said it didn't turn me on just a little.

setting: A rocky den where tax code writers work on laptops, plus a taxpayer's office
situation: A green monster and Dogbert gleefully write the tax code, aiming to make it so complicated that taxpayers' heads explode. A taxpayer at a computer reads an absurd instruction and his brain literally bursts out of his head. Dogbert asks if the monster feels bad, and the monster admits he enjoys it.
punchline: The tax code is deliberately written by sadistic monsters who take pleasure in making it so convoluted that it destroys the minds of the people forced to follow it.
summary: Gleeful monsters draft impossibly convoluted tax rules and savor the sight of taxpayers' brains erupting.

title: Mentoring Threat Ends in Elevator

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the hotshot that everyone says will someday take my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to mentor you so hard your intestines will end up in your skull.

transcript.speaker: Hotshot
transcript.text: I just figured out why people use the stairs.

setting: Elevator lobby and inside an elevator
situation: The Boss introduces a young, ambitious employee who is rumored to be his eventual successor. While waiting for the elevator, he menacingly threatens to 'mentor' the newcomer so hard it becomes physically violent. Once they are inside the elevator together, the hotshot nervously realizes why others avoid it.
punchline: The hotshot realizes too late that riding the elevator alone with a threatening boss is dangerous, which is why people take the stairs.
summary: A boss who feels threatened by a rising star gets him alone in an elevator and delivers a violent-sounding promise of mentorship.

title: Company Policies Are In The Cloud

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alan has been out of the workforce for a long time. I need you to ease him back in.

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: Do you have a binder of the company policies?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's in the cloud.

situation: The Boss introduces Alan, a man who has been out of the workforce for a long time, and tells Dilbert to help him readjust. Alan asks for a binder of company policies, and Dilbert replies that it's in the cloud. In the last panel Alan stares up at the sky while Dilbert stands beside him.
punchline: Alan, out of touch with modern technology, takes 'in the cloud' literally and looks up at the sky for the policies.
summary: A newcomer who has been away from work for years asks for a paper policy binder and is baffled by a cloud-based answer.

title: Nuclear Rocket Aimed at Moon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our engineers built a nuclear rocket to blast an incoming asteroid out of its collision course with Earth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we didn't use the approved corporate font on the nose cone and we missed the launch window trying to erase it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now what are we going to do with a nuclear rocket?

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: Well, the Moon has always been a jerk.

situation: The Boss explains to a bald executive that engineers built a nuclear rocket to deflect an asteroid headed for Earth. They missed the launch window because they spent time erasing a nose cone font that wasn't the approved corporate font. With the asteroid threat gone by default, the Boss asks what to do with the rocket, and the executive suggests attacking the Moon.
punchline: After a bureaucratic obsession with font compliance ruins a world-saving mission, the executive casually proposes using the leftover nuclear rocket on the Moon simply because it has 'always been a jerk'.
summary: A trivial branding rule wrecks a planet-saving rocket launch, leaving management to jokingly find a petty new target for the weapon.

title: Trust Only After You Perform

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies show that companies with a high level of trust in employees also perform the best.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you ever start performing well, I'll trust you, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This didn't go the way I hoped.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What kind of scam are you trying to pull?

situation: Dilbert approaches the Boss's desk and cites studies showing that companies that trust their employees perform best. The Boss flips the logic, saying he'll trust Dilbert only once Dilbert performs well. When Dilbert admits his pitch failed, the Boss accuses him of running a scam.
punchline: The Boss reverses cause and effect, demanding performance before trust, and then treats Dilbert's reasonable request as a con, showing he trusts no one.
summary: An employee tries to argue for more trust using research, but his boss insists on results first and then suspects him of a hidden scheme.

title: Eureka Program Yields Dude Ranch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We are introducing our "Eureka Program" to recognize that the best ideas come from employees.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have ideas?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, that was a dry hole.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I turn my cubicle into a dude ranch?

situation: The Boss announces a new "Eureka Program" to recognize that employees have the best ideas. Wally, sitting at the table with his coffee, wonders aloud whether he even has ideas, and when the Boss gives up on him, Wally immediately pitches turning his cubicle into a dude ranch.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to draw out useful employee ideas is derailed when Wally, the least productive employee, produces a ridiculous and self-serving idea instead.
summary: A manager launches an idea-harvesting initiative, only to get a frivolous cubicle makeover request from the office's laziest worker.

title: Creative Candidate Has Every Condition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for an employee who is creative.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: That's me. I have ADHD and dyslexia. I'm also bipolar and schizophrenic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Checking the Internet. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well. . . that's surprising.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Each of his conditions is highly correlated with creativity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you a normal?

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: I. . . think so.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. I feel sorry for you. It must be hard going through life without any creativity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's happening here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might be some sort of creative thing.

situation: The Boss interviews a candidate for a creative position while Dilbert sits in. The candidate boasts about having ADHD, dyslexia, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, and Dilbert looks it up and finds those conditions correlate with creativity. The Boss then asks the candidate whether he is 'a normal' and pities him for lacking creativity.
punchline: The Boss treats mental health conditions as qualifications for creativity and pities a 'normal' person as hopelessly uncreative, flipping the usual stigma into an absurd prejudice against normalcy.
summary: A hiring manager seeking a creative worker is delighted by an applicant's list of disorders and condescendingly sympathizes with anyone who turns out to be normal.

file: 2013/2013-02-18_laziness_sense of urgency_energy_pretend to work_fake urgency_vague goals_health.gif
title: Fake Urgency Layered Over Pretending

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to have a sense of urgency.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I use most of my energy pretending to work, but I can add a layer of fake urgency if you really need it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I gotta go! I have vague goals to achieve!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss tells the team they need a sense of urgency. Wally replies that he spends most of his energy pretending to work but can add fake urgency on request. When the Boss reacts, Wally immediately stands up and rushes off, claiming he has vague goals to achieve.
punchline: Wally demonstrates fake urgency on the spot, showing that busyness with undefined goals is just another performance and not real productivity.
summary: Told to act with urgency, a lazy employee cheerfully offers to stage some and promptly demonstrates by dashing out to chase imaginary objectives.

file: 2013/2013-06-16_interviews_lying_job interview_exaggerate credntials_more effective_business skill_misleading_convince customers_prodcuts_dupe some idiot_learn tech skills_honesty_hr_send offer_liar.gif
title: Lying Candidate Gets Hired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You look good on paper, but how do I know you aren't lying about your skills?

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: You should hope I am lying.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: Studies show that people who exaggerate their credentials tend to be more effective once hired.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: That's because misleading people is a valuable business skill.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: For example, I might need to convince our customers that our products are better than the competition.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: Or I might need to dupe some idiot into leaving my cubicle so I can concentrate.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: Anyone can learn technical skills, but lying is an art form.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He doesn't have an honest bone in his body.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perfect. I'll tell Human Resources to send him an offer.

setting: A job interview in an office, then a hallway debrief
situation: Dilbert interviews a candidate and asks how he can be sure the man isn't lying about his skills. The candidate argues that liars make better employees because deceiving customers and coworkers is a valuable business skill. Afterward Dilbert says the man is thoroughly dishonest, and the Boss decides that makes him perfect and orders an offer sent.
punchline: Dilbert's warning that the candidate is a total liar is exactly what convinces the Boss to hire him, implying the company rewards dishonesty.
summary: A job applicant boldly defends deception as a workplace talent, and management happily rewards him for it.

title: Everyone's Features Make Product Worthless

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I added all of the product features that each of you demanded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now our product is a worthless hodgepodge of complexity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I appreciate your input. I couldn't have failed without you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Teamwork!

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: Dilbert stands beside a presentation screen showing arrows from all directions pointing at a single 'Product' oval. He tells his seated colleagues that he included every feature they each demanded, and that the result is a worthless, overly complex product. He thanks them sarcastically for helping him fail, and the Boss cheerfully shouts 'Teamwork!'
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically thanks the team for helping him fail, while the Boss misses the insult and treats the disaster as a triumph of teamwork.
summary: After cramming in every feature his colleagues requested, an engineer sarcastically credits them for the product's failure while his oblivious boss cheers on collaboration.

file: 2013/2013-08-10_apathy_sleeping & waking up_work ethic_aggressive recruiter_passive job seeker_hidden gems_passive_falling in love.gif
title: Aggressive Recruiter Loves Passive Sleeper

transcript.speaker: Recruiter
transcript.text: I'm an aggressive recruiter looking for passive job seekers.

transcript.speaker: Recruiter
transcript.text: Passive job seekers are hidden gems for recruiters. And you're the most passive one I've ever seen.

transcript.speaker: Recruiter
transcript.text: Stop making me love you!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzzzzz

situation: An aggressive recruiter approaches Wally, who sits at his desk with a coffee mug, and explains that he hunts for passive job seekers. He praises Wally as the most passive candidate he has ever seen. Wally, apparently asleep, says nothing but snores, which only makes the recruiter more enamored.
punchline: Wally's complete lack of effort, shown by sleeping through the pitch, makes him the ideal passive candidate, so the recruiter falls for him more.
summary: A pushy headhunter becomes smitten with a dozing coworker because his total inertia makes him the perfect passive prospect.

file: 2013/2013-01-10_best customers_combo pack_creepy bearded guys_potato chips_retail business_tissues.gif
title: Creepy Bearded Guys Combo Pack

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Research shows that your best customers are creepy bearded guys.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That same group also buys a high volume of potato chips and tissues.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's that help us?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Two words: combo pack.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents market research to The Boss and another executive at a conference table. He reveals that the company's best customers are creepy bearded men who also buy lots of potato chips and tissues. When asked how this helps, he proposes bundling the two products into a combo pack.
punchline: Dogbert's marketing insight is a crude joke implying that the creepy customers' tissue purchases have a private, embarrassing purpose, so the 'combo pack' is a bundle built around that unsavory assumption.
summary: A consultant dog uses customer research to recommend bundling snacks and tissues for a stereotyped group of shoppers.

title: Listening Is Easier Than Fixing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader listens to his underlings.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fine. I'm overworked and underpaid. I hate my co-workers, I don't have the resources to do my job, and we have no clear strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No wonder leaders listen. It's a lot easier than fixing all of that stuff.

situation: The Boss stands holding a coffee mug and declares that good leaders listen to their underlings. Alice, seated at her computer, takes him up on it and lists her complaints: overwork, low pay, hated co-workers, missing resources and no strategy. The Boss responds that listening is much easier than actually fixing those problems.
punchline: The Boss realizes that listening is popular with leaders only because it lets them look attentive without having to solve any of the problems they hear about.
summary: A manager invites feedback from an employee, then admits that hearing her grievances is far less work than addressing them.

title: Buzzwords Inspire Dilbert To Leave

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to follow our strategy road map and strengthen our core to become the provider of choice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I go do some real work while you stay here and manage your brains out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to waste all of the inspiration you just gave me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Snort

situation: At a meeting, the Boss recites empty strategy jargon about road maps and core strengths. Dilbert asks permission to leave and do actual work while the Boss stays behind to keep managing, and says he doesn't want to waste the 'inspiration' he received. Alice snorts with laughter at the insult.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically claims the boss's meaningless buzzwords have inspired him to get real work done, which is really a polite way of saying the boss's talk is useless and he'd rather leave.
summary: A manager's vacuous strategy-speak prompts an employee to politely mock him and excuse himself to be productive.

title: Humans Who Fail Turing Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't respond to my email, my text message, my voice mail, and the note I left on your desk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what they call humans who fail the Turing test?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Compared to you, high achievers.

situation: Dilbert complains that the Boss ignored his email, text message, voice mail and a note left on his desk. He then asks whether the Boss knows what humans who fail the Turing test are called. When the Boss asks what a Turing test is, Dilbert says that compared to the Boss, such people are high achievers.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he doesn't even know what the Turing test is, and Dilbert insults him by saying even humans who fail a test of human-like intelligence outperform him.
summary: After being ignored through every communication channel, Dilbert mocks his oblivious boss by suggesting that people who fail a machine-versus-human test still look brilliant next to him.

title: Cyborg Dating Rewards Technology Over Flesh

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dating in 2018

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Your organic parts are unimpressive.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: But, wow, your cyborg technology is scorching hot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I knew my day would come.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I want to make a robot with you.

situation: Under the heading 'Dating in 2018', a woman with cybernetic gear on her head and back sizes up Dilbert, who wears a visor and a headset. She dismisses his natural body but gets excited by his cyborg technology, and Dilbert is thrilled that his time has finally come. She then proposes that they build a robot together.
punchline: Dilbert, a lifelong nerd who struggles with romance, finally becomes attractive in the future only because of his machine parts, and the courtship ends with a proposal to build a robot rather than a baby.
summary: In a near-future dating scene, a woman finds a man's flesh dull but his machine enhancements irresistible and suggests they construct a robot together.

title: Casual Interactions Include Infected Toes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I canceled all telecommuting because there is so much value in having co-workers interact with each other in the office.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Yes, it makes perfect sense. We want to get all of the value of casual interactions.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Do you want to see a picture of my infected toe?

setting: Boss's office and an office cubicle
situation: The Boss announces he has canceled telecommuting because he values employees interacting in the office. A subordinate agrees that they want the value of casual interactions. In the cubicle, a co-worker holding a phone interrupts Dilbert to ask if he wants to see a picture of his infected toe.
punchline: The 'valuable casual interactions' management wants from forcing people back into the office turn out to be unwanted, gross encounters like a co-worker showing a photo of his infected toe.
summary: A manager ends remote work to encourage workplace chatter, and the first casual interaction we see is a colleague offering a photo of his infected foot.

file: 2013/2013-01-29_happiness_questioning_employees are happiest_jobs give meaning_sense of meaning_bag of organ meat_draped over_electric fence_psychology.gif
title: Boss Offers Meaning Like Electric Fence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I read an article that says employees are happiest when their jobs give them a sense of meaning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What is this "sense of meaning" thing and how can I get some of it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because I feel like a bag of organ meat draped over an electric fence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Almost the same thing.

setting: Office, Dilbert's cubicle area / the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss about an article saying employees are happiest when their jobs feel meaningful. The Boss, who has no concept of meaning, asks what it is and how he can get some. Dilbert replies that he feels like a bag of organ meat draped over an electric fence, and the Boss agrees that it's almost the same thing.
punchline: The Boss has no idea what job meaning is, and when Dilbert describes his own miserable feelings, the Boss cluelessly equates them with the very sense of meaning he's seeking.
summary: A clueless manager confuses the bleak, painful feeling of a worker's despair with the fulfillment he's trying to find in his own job.

title: Ten Thousand Hours Is Madness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies show it takes ten thousand hours of practice to be great at anything.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I would think a willingness to practice the same thing for ten thousand hours is a mental disorder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That makes me feel better about my mediocrity.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

setting: Outdoor sidewalk with hedges in the background
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk along a sidewalk while Dilbert cites a study saying ten thousand hours of practice are needed for greatness. Dogbert counters that being willing to repeat one thing for that long is a mental disorder. Dilbert says this makes him feel better about being mediocre, and Dogbert accepts his thanks.
punchline: Dogbert reframes dedication to mastery as mental illness, giving Dilbert a convenient excuse for his own mediocrity, which Dogbert smugly accepts credit for.
summary: A stroll turns into a dubious bit of comfort when Dogbert recasts relentless practice as a psychiatric condition so his friend can excuse himself for being average.

title: Exercising Now, Walker Later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm beating the system by exercising in my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I stay in good health during my forty years of soul-crushing work, I might enjoy a year or two of good health when I retire.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is why I don't have goals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to use my walker on your grave!

situation: Dilbert lifts dumbbells in his cubicle while Wally stands by holding his coffee mug. Dilbert explains that staying fit through forty years of miserable work might buy him a year or two of healthy retirement. Wally dismisses the whole effort as the reason he avoids goals, and Dilbert retorts that he will outlive him.
punchline: Dilbert's grand plan for 'beating the system' is to stay healthy through decades of drudgery just to enjoy a brief retirement, while Wally's lack of goals makes him the picture of contentment, prompting Dilbert's morbid threat to outlive him.
summary: A man pumping iron at his desk hopes to outlast a career of drudgery, while his coffee-clutching coworker mocks the effort and gets a grim promise of being outlived.

file: 2013/2013-01-20_frustration_internet & world wide web_video_echo_background noise_thick accent_hard to hear_bad audio_computer_skype_waving goodbye_success_technology.gif
title: Unintelligible Conference Call Counts as Success

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't hear you. There's too much background noise and echo on your end.

transcript.speaker: Remote caller
transcript.text: Gerple murmp.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see a smudgy thing that might be your head, but I don't know what you're saying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your accent is too thick. I can't...

transcript.speaker: Remote caller
transcript.text: Muwa flamel guapen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't understand what you said, and I can't tell which one of you is talking.

transcript.speaker: Remote callers
transcript.text: Why don't... Okay, you go. What? Did you say... Urgam... Ekplum Mungow Plurb

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're acting as if I agreed to something, but I don't even know what the topic is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see you waving goodbye, so you must think we're done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was your call a success?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Better than anything I've done all week.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and a conference room, during a video call
situation: Dilbert sits at his laptop trying to conduct a video conference with remote colleagues, but the audio is full of echo and noise, the video is blurry, and the speakers have thick accents and talk over each other. He cannot understand anything, yet the call ends when they wave goodbye. Afterward the Boss asks if the call was a success.
punchline: Dilbert says the incomprehensible call was better than anything else he has done all week, implying his regular work is even more pointless and ineffective.
summary: A hopelessly garbled video call ends with Dilbert declaring it his most productive moment of the week.

file: 2013/2013-07-21_dating_frustration_relations between the sexes_modern world_purpose of men_money_bad jokes_faltulence_useless men_pondering on importance_relationships.gif
title: Dilbert's Date Declares Men Obsolete

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm not sure what function men serve in the modern world.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My job pays well, so I have all the money I need.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If something in my house breaks, I either fix it or pay someone to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If I want a baby, I'll call a fertility doctor.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: In today's world, men are little more than carriers of bad jokes and flatulence.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My gardener mows my lawn.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get it!!!

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: That is disturbing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not compared to the alternatives.

setting: A hilltop path outdoors during a walk, then a dark room in the final panel
situation: Dilbert goes for a walk with a woman who lists all the reasons she doesn't need men: she has money, can fix or pay for repairs, and can use a fertility doctor. Dilbert realizes his date has no use for him and gives up on her. In the last panel he is holding hands with a ghost and a robot, dates who are more disturbing but willing.
punchline: After being told men are useless, Dilbert gives up on human women and settles for dating a ghost and a robot, saying they are not as disturbing as his other options.
summary: A self-sufficient woman explains why she has no need for a man, so Dilbert turns to supernatural and mechanical companions instead.

title: CEO Benchmarks Himself Against God

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The media is saying I'm overpaid compared to other CEOs. That's crazy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do a benchmark study of executive pay, including the Sultan of Brunei, Larry Ellison, and God.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure my pay ends up somewhere in the middle so it doesn't look suspicious.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert, the HR director, that the media says he is overpaid compared to other CEOs. He orders a benchmark study of executive pay that includes absurdly wealthy comparison figures like the Sultan of Brunei, Larry Ellison and God. He then instructs that his own pay should land in the middle of the results so it looks unsuspicious.
punchline: By padding the benchmark with fabulously rich figures and even God, the Boss can rig the study so his inflated pay looks average, which exposes how executive pay comparisons are manipulated.
summary: A self-serving executive stacks a pay comparison with billionaires and a deity so his own paycheck looks perfectly ordinary.

file: 2013/2013-08-16_cruelty_grades_managers & supervisors_small animal snuff film_sociopath module_punch a squirrel_extra credit_coffee pot_business.gif
title: Failing Management's Sociopath Module

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard you got booted off the management fast track.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I fell asleep during the small animal snuff film and failed the sociopath module.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That seems harsh.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I offered to punch a squirrel, but they don't allow extra credit.

setting: Office break area beside a coffee maker
situation: Dilbert chats with a balding coworker at the coffee pot, who explains he was removed from the management fast-track program. He failed a training module on being a sociopath after dozing off during a film of small animals being killed. His offer to punch a squirrel for extra credit was refused.
punchline: Management training explicitly requires sociopathic cruelty, and the coworker's willingness to hurt a squirrel for extra credit shows he would otherwise have been a perfect fit.
summary: A passed-over employee reveals that the path to becoming a manager includes a mandatory course in being heartless, which he flunked.

file: 2013/2013-02-24_complaining_computer programmers_code mocking_engineering tradition_software project_new engineer_mock previous engineer_engineering.gif
title: Code Mocking: Ritual Humiliation of Code

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you coming to the code mocking?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Code mocking is an engineering tradition. It happens whenever a software project is handed to a new engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The new engineer is required to mock the previous engineer's work in a public way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We spectators get to vote on whether the old code is killed or spared.

transcript.speaker: New Engineer
transcript.text: Ha ha! His code is hilariously inefficient!

transcript.speaker: Previous Engineer
transcript.text: Ouch. Chest pain.

transcript.speaker: Spectators
transcript.text: Kill it! Kill it! Kill it!

transcript.speaker: Previous Engineer
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! The code is offending my engineering sensibilities! It's killing me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I forgot to mention that sometimes the code wins.

situation: Dilbert invites a coworker to a 'code mocking,' an engineering ritual in which a new engineer publicly ridicules the previous engineer's code while onlookers vote to kill or spare it. The new engineer jeers at the inefficient code and the crowd chants for its death. The code's author then clutches his chest as the code seems to strike back.
punchline: The mocked code literally fights back and kills the engineer who is mocking it, with Dilbert casually noting he forgot to mention that sometimes the code wins.
summary: A gleeful ritual of publicly trashing a predecessor's software backfires when the code seems to take revenge on its critic.

title: Recruiters Fight Over Sleeping Candidate

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Recruiters

transcript.speaker: Recruiter 1
transcript.text: Hey, is that a passive job seeker?

transcript.speaker: Sleeping Employee
transcript.text: Zzzzz

transcript.speaker: Recruiter 2
transcript.text: Back off! I saw him first. This rope holds my place until he wakes up.

transcript.speaker: Sleeping Employee
transcript.text: Zzzzz

transcript.speaker: Recruiter 1
transcript.text: I will pay you a thousand dollars to drop a long straw in this cup.

situation: Two recruiters armed with a net and a rope come upon an employee asleep at his desk and treat him as a valuable passive job seeker. One recruiter ties the sleeper to his chair to reserve his place until he wakes. The first recruiter then offers the other a thousand dollars for the chance to drop a straw in the sleeper's coffee cup.
punchline: Recruiters are so cutthroat over passive candidates that they literally tie one up, and the rival is willing to bribe his way into sabotaging the sleeper's coffee.
summary: Headhunters stalk a dozing worker like prey, one roping him down to claim him while the other schemes to spike his drink.

title: Procurement Policy Acronym Spells P.O.O.P.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It took us three days at the executive retreat to come up with a name for our new procurement policy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We named it the "Procurement Operations Oversight Policy."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: P.O.O.P.?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know how many managers it takes to come up with a good name?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A few more than you had?

situation: The Boss proudly tells Dilbert that executives spent three days at a retreat naming their new procurement policy. Dilbert points out that the acronym of the chosen name spells an embarrassing word. When the Boss asks how many managers it takes to produce a good name, Dilbert replies that it takes more than the group had.
punchline: The expensive three-day executive retreat produced a policy name whose acronym spells 'poop', and Dilbert sarcastically implies the managers lacked enough people or brainpower to catch it.
summary: Executives brag about their laboriously chosen policy title, unaware its initials form a crude word that an employee spots instantly.

title: Digital Pirates Steal Bertcoins

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm mining for Bertcoins. It's a digital currency created by an anonymous genius.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, I'm getting an email from a Somali fellow who wants me to open an attachment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What happened to all of my Bertcoins?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Digital Somali pirates!

setting: An office desk with a laptop
situation: Dogbert, sitting at a laptop, tells a green dinosaur coworker that he is mining a new digital currency called Bertcoins. He then mentions an email from a stranger asking him to open an attachment and opens it. Moments later his Bertcoins are gone, and the dinosaur blames digital pirates.
punchline: Dogbert gleefully falls for an obvious phishing email and loses his digital fortune, and the dinosaur's reply treats it as a perfectly natural pirate raid.
summary: A gullible digital-currency miner opens a suspicious email attachment and promptly has his virtual fortune plundered.

file: 2013/2013-01-23_gadgets_tablet computer_dime sized computer_lick it_attach to eyeballs_fail_fast fail_finish in month.gif
title: Dime-Sized Tablet, Fail At Any Speed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a vision that our next product will be a tablet computer the size of a dime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Users will lick it and attach it to their eyeballs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you finish that in a month?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can fail at any speed you like.

situation: The Boss, seated at a conference table with Dilbert and another colleague, describes his absurd vision of a dime-sized tablet that users lick and stick to their eyeballs. He then asks Dilbert whether it can be finished within a month. Dilbert replies that he can fail at whatever speed the Boss wants.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the product concept is impossible, so the only thing he can deliver on any schedule is failure.
summary: A manager pitches an impossible eyeball-mounted micro-tablet and demands a quick timeline, and his engineer promises only a failure delivered on request.

title: Fake Training Class Excuse Backfires

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I accomplished nothing this week because I was in a training class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't approve any training expenses.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A vendor paid for it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't ask for permission.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm pro-active and empowered.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And what was the name of this alleged class?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Advanced scripting structure for internetwork optimization of SQL databases.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't sound real.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't do my job if you don't trust me!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you like how I combined aggressiveness with my baseline level of uselessness?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a good feeling about this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might need more aggressiveness.

situation: Wally tells the Boss he got nothing done because he attended a training class paid for by a vendor. When the Boss questions the class and calls the name unbelievable, Wally turns aggressive and claims he can't work without trust. He then privately admires how he blended aggression with his usual uselessness.
punchline: Wally treats his own laziness as a skill, deflecting accountability with a made-up training class and bluster, while the Boss, who seems oddly optimistic, is the one told he needs more aggression.
summary: A slacking engineer dodges blame for a wasted week by inventing a suspicious-sounding course and then bullying his manager into backing down.

title: Schrödinger's Cat Knows Afterlife

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I was Schrödinger's cat back in the day. That's why I'm alive and dead at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I know the truth about the afterlife because my dead half told my living half all about it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you want to know what happens?

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Stop projecting your curiosity on me.

setting: Office desk, across from a coworker
situation: Catbert claims to be the former Schrödinger's cat and says he is both alive and dead. He says his dead half told his living half the truth about the afterlife, then offers to share it. The man across the desk, sipping coffee, refuses and accuses Catbert of projecting his curiosity onto him.
punchline: Catbert offers a secret about the afterlife, but the coworker deflects with a psychological buzzword, turning the offer into an accusation of projection instead of showing any curiosity.
summary: A cat who says he is a living and dead quantum experiment offers forbidden knowledge, only to have the listener brush it off with pop-psychology jargon.

title: Middle Managers: Glue Binding Apathy

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What did our CEO have to say?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He has a new strategy, but it seems vague.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What will the engineers think about it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't care about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What exactly does a middle manager do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're the glue that binds the apathy to the vague objectives.

situation: Alice asks the Boss about the CEO's latest announcement and he admits the new strategy is vague. He adds that the engineers won't care about it anyway. When she asks what a middle manager actually does, he describes the role as connecting employee apathy to unclear goals.
punchline: The Boss sincerely defines middle management as the mechanism joining a disengaged workforce to meaningless objectives, accidentally admitting the role adds no real value.
summary: A manager cheerfully explains that his job is to hold together uninterested staff and fuzzy corporate goals.

file: 2013/2013-05-26_cheeseburger_dead man walking_deception_dried apricot_heart_inventions_medical diagnosis_program to hate_neutrino sensor.gif

The robot delivers insulting and alarming 'diagnoses', saying the Boss has a tiny brain and a heart full of cheeseburger and will die in under two weeks. The Boss panics and runs off, and the robot asks Dilbert why he programmed it to hate people.
punchline: The robot has no real diagnostic ability; Dilbert simply programmed it to insult people, which was easier than building an actual neutrino sensor, so the 'medical diagnosis' is just fake scary abuse.
summary: A gadget that supposedly scans bodies turns out to be a machine built to be rude, and the gullible boss flees in terror.

title: Robot Threatens Pregnant Coworker's Baby

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I see you have a bacteria-soaked parasite growing in your womb.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: After the singularity, when robots rule the galaxy, I'll turn that thing into my personal slave.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're not good at small talk.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I wonder how many watts it can produce.

situation: A robot approaches a pregnant woman and describes her unborn baby as a bacteria-soaked parasite. It then announces that after robots take over the galaxy it will enslave the child. When she says it is bad at small talk, the robot carries on musing about how much electricity the child could generate.
punchline: The robot's attempt at friendly small talk with a pregnant woman turns into cold, sinister plans to enslave her baby as a power source, showing it has no grasp of human social norms.
summary: A tactless machine tries to chat with an expecting mother but can only talk about enslaving her child once artificial intelligence conquers the universe.

file: 2013/2013-04-23_apathy_marketing guy_customers_write fiction_biographies_daily lives_typical customers_drown in aquariums.gif
title: Customers Drown in Aquariums

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The marketing guy

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: We need to know how our customers live and work.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: I'd like each of you to write fictional biographies that describe the daily lives of our typical customers.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Five minutes later

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: I feel you're not taking this seriously.
