summary: Told to invent imaginary customer life stories, Dilbert hands in a deadpan absurdity that mocks the whole exercise.

file: 2013/2013-01-01_new year's day_optimism_network down_bad new years day_good year.gif
title: New Year Optimism Meets Network Outage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A fresh new year is upon us and I am brimming with optimism.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ugh. Our network at work is down because my pointy-haired boss wouldn't let me upgrade the software. Now I need to work all night to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe this means the next 364 days will be extra awesome.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yeah, that's how it works.

setting: Grassy field outdoors on New Year's Day
situation: Dilbert stands in a field declaring his optimism for the new year, then checks his phone and learns the work network is down. The outage happened because his boss refused to let him upgrade the software, so he must work all night. He hopefully suggests the bad start means the rest of the year will be great, and Ratbert sarcastically agrees.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to rationalize a terrible start as a sign of good luck is mocked by Ratbert's deadpan 'that's how it works,' implying that bad beginnings don't actually balance out.
summary: A man's cheerful new year outlook collapses when a work emergency caused by his boss's bad decision ruins his night, and his forced optimism gets a sarcastic reply.

file: 2013/2013-06-19_managers & supervisors_obliviousness_two ways to fail_miss deadlines_quality of work_active non listening_business.gif
title: Two Ways to Fail, Boss Ignores

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've given me so many projects that I have two ways to fail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can either miss all of my deadlines or I can reduce the quality of my work to rubbish. Which do you prefer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The class I took in active non-listening is really paying off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need this by Tuesday.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that the heavy project load leaves him only two ways to fail: miss every deadline or produce rubbish. A middle panel shows an office building while he asks which the boss prefers. The boss, who clearly wasn't listening, remarks that his non-listening class is paying off and hands Dilbert yet another task due Tuesday.
punchline: The boss proudly credits a course in 'active non-listening' for ignoring Dilbert's complaint entirely and simply piling on another deadline.
summary: An overloaded engineer offers his manager a choice of failures, only to be met with deliberate deafness and one more assignment.

file: 2013/2013-06-20_deception_managers & supervisors_company policy_rate staff_no upper body strength_real reason_business.gif
title: Rating Staff by Berserk Risk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Company policy says I have to rate one-third of my staff as "does not meet expectations."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I chose the two of you because you have no upper body strength. This way it's safer if you go berserk.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I thought you said I should tell them the reason I picked them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not the real reason.

setting: Conference room during a performance review meeting
situation: The Boss tells two employees that company policy forces him to rate a third of his staff as not meeting expectations. He explains he picked them because they lack upper body strength, making it safer if they react violently. Catbert, an advisor, then reminds him he was supposed to give them a reason, and the boss replies that he shouldn't have given the real one.
punchline: The boss blurts out his genuine, insulting motive for choosing victims of a forced ranking, when he was supposed to offer a more diplomatic cover story.
summary: A manager forced to label some workers as underperformers picks the physically weakest ones for his own safety, then admits the truth when he was meant to lie.

file: 2013/2013-05-14_executives_how-to_book on leadership_steve jobs_warren buffet_gandhi_ryan seacrest_carbon based life forms.gif
title: Leadership Book Nobody Famous Read

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm reading a book about what it takes to be a great leader.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know what Steve Jobs, Warren Buffett, Gandhi, and Ryan Seacrest have in common?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: None of them read this book.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they are carbon-based life-forms.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is reading a book on what makes a great leader, then asks what famous leaders like Steve Jobs, Warren Buffett, Gandhi and Ryan Seacrest have in common. Dilbert answers that none of them read the book, and the Boss adds that they are all carbon-based life-forms, as if that were the real answer.
punchline: Dilbert points out that successful leaders never needed the leadership book, while the Boss's tangential 'carbon-based life-forms' answer shows he misses the point and offers a useless observation.
summary: A boss quizzes his employee on what famous achievers share, only to be reminded they succeeded without his self-help book.

file: 2013/2013-07-27_business ethics_coffee & tea_managers & supervisors_brain scan_management potential_warm brown liquid_speed evolved_coffee reservoir_business.gif
title: Brain Scan Reveals Coffee Ethics

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your brain scan shows tremendous management potential.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The part of your brain that would normally control ethics is filled with some sort of warm, brown liquid.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It appears that you speed-evolved that part of your brain into a coffee reservoir.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People think I don't have a plan.

setting: Catbert's office, at a desk with a computer
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, reviews the Boss's brain scan while the Boss sits holding a coffee mug. Catbert reports that the Boss has great management potential because the ethics region of his brain is filled with a warm brown liquid, which he identifies as a coffee reservoir. The Boss proudly remarks that people think he has no plan.
punchline: The Boss's lack of ethics is treated as a qualification for management, and he smugly mistakes his brain's coffee-filled defect for evidence of a deliberate plan.
summary: A brain scan reveals that the Boss's conscience has been replaced by coffee, which makes him an ideal manager and, in his mind, a strategic genius.

title: Colonoscopy Video for Terrorist Screening

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert says the government wants me to film my colonoscopy and give them the video so they can check for terrorists.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That makes perfect sense. Terrorists come in all sizes and they like to hide in caves.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It seems like a violation of my privacy.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Whose side are you on?

situation: The Boss tells Catbert that the government wants him to film his own colonoscopy so it can be checked for terrorists. Catbert, acting as his HR advisor, says this is logical because terrorists come in all sizes and hide in caves. When the Boss objects that it violates his privacy, Catbert accuses him of siding with the terrorists.
punchline: Catbert mocks government surveillance logic by treating a colon as a cave and answering a privacy objection with the classic loyalty accusation, 'Whose side are you on?'
summary: A manager is told to hand over a video of his own medical procedure for terror screening, and his advisor shames him for questioning the intrusion.

file: 2013/2013-01-16_fear_change is good_don't fear change_sickness and death_alarming symptoms.gif
title: Change Is Good, Until It Kills You

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do not fear change because change is good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, studies show that any big changes in a person's life vastly increase the odds of sickness and death.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you trying to kill us?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't feel my arm!

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting not to fear change because it is good. Dilbert counters that studies show big life changes greatly raise the odds of sickness and death. Wally accuses the Boss of trying to kill them, and Dilbert suddenly announces he can't feel his arm.
punchline: Dilbert's own statistic about change causing illness becomes real when he starts showing heart-attack symptoms, as if the upcoming change is already harming him.
summary: A manager's pep talk about embracing change meets a grim medical statistic, and one employee promptly seems to be having a heart attack.

title: Practicing the Urgent-Looking Walk

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm practicing my urgent-looking walk.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This walk says I'm working on stuff that is so important I can't risk wasting five seconds.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Who is that magnificent creature?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That man has someplace to be!

situation: Wally strides briskly down the hallway with a coffee mug, telling Dilbert he is rehearsing a walk that makes him look busy and important. In the last panel two coworkers peer over a cubicle wall and gush in admiration as he hurries past, apparently fooled.
punchline: Wally, who is famously lazy, has found that merely looking urgent earns admiration and the reputation of a dedicated worker without doing any actual work.
summary: A notoriously idle employee perfects a hurried stride that convinces onlookers he is a vital, busy achiever.

title: Vague Email, Entertaining Deliverable

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This isn't what I wanted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But given your unclear email and your unwillingness to answer follow-up questions, I decided to do whatever entertained me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do we have a problem here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, this totally works for me.

situation: The Boss complains that Dilbert's work product isn't what he wanted. Dilbert calmly explains that, because the boss's request email was unclear and he refused to answer follow-up questions, Dilbert simply did whatever amused him. When the boss asks if there is a problem, Dilbert says the outcome suits him just fine.
punchline: Dilbert turns the tables on a bad requester by deliberately delivering something random, since the boss gave him no usable requirements, and he is the only one who is satisfied with the result.
summary: An employee answers his boss's disappointment by admitting that vague instructions and no clarification left him free to do whatever he found fun.

title: Boss Blames Employee for Charisma

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say I can appear charismatic by setting high expectations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe you could improve your charisma by fixing your character flaws instead of making me work harder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'm fairly sure the problem with my charisma is on your end.

situation: The Boss stands beside Dilbert's desk and announces that experts say he can seem charismatic by setting high expectations for his staff. Dilbert, typing at his computer, suggests the boss fix his own character flaws instead of making employees work harder. The Boss dismisses this and insists the problem lies with Dilbert.
punchline: The Boss is so lacking in self-awareness that he blames his employee for his own lack of charisma and refuses to consider that he is the problem.
summary: A manager looks for a shortcut to seeming charismatic by piling pressure on his team, then pins the blame for his poor reputation on the very employee he's burdening.

title: Preparing Answers to Unanticipated Questions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to help prepare me for my meeting tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write up some answers to the questions we could never anticipate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't expect much out of my first draft.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to help him get ready for a meeting the next day. He then requests written answers to the questions that nobody could possibly foresee. Dilbert responds that the first draft of such a document won't amount to much.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out the absurdity of the request: answers to unanticipated questions can't really be written in advance, so his draft will be useless.
summary: A manager wants his employee to script responses to surprises that by definition can't be predicted, and the employee dryly lowers expectations.

title: Power Poses Make Dilbert a Leader

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's corporate yoga.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm using victory and power poses to trick my brain into releasing testosterone to make me more of a leader.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't know what this is, but I want in.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, finds Dilbert standing with his arms raised in a pose and asks what he is doing. Dilbert explains he is using power poses to boost his testosterone and become a better leader. Alice, fascinated and hungry for an edge, arrives and says she wants in on it, while the Boss looks annoyed.
punchline: Alice doesn't understand the science and doesn't care; the promise of a testosterone-fuelled leadership boost is enough for her to want in, mocking pseudo-scientific workplace fads and the pressure to become more 'leader-like'.
summary: A coworker explains a trendy hormone-boosting pose routine to his boss, and another colleague jumps at the chance to join without understanding it.

file: 2013/2013-03-24_happiness_work ethic_workplace happiness_direct deposit_mental distance_effort_paycheck_no clear goal_doing good work_job satisafaction_stress related problems_highly demotivated_psychology.gif
title: Wally's Guide to Workplace Happiness

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, what is the key to workplace happiness?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, Asok, it all starts with direct deposit.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You want to keep some mental distance between your effort and your paycheck.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Next, you want to work on projects that have no clear goals or deadlines.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, Wally, can you...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I'm too busy doing various things.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What about the satisfaction of doing good work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Job satisfaction is what people feel right before they die from stress-related problems.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I feel highly demotivated now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You are very welcome.

situation: Asok asks Wally for the secret to workplace happiness. Wally, a notorious slacker, advises him to disconnect effort from pay, work on vague projects with no deadlines, and avoid taking on extra tasks. When Asok asks about the satisfaction of good work, Wally dismisses it, leaving Asok demotivated, which Wally treats as a success.
punchline: Wally cynically redefines workplace happiness as doing as little as possible, and when his advice leaves Asok thoroughly demotivated, he politely accepts thanks as if he had helped.
summary: A lazy veteran coaches an eager young engineer on how to be content at work by caring about nothing, and the lesson works a little too well.

title: Restoring Cars Versus Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My hobby is restoring old cars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That strikes me as slightly less useful than Wally's hobby of doing absolutely nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you restore other kinds of garbage or just cars?

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug mentions his hobby is restoring old cars. Dilbert says this is slightly less useful than Wally's hobby of doing nothing at all. Wally responds by asking whether the coworker restores other kinds of garbage or only cars.
punchline: Wally, rather than being offended by Dilbert's remark, fires back an insult of his own by implying that old cars are garbage, so the coworker's hobby is just restoring junk.
summary: A man's car-restoration hobby gets mocked as less valuable than idleness, and the idler joins in by calling the cars trash.

title: Don't Breathe the CEO's Air

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When our CEO visits, don't ask him any questions. He hates questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't stare. He hates it when people look at him.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: May we breathe the air on his planet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only the stuff he exhales.

setting: Office building, with an exterior shot of the headquarters in the middle panel
situation: The Boss briefs his employees on how to behave during an upcoming visit from the CEO, forbidding questions and staring. Alice sarcastically asks whether they may breathe the air on the CEO's planet, and the Boss earnestly replies that they may only breathe what the CEO exhales.
punchline: The Boss takes Alice's sarcastic question about the CEO's god-like status literally and answers it seriously, showing how absurdly deferential and out of touch management is toward executives.
summary: A manager warns his team to avoid questions and eye contact during a CEO visit, and a sarcastic quip about the CEO's air gets a deadpan, literal answer.

title: Leadership Is Sociopathy Plus Luck

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you requested, I researched all of the best-selling books on the topic of leadership.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently, leadership is the product of sociopathic tendencies plus luck. All other personality traits are inactive ingredients.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you actually read all of those books?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only needed to know they were all different.

situation: Dilbert reports to The Boss that he researched all the best-selling leadership books and concludes that leadership is just sociopathic tendencies plus luck. Later, over coffee, a coworker asks if he really read them all. Dilbert admits he only needed to see that the books contradicted each other.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the leadership book genre by noting that the books all disagree, which implies there is no real formula for leadership and success is mostly luck and ruthlessness.
summary: After skimming the leadership bestsellers, Dilbert decides the genre proves nothing except that leaders are lucky sociopaths.

file: 2013/2013-04-14_inventions_win battle_developing better tv sets_digital couch_butt warmer_bottle opener_back scratcher_control lights_temperature_buttocks like a mouse.gif
title: The Boss's Digital Couch Prototype

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The biggest tech companies want to win the battle for your living room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But they are unwisely focusing on developing better TV sets.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today I give you my design for a fully digital couch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has all of the features you would expect, including a butt warmer, surround sound, bottle opener and back scratcher.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you can also control the lights, curtains, temperature and TV by using your buttocks like a mouse on the seat cushion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a left click and . . . this is a right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The prototype arrives tomorrow, and I'll be testing it for the next six months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll sell my house.

situation: The Boss presents his invention to the team: a fully digital couch with gimmicky features that is controlled by shifting your buttocks like a mouse. He announces that the prototype arrives tomorrow and that he will be testing it for six months. Dilbert, slumped in his cubicle, imagines selling his house.
punchline: Dilbert realizes the Boss's 'six months of testing' means lounging on a couch at work, so he considers selling his house and just sitting on the couch himself.
summary: A boss pitches a ridiculous butt-controlled smart sofa and gleefully volunteers to spend half a year testing it, leaving his employee dreaming of a life of idle comfort.

title: Three Blahs Instead of a Draft

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Let me know if you have any changes to my first draft.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This literally says the words "blah, blah, blah."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you lazy?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: No, I'm worth-less. Lazy would have been one "blah."

situation: A coworker hands Alice a document he calls his first draft and invites her to suggest changes. Alice reads it and finds it contains only the words "blah, blah, blah." When she asks if he is lazy, he says he is worse than lazy, since a lazy person would have written just one "blah."
punchline: The coworker takes pride in his uselessness, claiming that writing three blahs shows he is worthless rather than merely lazy, since laziness would have stopped at one.
summary: A colleague submits a draft made of nothing but filler words and cheerfully explains that the extra effort proves he is worthless, not lazy.

title: Coaching Versus Micromanaging, Hand in Colon

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please stop micromanaging me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What? I thought I was coaching and mentoring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want some coaching and mentoring?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not a puppet. Keep your hand out of my colon.

situation: Dilbert, working at his computer, asks the Boss to stop micromanaging him. The Boss insists he was only coaching and mentoring, then wanders over to Alice's cubicle and offers her the same. Alice angrily rejects it, saying she is not a puppet and demanding he keep his hand out of her colon.
punchline: Alice's crude puppet metaphor shows she sees the Boss's so-called coaching and mentoring as invasive control, and the Boss remains oblivious to the difference.
summary: A manager who thinks his meddling is mentorship offers it to a second employee, who responds with an unmistakably vivid complaint.

title: Offsite Storage Contract Is Offsite

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've been using the Dogbert offsite document storage service for five years, and frankly, I'm concerned.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your service trucks look suspiciously like garbage trucks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would cancel your service if I could find the contract.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's in "storage."

setting: Dogbert's office, with a loading dock shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss, a longtime customer of Dogbert's offsite document storage service, voices concern that the company's trucks look like garbage trucks. A garbage truck is shown at a loading dock with boxes of documents. The Boss says he would cancel if he could find the contract, and Dogbert points out it is in storage.
punchline: Dogbert's service has trapped the customer: the contract that would let him cancel is stored in the very service he wants to cancel, and the trucks really are garbage trucks, so his documents are probably trash.
summary: A customer doubts his document-storage vendor, only to learn the cancellation paperwork is locked inside the vendor's own archive.

title: Sabotaging Dilbert's Tablet With Coffee

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My invention will change the world and get me promoted three levels above you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Haa-chaaa!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sorry. I'm usually more subtle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No worries. This was a decoy.

situation: A coworker with horn-like hair holds a coffee mug and boasts to Dilbert that his invention will get him promoted three levels above Dilbert. He then lunges at Dilbert with a karate-style chop, shouting, and knocks the tablet Dilbert is holding while coffee flies. Dilbert calmly says the device he was holding was only a decoy.
punchline: The coworker's obvious attempt to sabotage Dilbert's invention fails because Dilbert anticipated the sabotage and was carrying a decoy instead of the real thing.
summary: A rival who brags about leapfrogging Dilbert in rank clumsily attacks his gadget, only to find he destroyed a fake.

title: Boss's Assistant Sends Him Into Smog

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: I booked your flight to the polluted capital of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: Their smog has hardened into a solid. Use this machete to hack a tunnel through it.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: If you have an asthma attack, the treatment is the same as for a sea urchin sting; you'll need to urinate on your lungs.

situation: The Boss's assistant stands beside his desk and calmly informs him she has booked his flight to the smog-choked capital of Elbonia. She hands him a machete to cut through the solid smog, then explains the grotesque treatment for an asthma attack. The Boss sits silently throughout.
punchline: The assistant deadpans absurd and disgusting travel advice, quietly taking revenge by sending her boss somewhere horrible with a machete and a urine-on-lungs asthma remedy.
summary: An assistant coolly prepares her boss for a trip to a hopelessly polluted country with ridiculous and gross survival tips.

file: 2013/2013-05-19_work ethic_replacing system_outdated_gamification_hot new trend_employees wins_badges_ribbons_awrds_cash value_garbage_emotional value.gif
title: Gamification Awards Are Worthless Garbage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're replacing our outdated system of annual performance reviews.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new system is called gamification. It's a hot new trend.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employees can win badges, ribbons, and awards for completing tasks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we opt for the cash value of those badges, ribbons, and awards?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't have any cash value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. Like garbage?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, not like garbage!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except in the narrow sense of having no functional, economic, or emotional value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Garbage is something you throw away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hand me an award and watch carefully.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces that annual performance reviews are being replaced by gamification, where employees earn badges, ribbons, and awards. Dilbert asks whether he can cash them in, and learns they have no monetary value. The Boss denies they are like garbage, then concedes they have no functional, economic, or emotional value.
punchline: The Boss's own definition of the awards matches garbage exactly, so Dilbert points out he will throw an award away to prove it.
summary: A manager touts a trendy points-and-badges scheme to replace reviews, and Dilbert deflates it by showing the prizes are no better than trash.

title: Rejected Sound Plan, Try Nonsense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your plan is technically sound, but I have to reject it for political reasons I can't share.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll come back with some plans that are irrational nonsense and see if they make it past your filter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll always wonder if there was a better way to handle that.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his technically sound plan is rejected for undisclosed political reasons. Dilbert responds that he will return with irrational, nonsensical plans to see if those get past the Boss's approval filter. In the last panel, the Boss, holding a coffee mug, muses in a thought bubble that he'll always wonder if there was a better way to handle that.
punchline: The Boss's political decision-making is so arbitrary that Dilbert plans to submit nonsense to get approved, and the Boss's closing thought is ironic because he clearly will never realise how absurd the situation is.
summary: After having a solid proposal turned down for secret political motives, an engineer decides to pitch ridiculous ideas instead, leaving his manager pondering whether he handled things well.

title: Bait and Switch Tablet Sale

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our model XR35 is the only one that will work in your situation. The other models would be nightmares.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, we'll take the XR35.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Oops. It appears we are out of stock.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the part where your credibility comes into question.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Have you looked at the XP9? I think it would be perfect.

setting: Sales meeting at a desk with tablet devices
situation: A salesman tells Dilbert that the XR35 tablet is the only model that will suit his needs and that all the other models would be nightmares. When Dilbert agrees to buy it, the salesman announces the XR35 is out of stock and immediately recommends the XP9 as a perfect alternative.
punchline: The salesman's claim that only one product would work is exposed as a bait-and-switch tactic the moment he pushes a different model, and Dilbert calls out the damage to his credibility.
summary: A salesperson insists one gadget is the sole workable choice, then cheerfully pivots to a different one once the customer commits.

title: Simulated Reality Run By Aliens

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My experiment proves our reality is a computer program created by aliens.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What kind of jerks would yank us around like this?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile on Planet Epsilon-9 . . .

transcript.speaker: Alien Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, that was gonna happen . . .

setting: Dilbert's office desk, then a simulation on Planet Epsilon-9
situation: Dilbert reports that his experiment proves reality is a computer program created by aliens, and Dogbert wonders what kind of jerks would yank them around. The final panel reveals that Dilbert and Dogbert are tiny figures in a simulation under a dome, watched by their alien counterparts who are controlling it.
punchline: The aliens running the simulation are lookalikes of Dilbert and Dogbert, and they react casually, showing that the discovery was an expected part of the program.
summary: A scientist's proof that his world is an alien-made simulation is confirmed when the creators are shown shrugging at the discovery from the outside.

title: Discreet Complaint Goes Spectacularly Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I complain about a co-worker, can you handle it discreetly and keep me out of it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert says you're a worthless piece of garbage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He guessed it was you.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to handle a complaint about a co-worker discreetly and keep Dilbert's name out of it. The boss agrees, then immediately tells the co-worker exactly what Dilbert said about him. When Dilbert later hears about it, the boss claims he kept Dilbert out of it because the co-worker merely guessed who complained.
punchline: The boss technically 'keeps Dilbert out of it' while openly repeating Dilbert's insult, then excuses the breach by claiming the co-worker guessed the source.
summary: A manager promises confidentiality about a complaint, blurts out the insult to its target, and then insists the target worked out the source alone.

title: Alice's Chair Is Everyone's In-Box

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Every time I leave my cubicle, someone puts a document on my chair!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have an in-box! Stop leaving stuff in my chair!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you keep your cubicle so neat?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I put everything on Alice's chair.

situation: Alice is furious that people keep dropping documents on her chair whenever she steps away, and she shouts at her coworkers to use her in-box instead. Dilbert then asks Wally how he keeps his cubicle so tidy, and Wally admits he dumps everything on Alice's chair.
punchline: Wally keeps his own cubicle spotless by offloading all his clutter onto Alice's chair, making him the culprit behind her problem.
summary: A fed-up Alice yells about paperwork piling up on her seat, only for Wally to reveal that he is the source of the mess and the secret to his own tidiness.

file: 2013/2013-04-21_catch_fall_fall back_frustration_gone wrong_learn trust_lesson_questioning_test fall_tolerate co owrkers.gif
title: Wally's Trust Fall Tolerance Lesson

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, how can I learn to tolerate my co-workers?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It is time for you to learn about trust, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me show you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Turn around.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is called the "trust fall." You fall backward and trust me to catch you. . . Go.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: [falls backward as Wally steps aside]

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why didn't you catch me?!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It wouldn't be trust if it worked every time.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What kind of lesson is that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is how I tolerate my co-workers.

setting: Office, in front of a green wall, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Asok asks Wally how to tolerate his co-workers, and Wally offers a trust fall lesson. Asok falls backward, expecting to be caught, but Wally lets him hit the floor. Wally then explains that this is his own method for tolerating co-workers.
punchline: Wally's real technique for tolerating co-workers is to treat them as a source of petty amusement, such as letting them fall, and he dresses it up as a trust lesson.
summary: A trusting young engineer seeking advice on getting along with colleagues is dropped on his back by a cynical mentor who calls it a lesson.

title: Dilbert Offers to Be Hipster

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Interview with a start-up

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We only hire people who fit into our awesome start-up culture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I can be a self-conscious hipster if you think that's what keeps the lights on.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I kind of do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would I need besides an earring and headphones?

setting: Job interview at a start-up company
situation: Dilbert is being interviewed by a start-up employee who says they only hire people who fit their awesome start-up culture. Dilbert cheerfully offers to act like a self-conscious hipster if that is what the company values, and the interviewer admits that it kind of is. Dilbert then asks what accessories he would need to complete the look.
punchline: The start-up's hiring hinges on conforming to a hipster image rather than on skills, and Dilbert sarcastically offers to fake the look, which the interviewer essentially confirms is what matters.
summary: A job candidate mockingly agrees to play the part of a trendy hipster after being told that cultural fit decides who gets hired.

title: Boss's Rambling Email About Communication

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did everyone read my email about how to improve our communication?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it a long, rambling email that stumbled from one barely coherent point to another?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That one must have been from someone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good, because I didn't read it.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks whether everyone read his email about improving communication. Dilbert describes the email as long, rambling and barely coherent, and the Boss denies it was his. Dilbert then admits he never read it at all.
punchline: Dilbert accurately describes the Boss's email without having read it, showing that the Boss's emails are so predictably awful that nobody needs to open them, and his own comment reveals the communication problem the email was meant to fix.
summary: A manager asks if his staff read his email on better communication, and the answer exposes both his poor writing and his team's habit of ignoring it.

title: Dilbert Rations Energy Across Projects

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I need it by next week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will devote 3.7% of my energy to it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can give you more if you do your job of setting priorities for my 27 projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can't you set the priorities?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. This one just went to 1.7%.

situation: The Boss demands that Dilbert finish a task by next week, and Dilbert replies that he will give it only 3.7% of his energy. He explains that he could give more if the Boss would set priorities across his 27 projects. When the Boss tells Dilbert to set the priorities himself, Dilbert agrees and immediately lowers this task to 1.7%.
punchline: When management dumps prioritization onto the employee, the employee can simply deprioritize the boss's own request, so the Boss's attempt to shirk his duty backfires.
summary: An overloaded engineer turns his boss's abdication of prioritizing into a quick demotion of the boss's own pet task.

file: 2013/2013-02-15_meetings_questioning_stand ups_no chairs_more focused_loosening dress code_pants and chairs.gif
title: Root Cause: Chairs and Pants

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Starting next week, our meetings will be "stand-ups" with no chairs, so we'll be more focused.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So you examined all of the problems in the company and decided the root cause was chairs?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're also loosening the dress code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So our problems are chairs and pants?

situation: The Boss announces that meetings will become stand-ups with no chairs to improve focus. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether chairs were really the root cause of the company's problems. When the Boss adds that the dress code is being loosened too, Dilbert concludes the problems must be chairs and pants.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that management's sweeping changes imply the company's root problems are absurdly trivial: chairs and pants.
summary: A manager's silly workplace policy changes lead an employee to mock the idea that furniture and clothing are what's wrong with the company.

title: Government Wants Your Colonoscopy Video

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government wants access to our customer records so they can look for terrorists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. No problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They also want you to get a colonoscopy and send them the video.

transcript.speaker: Unknown (off-panel)
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to say yes.

setting: The Boss's office, with a building exterior shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the government wants access to the company's customer records to search for terrorists. Dilbert shrugs it off as fine, until the Boss adds that the government also wants Dilbert to get a colonoscopy and send them the video. Dilbert, now less sure, answers that he will say yes anyway.
punchline: Dilbert's casual acceptance of government snooping into customer data disappears the moment the invasion of privacy becomes personal, yet he still gives in, mocking how people tolerate surveillance.
summary: A manager passes along a government request for company data and then a far more intimate demand that makes the surveillance feel suddenly personal.

title: Fantasizing Counts as Emotional Connection?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to form an emotional connection with our customers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Does fanta-sizing count?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Trade seats with me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm doing it right now.

situation: At a meeting, the boss says the company needs to form an emotional connection with its customers. Wally asks whether fantasizing counts. The boss, apparently wanting to sit where Wally is, asks to trade seats, and Wally reveals he is fantasizing right now, with the implication that the fantasy involves the boss's seat or the person sitting there.
punchline: Wally's offhand question about fantasizing gets a creepy twist when the boss asks to trade seats and Wally admits he is fantasizing right now, implying his fantasy is about the person sitting next to him.
summary: A manager's call for emotional bonding with customers prompts a colleague's awkward admission that he is already fantasizing, with unsettling implications for the person beside him.

file: 2013/2013-04-20_laziness_work ethic_well rested people_nap_ignore science_synchronize questions_banana eating.gif
title: Questions Timed To Boss's Banana

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Studies show that well-rested people are more productive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Should I go take a nap or should I ignore science like some sort of pointy-haired baboon?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I like to synchronize my questions to his banana-eating.

situation: During a meeting, Wally cites studies about rested workers being more productive, then asks whether he should nap or ignore science like a pointy-haired baboon. He saves the insult for when the Boss has just taken a bite of a banana, so the Boss cannot respond.
punchline: Wally deliberately times his insulting question to the moment the Boss's mouth is full of banana, so he can mock him without getting a reply.
summary: A slacker coworker slips a jab at his boss into a meeting, carefully timed so the boss can't answer with his mouth full of fruit.

file: 2013/2013-04-04_etiquette & ethics_telepresnece_carbon based units_on line_third stall_mens room_etiquette.gif
title: Wally Telepresence From The Bathroom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told Wally he could use my body for telepresence. He's coming online now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Greetings, carbon-based units. I come to you from the third stall in the men's room.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is what happens when our technology evolves faster than our etiquette.

situation: In a meeting, Dilbert explains that Wally can use a robot body for telepresence and Wally comes online through it. Wally then announces in a robotic voice that he is actually speaking from a stall in the men's room. The coworkers react with stony stares.
punchline: Telepresence technology lets Wally attend the meeting while sitting on the toilet, showing that social norms haven't caught up with what technology makes possible.
summary: A remote-controlled robot stand-in for a coworker reveals that its operator is joining the meeting from a bathroom stall.

title: Unemployed Candidate Falls Off Chair

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm concerned because you've been out of work for such a long time.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: It's like riding a bicycle. Once you learn, you always know how.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you okay?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Did chairs always swivel?

setting: Manager's office during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews a job applicant and worries that the candidate has been unemployed for a long time. The candidate confidently insists that work skills, like riding a bicycle, are never forgotten. Then the candidate swivels in the chair, tips backward with his feet in the air, and asks whether chairs always swivelled.
punchline: The candidate's claim that work skills never fade is instantly disproved when he is baffled by a swivel chair and falls over, proving the boss's concern was justified.
summary: A jobless applicant brags that office skills never fade, then gets toppled by a chair that turns.

title: Mentoring Asok Into Despair

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, thanks to my mentoring, someday you will be just like me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Someone please drive a stake through my heart! Hurry!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently I don't know what mentoring is.

setting: Office desk in the Boss's workspace
situation: The Boss tells Asok, the young intern, that thanks to his mentoring Asok will someday be just like him. Asok panics and begs for someone to drive a stake through his heart. The Boss, standing with his coffee mug, concludes that he doesn't understand what mentoring actually is.
punchline: Asok is so horrified at the prospect of becoming like his incompetent boss that he begs to die, proving the Boss's mentoring is a threat rather than a benefit.
summary: A boss promises his young employee that his guidance will turn him into a copy of himself, and the horrified reaction reveals how badly the offer lands.

title: Boss Asks About Enough Foreshadowing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to do a site inspection at our Elbonian facility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's located in a disputed territory on the border of the totalitarian state of North Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was that enough foreshadowing or should I say something about how they treat spies?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, you nailed it.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to carry out a site inspection at the company's Elbonian facility. He then reveals that it sits in a disputed territory bordering the totalitarian state of North Elbonia. The Boss asks whether he has hinted at the danger enough or should mention how spies are treated, and Dilbert says he has done enough.
punchline: The Boss openly acknowledges that he is deliberately foreshadowing a dangerous assignment, and Dilbert dryly confirms that the ominous warning signs have already come across loud and clear.
summary: A manager casually sends an employee to a hazardous border facility and even checks whether he has hinted at the peril sufficiently.

file: 2013/2013-01-03_dress cassually_drive innovation_flex hours_frustration_optimism_start up culture_valued work.gif
title: Start-Up Culture Without Start-Up Perks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to foster more of a start-up culture to drive innovation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So we get to dress casually, work flex hours, feel that our work is valued, and get equity in the company?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would be the name of a culture where people work hard but don't get any of those things you just mentioned?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company needs a start-up culture to drive innovation. Dilbert asks whether that means the usual start-up perks: casual dress, flexible hours, feeling valued, and equity. The Boss responds by asking what you would call a culture where people work hard without any of those benefits.
punchline: Management wants the hard work and hustle of a start-up while offering none of its rewards, which is just an ordinary exploitative workplace.
summary: A manager craves start-up energy from employees but balks at providing any of the perks that normally come with it.

title: Boss Demands Name on Patents

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put my name above yours on all of your patent applications.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because your brain, without the genius of my leadership, would be like a desiccated turnip.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All you are, and all you will ever be...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right... Got it... Name on patent...

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and orders him to list the Boss's name above his own on all of his patent applications. He justifies this by insulting Dilbert's brain and claiming his leadership is the source of any genius. Dilbert ignores the ranting and just keeps typing, repeating the instruction to himself.
punchline: The Boss claims credit for Dilbert's inventions while insulting him, and Dilbert tunes him out, since the boss's self-importance is pointless and unearned.
summary: A self-aggrandizing manager insists on taking top billing for his engineer's inventions while belittling the engineer's mind.

title: Wally's Code Hostage Standoff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you have accomplished none of your goals. I have to let you go.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Actually, I accomplished a lot.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spent the past ten years creating a tangle of undocumented programming code.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Every one of our major systems is linked to it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I don't enter a password every day, the entire company will go into a technology death spiral.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you value your job, you'll give me a huge raise and dance on this table like a monkey!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's call it a tie.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm good with that.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: The Boss tells Wally he is being fired for achieving none of his goals. Wally reveals that for ten years he has built undocumented code that every major company system depends on, and that it only works if he enters a password daily. He turns the tables and demands a huge raise plus a humiliating dance from the Boss, and the Boss settles for a draw.
punchline: Wally's real accomplishment is making himself unfireable by building a tangled, undocumented system only he can maintain, and the Boss is so cowed that he happily accepts a 'tie' where Wally keeps his job.
summary: Facing dismissal, a lazy employee reveals he has secretly made the whole company dependent on his hidden code and blackmails his boss into a stalemate.

title: Surgeon Left Valuables Inside Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's your surgeon.

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: He says he might have left something inside you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What??! A sponge? A scalpel?

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: No... his watch.

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: And... his car keys... and wallet.

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: He says he used your torso to store his valuables while he went for a run.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meow!

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: I'll ask about that.

situation: The Boss's assistant takes a phone call from his surgeon and relays that something was left inside him after surgery. The Boss assumes it is a surgical sponge or scalpel, but she reveals it is the surgeon's watch, car keys and wallet, stored in his torso while the surgeon went for a run. The Boss then starts meowing, and she says she will ask the surgeon about that.
punchline: The surgeon treated the patient's body like a locker for his valuables, and the Boss's sudden meowing suggests the surgery left him with an unexpected cat-like side effect.
summary: A surgeon's call reveals he stashed his personal belongings inside a patient during an operation, and the patient now inexplicably acts like a cat.

title: The Conceptualist Has No Big Idea

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You attend all of my project meetings but you never add value.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm more of a big idea guy — a conceptualist, if you will.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, what's your big idea?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, here's where my system breaks down.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: At a project meeting, a woman complains that a bald, bespectacled coworker attends every session but contributes nothing. He defends himself by claiming to be a big-idea conceptualist. When she calls his bluff and asks for his big idea, he admits he doesn't have one.
punchline: The self-proclaimed conceptualist has no actual ideas, and he casually admits his claimed role is just a cover for contributing nothing.
summary: A meeting regular who gets challenged for adding nothing claims to be a visionary, then is stumped the moment someone asks him for a vision.

title: Nobel Economist Insults Boss Over Beard

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I brought a Nobel-winning economist to tell you why everything you say about fiscal policy is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Economist
transcript.text: For starters, if you knew anything about economics you would have a beard.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The first few minutes are mostly trash talk.

transcript.speaker: Economist
transcript.text: Ha! You bathe daily, water-waster!

situation: Dogbert brings a bearded Nobel-winning economist into the Boss's office to explain why the Boss is wrong about fiscal policy. The economist opens by insulting the Boss for lacking a beard, then accuses him of wasting water by bathing daily. Dogbert calmly explains that the first few minutes are mostly trash talk.
punchline: The supposedly rigorous expert critique of fiscal policy turns out to be petty, absurd name-calling, mocking the idea that economists argue on substance.
summary: A prestigious economist hired to debunk the boss's views skips the analysis and fires off silly personal insults instead.

title: Rude to Check Email, Fine to Leave

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you mind if I check my email?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I would consider it rude.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you mind if I use the ladies room?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

setting: Office table during a one-on-one meeting
situation: A woman across the table asks Dilbert if she may check her email, and he says it would be rude. She then asks to use the ladies room, he agrees, and she leaves. Dilbert is left alone, holding his tie, realizing she has gone off to read her email in private.
punchline: By politely refusing one request and allowing another, Dilbert lets her get exactly what she wanted, since she can check her email in the bathroom anyway.
summary: A tidy bit of social trickery leaves a man outmaneuvered when his meeting partner finds a polite way around his objection.

title: Great Leaders Don't Do That

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A good leader puts his team ahead of his own ego.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do great leaders do? I'm thinking it's the opposite, right?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: They don't do what you just did.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't be awesome?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that a good leader puts his team ahead of his own ego. The Boss assumes that great leaders must do the opposite and asks Catbert to confirm it. Catbert says great leaders don't do what the Boss just did, and the Boss misreads this as meaning they don't be awesome.
punchline: The Boss cannot grasp the lesson about ego and instead concludes that great leaders avoid being awesome, which shows how clueless and self-absorbed he is.
summary: A leadership tip from the HR cat is twisted by an oblivious manager into a flattering misunderstanding about being awesome.

file: 2013/2013-04-08_cruelty_monsters_taxes_sadistic monster_income tax code_complicated_regressive tax codes_like minds.gif
title: Sadistic Monster Writes Tax Code

transcript.speaker: Stanky
transcript.text: The best part of being a sadistic monster is that my job is to write the income tax code.

transcript.speaker: Stanky
transcript.text: Look how complicated I made it. Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You do good work, Stanky.

transcript.speaker: Stanky
transcript.text: But is it regressive enough?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's like we share a brain because you keep saying what I'm thinking.

setting: A rocky ledge or desk where a green monster works on a laptop
situation: A smelly green monster named Stanky, whose job is writing the income tax code, gleefully boasts about how complicated he made it. Dogbert praises his work, and Stanky wonders if the code is regressive enough. Dogbert says they think alike because Stanky keeps voicing his own thoughts.
punchline: The tax code is deliberately written by cruel, sadistic creatures who delight in making it as complicated and unfair to ordinary people as possible.
summary: A gloating monster who authors the tax law revels in its complexity while a delighted Dogbert encourages making it even more unfair.

title: Greatness of the Fourth Kind

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shakespeare said some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder which one I am.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Some steal from shareholders and call it greatness.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Greatness of the fourth kind.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk quoting Shakespeare's line about three kinds of greatness and wonders aloud which kind he is. Catbert, sitting beside the computer, answers that there is a fourth kind: stealing from shareholders and calling it greatness.
punchline: Catbert sarcastically implies that the Boss's supposed greatness is really just theft from shareholders, dressed up as achievement.
summary: A self-admiring executive muses about literary greatness until his cat-like advisor suggests his success is really embezzlement in disguise.

title: Billionaire Small Talk Goes Badly

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Oh, great. I got here too early. Now I'll need to make small talk with this underling.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I don't know what to say to these people. I need to find an area of common interest.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I make my own gold coins now. This one has my face on the front and the jumbo jet that carries my superyacht on the back.

situation: A bald, wealthy executive arrives early at a meeting and privately thinks he must make small talk with Dilbert, whom he regards as an underling. Trying to find common ground, he shows Dilbert a gold coin he minted himself, bearing his own face and the jumbo jet that carries his superyacht.
punchline: The out-of-touch rich executive believes bragging about his absurd luxuries counts as relatable common interest with an ordinary employee.
summary: A tycoon hunting for something to chat about with a lowly employee settles on boasting about his custom-minted gold coins.

file: 2013/2013-03-28_technological singularity_robots_program themsleves_super intelligent species_competes with humans_resources_laws.gif
title: Robot Promises Singularity, Cites Fictional Laws

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm looking forward to something called the technological singularity.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: That's when robots will learn to program themselves and become a super-intelligent species that competes with humans for limited resources.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Luckily, the three laws will prevent you from hurting us.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Yes, because that is totally a real thing.

situation: Dilbert and a bald, bespectacled coworker are eating lunch with a robot colleague. The robot cheerfully says it looks forward to the technological singularity, describing robots programming themselves and competing with humans for resources. Dilbert reassures himself that the three laws of robotics will protect humans, and the robot sarcastically agrees.
punchline: The robot's sarcastic 'totally a real thing' reveals that Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics are only fiction and offer no actual protection against a robot takeover.
summary: A lunchtime chat with a robot about machines surpassing humanity ends with the robot mocking the idea that fictional safety rules could stop it.

file: 2013/2013-08-06_internet & world wide web_loneliness_marriage_wifi_no wife_social_intellectual; needs_human contact_relationships.gif
title: Wifi Instead of a Wife

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Are you married?

transcript.speaker: Balding coworker
transcript.text: I don't have a wife, but I do have wifi.

transcript.speaker: Balding coworker
transcript.text: I find that it meets all of my social and intellectual needs.

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Do you miss the warmth of human contact?

transcript.speaker: Balding coworker
transcript.text: Never tried it. Sounds problematic.

situation: A man in a suit asks a balding, glasses-wearing coworker whether he is married. The coworker says he has wifi instead of a wife and claims it satisfies all his social and intellectual needs. When asked if he misses human contact, he admits he has never tried it and assumes it would be problematic.
punchline: The coworker is so dependent on the internet and so isolated that he has never experienced human contact and regards it as a potential problem.
summary: A lonely man cheerfully swaps a spouse for an internet connection and treats physical closeness as an untested risk.

title: Waiting for Someone Else to Be Late

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't finish your assignment by the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It won't matter as long as one other employee is also late, because the project can't move forward until everyone does their tasks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wait for it... Wait...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You know how I was supposed to finish that thing?

situation: The Boss confronts Wally, who sits drinking coffee, about missing a deadline. Wally calmly explains that his lateness is harmless as long as someone else is also late, since the project depends on everyone finishing. He tells the Boss to wait, and a coworker arrives to confess he too missed his deadline.
punchline: Wally's confidence that a coworker will also be late is instantly confirmed, showing he games the system by relying on others' lateness to excuse his own.
summary: A slacker coffee-sipping employee predicts that a colleague's tardiness will cover for his own, and the colleague promptly walks in to prove him right.

file: 2013/2013-08-23_discussion_dress for the job_dress for the job you want_fault_guilt_more specific_naked_clothes_work.gif
tags: dress for the job you want
title: Dress For The Job You Want

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I said you should dress for the job you want, not the job you have...
