transcript.text: I shouldn't have needed to be more specific than that.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You have a way of making everything sound like it's my fault.

setting: Office, in a meeting across a desk, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: The Boss lectures an employee about his earlier advice to dress for the job he wants rather than the job he has. The middle panel shows an office building as the Boss complains he shouldn't have needed to be more specific. In the last panel the employee is seen sitting at the desk apparently naked, with only a coffee mug in front of him, and complains that the Boss blames him for everything.
punchline: The employee took the dress-for-the-job-you-want advice absurdly literally, showing up unclothed, yet still protests that he is being unfairly blamed.
summary: A manager scolds a worker over his dress, only to reveal the worker has shown up wearing nothing at all and is offended at being blamed.
keywords: dress for the job you want

title: The Noncommittal Committee Won't Decide

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Noncommittal Committee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does everyone agree with the plan?

transcript.speaker: Committee member (woman in orange)
transcript.text: It depends.

transcript.speaker: Committee member (bald man)
transcript.text: Ask me later.

transcript.speaker: Committee member (man in purple)
transcript.text: Eh.

transcript.speaker: Committee member (woman in green)
transcript.text: I'll think about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Make a decision!!!

transcript.speaker: Committee member
transcript.text: Is this your first day?

setting: Conference room during a committee meeting
situation: Dilbert presents a plan to a committee and asks whether everyone agrees. Each member responds with a vague, evasive non-answer, so he loses his temper and shouts at them to decide. One of them calmly asks if it is his first day, implying that dodging decisions is normal there.
punchline: The committee's whole purpose is to avoid committing to anything, so Dilbert's demand for a decision shows he doesn't understand how the organization works.
summary: A group of evasive committee members dodges every attempt to get a straight answer, and the exasperated presenter is treated like a naive newcomer for expecting one.

title: Microwave Beeps Mean Please Kill Me

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You keep giving me trivial assignments that make me doubt my self-worth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Chill out. You don't hear the microwave whining all day long.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: He doesn't know that the machine word for "please kill me" is "beep."

transcript.speaker: Microwave
transcript.text: Beep

setting: Boss's office, then a break room counter
situation: A robot employee complains to the Pointy-Haired Boss that the trivial assignments he gives it make it doubt its self-worth. The Boss dismisses the complaint by pointing out that the microwave never whines. The robot then walks to the microwave, which beeps, and explains that beeping is the machine language for 'please kill me'.
punchline: The Boss thinks the microwave is content with menial work, but the robot knows its beeping is actually a cry of despair, implying that machines suffer in silence from meaningless tasks.
summary: A depressed robot worker is told by its oblivious boss to stop complaining like the microwave, only to reveal that the microwave's beeps are secretly pleas for death.

file: 2013/2013-08-26_employees_ignorance (knowledge)_new guy_first day_calling in sick_message_problem getting dressed_head in arm hole_boss can relate_business.gif
title: New Hire's Absurd Sick Excuse

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: It's the new guy's first day and he's calling in sick.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: His message says he was putting on his shirt and got his head caught in an arm hole.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good hire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had that same problem with my pants.

situation: A receptionist at her desk, phone to her ear, reports that the new employee has called in sick on his first day. His message claims he got his head stuck in a shirt's arm hole while dressing. She sarcastically calls him a good hire, and The Boss says he once had the same problem with his pants.
punchline: The Boss relates to the new hire's dressing mishap, revealing his own incompetence at something as basic as putting on pants, while the receptionist's 'good hire' is dripping with sarcasm.
summary: A new employee skips his first day because of a clothing mishap, and his boss cheerfully admits he has struggled with the same kind of trouble.

file: 2013/2013-09-07_civil liberties_law enforcement officers_surveillance_stole sensitive info_spy software_stealing back.gif
title: Stealing Back Stolen Surveillance Data

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: You hacked into a government database and stole sensitive information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, it was my company's information that your spy software stole first. I was just stealing it back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So we're good here, right?

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: Yeah, that's how it works.

situation: Two government agents in dark suits and sunglasses confront Dilbert at his desk, accusing him of hacking a government database and stealing sensitive information. Dilbert argues that the data was originally his company's, taken first by the government's spy software, so he merely reclaimed it. The agent agrees that this is how it works.
punchline: The government accepts Dilbert's 'stealing it back' defense because it is the same logic that justifies their own spying, exposing the hypocrisy of surveillance.
summary: Caught hacking a government system, Dilbert claims he only retrieved data that the agents' own spyware had taken from his company, and they reluctantly concede the point.

file: 2013/2013-09-20_ignorance (knowledge)_managers & supervisors_work ethic_project_unstable applcation_data model_overly complex relational databse_lazy_business.gif
title: Does That Mean Lazy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's taking you so long on the project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The application is unstable because the data model is driven by an overly complex relational database and there was no integration testing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does any of that mean the same thing as "lazy"?

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why the project is taking so long. Dilbert gives a detailed technical explanation involving an unstable application, a complex relational database, and missing integration testing. The Boss, who understood none of it, asks whether any of it just means Dilbert is lazy.
punchline: The Boss cannot follow the technical explanation, so he assumes it is jargon covering for laziness, showing how managers dismiss legitimate engineering problems as excuses.
summary: A manager demands to know why a project is late, and when given a technical diagnosis, he wonders aloud if it is all just a fancy way of saying the engineer is slacking.

title: Government Wants to Weaponize Internet Browser

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: I'm from the government. We've been monitoring your internet activity.

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: Half of my department went blind and the other half needs counseling.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds like not my problem.

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: We'd like to weaponize you.

situation: A government agent in a dark suit and sunglasses visits Wally at his desk and says his agency has been monitoring Wally's internet activity. The agent, who now carries a white cane, explains that half his department went blind and the other half needs counseling from what they saw. Wally shrugs it off as not his problem, and the agent says they want to weaponize him.
punchline: Wally's web browsing is so disturbing that it blinded and traumatized government surveillance staff, and the government now sees that harm as a weapon worth recruiting him for.
summary: A surveillance agent left sightless by what he saw in an employee's online habits recruits that employee as a potential weapon.

title: Testing X-Ray Phone on Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I added a biometric sensor to our smartphone prototype.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: ZZEEEP

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It uses x-rays.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should have tested it on animals first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I look like an animal hater?

situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a smartphone prototype with a new biometric sensor. He demonstrates it by pointing it at the Boss, whose skeleton glows in an x-ray flash, and explains it uses x-rays. The Boss, now disheveled and singed, suggests animal testing, and Dilbert responds by implying he chose the Boss as the test subject rather than harm animals.
punchline: Dilbert says he didn't test the dangerous device on animals because he's not an animal hater, implying he'd rather irradiate his boss instead.
summary: An engineer demonstrates a gadget that zaps his boss with radiation and then defends skipping animal trials on ethical grounds.

title: Engineer Pitches Himself at Party

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi. I'm an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That means I have excellent employment potential and I can fix things around the house.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How are your social skills?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. Look who wants the moon.

setting: A social gathering or cocktail party
situation: Dilbert introduces himself to a woman holding a martini and lists the practical benefits of dating an engineer: job security and home-repair skills. When she asks about his social skills, he responds sarcastically that she is asking for far too much.
punchline: Dilbert treats a basic expectation of decent social skills as an unreasonable demand, implying engineers cannot offer them.
summary: An engineer at a party sells himself as a stable, handy partner, then balks when asked to also be sociable.

title: Optogenetic Device Rewrites Coworker's Preferences

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard that Marketing's optogenetic device tweaked some of your preferences.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yup.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now I'm a gay anarchist who loves football and string cheese.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a big adjustment.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Well, the cheese part came easily...

setting: Office building, with coffee mugs in hand
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he has heard that Marketing's optogenetic device altered some of his preferences. The coworker, holding a coffee mug, lists his dramatically changed new identity as a gay anarchist who loves football and string cheese. Dilbert says that sounds like a big adjustment, and the coworker says the cheese part was the easy bit.
punchline: After being reprogrammed into a sweeping new identity, the coworker says the only effortless change was the trivial one, loving string cheese.
summary: A coworker reprogrammed by a mind-altering gadget lists his startling new traits, then admits only the snack preference came easily.

file: 2013/2013-09-15_frustration_managers & supervisors_product changes_change orders_new features_online change order system_old forms_change order_managemet_better plan_business.gif
title: Change Orders Require Change Orders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't make any product changes without change orders.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When users ask for new features, direct them to the online change order system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That system only has the old forms.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell someone to put the new ones on there.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That would require a change order.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we could tell users our sense of hope was killed by something called management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then we could sort of slump over like we're waiting for death's cold embrace.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll get back to you if I think of a better plan.

situation: The Boss orders his team to route all product changes through the online change order system. Dilbert points out the system only contains the old forms, and when the Boss says to add the new ones, Wally notes that would itself require a change order. Dilbert sarcastically suggests telling users that management killed their hope, and the team slumps over the table while the Boss says he'll think of a better plan.
punchline: The change order process is so circular that updating the change order forms requires a change order, leaving the team so defeated they slump over the table, and the Boss's only response is to promise a better plan later.
summary: A rigid approval rule traps a team in a loop where fixing the paperwork system needs the very paperwork it lacks, driving them to dramatic despair.

file: 2013/2013-11-04_burglars & robbers_frustration_lab_stealing back cables_worse problem_boss_adds fuel to fire.gif
title: Cable Thief Complains About Cable Thieves

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every time I leave the lab, some jerk steals my cables and replaces them with their bad ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I have to spend hours stealing back one cable at a time and testing each one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Doesn't that make YOU one of the cable-stealing jerks?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've never met a problem you couldn't worsen.

setting: The Boss's office, sitting across a desk
situation: Dilbert complains to the Boss that someone keeps swapping his good lab cables for bad ones, forcing him to spend hours stealing them back and testing each one. The Boss points out that this makes Dilbert one of the cable thieves himself. Dilbert responds by insulting the Boss's tendency to make problems worse.
punchline: The Boss's observation that Dilbert is also a cable thief is accurate, but Dilbert deflects the uncomfortable truth by sarcastically accusing the Boss of making every problem worse.
summary: After griping about cable thieves in the lab, Dilbert is told he is one of them and snaps back that the Boss only ever aggravates situations.

title: Immortal Mordac Gets Outsourced Prediction

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services, and I am immortal!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, in a few years your function will be either distributed across existing organizations or outsourced.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Well, that was a total buzzkill.

situation: Mordac, the head of IT security, stands over Dilbert at his computer and proudly declares himself immortal. Dilbert calmly points out that within a few years his department will likely be dissolved into other groups or outsourced. Mordac walks away deflated.
punchline: Mordac boasts of immortality, but Dilbert reminds him that his job, unlike his life, is far from permanent, since IT functions routinely get outsourced or absorbed.
summary: A boastful IT gatekeeper claims eternal life until a coworker predicts his department will soon be dispersed or sent to an outside vendor.

title: Salesman Offers Chair Assault Instead

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Salesman vs. Engineer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you offer us a discount?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I had something like that in mind, except instead of giving a discount, I would hit you with a chair and run away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't do that.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Okay, but I'll have to charge you extra.

setting: Sales meeting table in an office
situation: Dilbert, the engineer, asks a salesman across the table for a discount. The salesman responds that he was considering hitting Dilbert with a chair and running away instead. When Dilbert begs him not to, the salesman agrees but says he must charge extra for the favor.
punchline: The salesman turns not assaulting the customer into an upsell, treating the absence of violence as a premium feature that costs more.
summary: A salesman answers a request for a price break with a threat of violence, then bills extra for holding back.

file: 2013/2013-09-06_civil liberties_surveillance_lost data_company data_backups_governments secret database_recors_working fine.gif
title: Recovering Backups From Government Surveillance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We lost all of our company data and our backups, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I hacked into our government's secret database where they keep records of everything we say or do and got it all back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I feel as if I should be doing something now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nah. Everything is working fine.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the company lost all its data and backups. He then explains he hacked into the government's secret surveillance database, which records everything people say and do, and restored all the data from it. The Boss feels he ought to react or act, but Dilbert says everything is fine.
punchline: The government's mass surveillance database works as a flawless backup system, so the only thing the Boss can do is accept that the invasion of privacy has conveniently solved the problem.
summary: A lost-data crisis vanishes when an employee retrieves everything from the state's all-seeing records of citizens' activity.

title: Best Practices That Fit Like Gloves

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll teach you the best practices of companies that have nothing in common with yours.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Those practices will fit your company like a foot in a glove.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Close enough.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, offers the Boss best practices taken from companies that have nothing in common with his. He then garbles the idiom, saying they will fit like a foot in a glove. The Boss, now wearing a glove on his foot, thinks 'close enough' and accepts the advice.
punchline: The Boss is so undiscerning that he accepts irrelevant best practices and a mangled idiom without objection, mirroring how companies adopt mismatched management fads.
summary: A consultant dog sells a gullible executive advice borrowed from unrelated firms, and the executive happily accepts it despite the botched metaphor.

title: Likes Job, Hates Everything About It

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like my job. But I don't like any of the tasks... or any of the people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like the commute... and I'm paid less than I'm worth... and I'm not making the world a better place.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Are you sure you like your job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you ask?

setting: Grassy hilltop outdoors, near a cliff edge
situation: Dilbert stands on a grassy cliff talking with Ratbert and announces that he likes his job. He then lists a string of complaints about the tasks, the people, the commute, his pay, and the lack of meaningful impact. Ratbert asks if he is really sure he likes it, and Dilbert genuinely doesn't understand why he would ask.
punchline: Dilbert claims to like his job while listing every aspect of it he dislikes, and he is oblivious to the contradiction when Ratbert questions him.
summary: A man insists he is happy at work while cataloguing every single thing wrong with it, then puzzles over why anyone would doubt him.

file: 2013/2013-09-08_death & dying_negotiating_work ethic_raise_workload_incentive_work harder_disgruntled_no meaning_dreams lie broken.gif
title: Raise Offer Costs More Than It Pays

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you finish your project in twelve months, I'll give you a five percent raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would gladly give up five percent of my future pay to avoid a doubling of my workload.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't understand. I'm giving you an incentive to work harder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm pretty sure you're charging me five percent of my future pay to sit here and feel disgruntled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it's working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate you more than ever and I no longer find meaning in my work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My dreams lie broken and empty beneath the ruins of my optimism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're negotiating or dying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a little of both.

situation: The Boss offers Dilbert a five percent raise if he finishes his project in twelve months. Dilbert argues the offer is really a charge on his future pay that only makes him miserable, then announces it's working: he hates the Boss and has lost all meaning in his work. The Boss can't tell whether Dilbert is negotiating or dying.
punchline: Dilbert flips the incentive on its head, claiming the 'raise' is a fee for feeling disgruntled, and his despair is so complete that even the Boss can't tell whether he's bargaining or giving up on life.
summary: A boss's attempt to motivate with a small future raise instead drives his employee into theatrical despair.

file: 2013/2013-11-23_managers & supervisors_obliviousness_great leader_hires good people_no budget_micromanaging_half wits_afford_business.gif
title: Micromanaging the Half-Wits I Can Afford

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A great leader hires good people and gives them the freedom to do their jobs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I don't have the budget to hire good people. So I settle for micromanaging the half-wits I can afford.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your boss was just in here saying the same thing.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk and lectures Catbert, the red-furred human resources director, about what makes a great leader. He admits he can't afford good people, so he micromanages cheap, mediocre staff instead. Catbert replies that the Boss's own boss was just there saying the same thing about him.
punchline: The Boss's self-justifying excuse for micromanaging his staff applies equally to himself, since his own boss regards him as one of the half-wits he can afford.
summary: A manager blames his tight budget for micromanaging mediocre employees, only to be told his own superior says exactly the same about him.

title: Peers Hate Every Idea But Their Own

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to vet my idea with my peers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To save time, I am willing to stipulate that you hate all ideas that are not your own.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All in favor?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hate this idea, too.

situation: Dilbert stands before a group of seated coworkers, including Wally and Alice, and explains he has been asked to vet his idea with them. To save time he skips the discussion and assumes they hate every idea that isn't theirs, then calls for a vote. Alice confirms his assumption by saying she hates this idea too.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical shortcut around the peer review is proven right immediately, because his coworkers reflexively reject any idea that isn't their own.
summary: Expecting reflexive rejection from his colleagues, Dilbert tries to skip the idea review with a quick vote, and one of them promptly proves him right.

file: 2013/2013-10-22_choosing_stress_vacations_unlimited vacation days_torpedo career_source of stress_set up_manipulate.gif
title: Unlimited Vacation Is a Trap

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're jumping on the fad of giving employees unlimited vacation days.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The only gating factor will be the knowledge that taking any time off whatsoever will torpedo your career.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So... now our vacations will be a source of stress?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Only as much as you want. It's totally up to you.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces to Alice and Dilbert that the company is adopting unlimited vacation days. He then explains that the only limit is the knowledge that taking any time off will ruin your career. Alice points out that this makes vacations a source of stress, and Catbert cheerfully says it's entirely up to her.
punchline: Unlimited vacation is a sham perk because employees will fear career damage if they use it, so the policy costs the company nothing while Catbert pretends the stress is the employees' own choice.
summary: A malevolent HR chief unveils a limitless time-off policy whose real constraint is the career penalty for ever using it.

title: Boss Rewards Staffing Blunder With Head Pat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Boss
transcript.text: I read an article that says leaders should acknowledge the achievements of their underlings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you done anything lately that warrants some praise?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Well ... I'm under budget because I forgot to staff one of our projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I think I'm supposed to pat you on the head or something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's try that and see how we feel.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Stop leaning in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Feels ... so ... good.

situation: After reading an article about praising underlings, the boss asks an employee to name an achievement worth recognizing. The employee offers that he is under budget only because he forgot to staff a project, and the boss accepts this as good enough. The boss then awkwardly pats the employee's head and ends up enjoying it far too much.
punchline: The boss will praise any achievement, even an accidental one caused by negligence, and then obviously relishes the head pat far more than the employee does.
summary: A manager hunting for something to compliment settles on a budget saving that came from an oversight, then gets carried away with the reward ritual.

title: Evil Genius Replaces Marketing Department

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We replaced our entire marketing department with one evil genius.

transcript.speaker: Evil Genius
transcript.text: My optogenetic* technology can re-wire the neural pathways of our customers and change their preferences.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Already works on mice

transcript.speaker: Evil Genius
transcript.text: You like gray.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I like to be gay.

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that the marketing department has been replaced by a single evil genius. The genius explains his optogenetic device can rewire customers' brains to change their preferences, then zaps a coworker while saying he likes gray. The zapped coworker instead blurts out that he likes to be gay.
punchline: The mind-control device malfunctions on its first human test, producing a wildly different result than intended, showing that replacing marketing with a sketchy gadget is a bad idea.
summary: A mad scientist who took over a company's marketing duties tests his brain-rewiring ray on a coworker and gets an unintended outcome.

title: Leader in the Mold of Jobs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see myself as a leader in the mold of Steve Jobs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try rinsing your entire body with vinegar. That might remove his mold.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are we talking about the same thing?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please don't touch anything I own.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss announces that he sees himself as a leader in the mold of Steve Jobs. Alice deliberately misreads 'mold' as the fungus and suggests he rinse his whole body with vinegar to remove it. When he asks if they mean the same thing, she tells him not to touch anything she owns.
punchline: Alice plays on the double meaning of 'mold' to imply the Boss is not a visionary but a contaminant she wants nowhere near her belongings.
summary: A boss's grand self-comparison to a famous tech visionary is answered with a pointed pun about fungus and a warning to keep his hands off her things.

title: Price War Strategy From Executive Retreat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new strategy is to lower our prices to increase sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So our strategy is to start a price war and drive our profit margin to zero?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It made sense at the executive retreat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Was alcohol involved?

situation: The Boss announces to his team that the company's new strategy is to cut prices to boost sales. Dilbert points out that this amounts to starting a price war that will push profit margins to zero. The Boss defends it by saying it made sense at the executive retreat, and Alice asks whether alcohol was involved.
punchline: Alice implies that only drunken executives could come up with such a self-destructive strategy, and the Boss's excuse about the retreat makes that seem plausible.
summary: A manager unveils a ruinous discount plan born at a leadership getaway, and a skeptical coworker wonders if drinking explains it.

title: Revising Expectations Means They Were Faulty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to great leadership is setting clear expectations and periodically revising them as conditions change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you plan to revise expectations, that tells me you know them to be faulty now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Stop inspiring me so much.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss lectures about leadership, saying expectations should be set clearly and then revised as conditions change. Dilbert points out that planning to revise them implies the current expectations are already known to be flawed. The Boss weakly concedes, and a bald coworker sarcastically tells him to stop inspiring everyone.
punchline: The Boss's leadership advice accidentally admits that he knowingly sets flawed expectations, and the coworker's sarcastic remark underlines how uninspiring the advice really is.
summary: A manager's leadership maxim about adjusting goals gets undercut by an employee's pointed logic and a coworker's dry sarcasm.

title: Introvert Experiences Coworker As Furniture

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You claim to be an introvert and yet you never seem to be drained when you talk to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you don't put off a human vibe. I experience you the same way I experience birds, furniture, and robots.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You totally get me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't talk.

setting: Office, with both men holding coffee mugs
situation: A bald coworker in glasses points out that Dilbert says he is an introvert but never seems worn out when talking to him. Dilbert explains that he doesn't perceive the coworker as a human at all, but as something like a bird, furniture or a robot. The coworker takes this as a compliment and says Dilbert understands him, and Dilbert tells him to stop talking.
punchline: Dilbert's insult, that the coworker is so lacking in human presence that he is as draining as furniture, is taken as a compliment, and Dilbert then shuts down the conversation.
summary: An introvert reveals he feels no social fatigue around a colleague because he doesn't register him as a person, and the colleague happily misreads it as being understood.

title: Boss Punches Himself Before Billion-Dollar Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd you get the black eye?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was pulling up my blanket in bed. My hand slipped and I punched myself in the face.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, let's make some billion-dollar technology decisions.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss how he got a black eye, and the Boss explains that he accidentally punched himself in the face while pulling up his blanket in bed. Dilbert, having heard this clumsy explanation, immediately proposes they start making huge technology decisions together.
punchline: Dilbert's abrupt switch to billion-dollar technology decisions implies that a boss who injures himself with a blanket is exactly the kind of person who ends up controlling enormous IT budgets, and that those decisions will be made with that level of competence.
summary: After a manager admits his own bedtime clumsiness gave him a shiner, his employee casually moves on to spending billions on technology.

title: Kids Photo Is Strictly Business

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that a picture of your kids? No personal items are allowed in cubicles!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's not personal. My kids are only in it for the money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's more of a gray area than you'd think.

situation: The Boss spots a photo of an employee's kids in his cubicle and points out that personal items are banned. The employee claims the photo isn't personal because his kids are only in the picture for the money. The Boss, now holding a coffee mug and apparently conceding the point, muses that the rule is a gray area as Catbert sits on a desk nearby.
punchline: The employee cynically argues his kids are mercenary, making the photo a business matter rather than a personal one, and the Boss accepts the logic, showing how flimsy the rule is.
summary: A manager cracks down on family photos at work until an employee reframes his children as purely financially motivated, which somehow muddies the rule.

title: Dilbert's Egg Starts Liar Business

transcript.speaker: Egg figure
transcript.text: I'm starting a new business as a professional liar.

transcript.speaker: Egg figure
transcript.text: I'll provide alibis, job references, annual reports, and that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were you born evil?

transcript.speaker: Egg figure
transcript.text: It feels as if someone else had a hand in it.

characters: Egg figure (a small egg-shaped puppet-like character)
setting: Dilbert's bedroom, beside a dresser with a mirror
situation: While Dilbert gets dressed and puts on his tie, a small egg-shaped figure standing on the dresser announces it is starting a business as a professional liar, offering alibis, job references and annual reports. Dilbert asks if it was born evil. The mirror reveals a man's hand operating the egg like a puppet, and the egg says it feels like someone else had a hand in it.
punchline: The egg puppet's evil streak is literally the doing of its puppeteer, who has a hand inside it, so the puppet's 'someone else had a hand in it' is a pun on being manipulated.
summary: A hand puppet cheerfully announces plans to sell lies for a living, then blames its wickedness on the hand literally inside it.
keywords: someone had a hand in it

file: 2013/2013-10-20_dating_internet & world wide web_social media cosultant_one like_less than ten thousand_insulting_elbonian_inflate your like count_socialize_wine glasses_bar wine_kiss_relationships.gif

transcript.speaker: Woman

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're giving me ONE like?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Anything less than ten thousand likes is an insult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be right back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hired an Elbonian to artificially inflate your like count.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Like, like, like, like, like, like, like, like, like.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am not paying that guy.

setting: A bar or social gathering with wine glasses
situation: Dilbert meets a woman at a party who works as a social media consultant. When he tells her he likes her, she is insulted that it's only one like and demands ten thousand. Dilbert fetches an Elbonian to inflate her like count, and the Elbonian hugs her while repeating 'like'.
punchline: Dilbert literalizes the demand for likes by hiring an Elbonian who physically hugs her while chanting 'like', then decides he refuses to pay for it, cheaply dodging the cost of his own gesture.
summary: A woman who consults on social media scorns a single compliment, so a date hires a foreign worker to flood her with likes in person.

title: Good Sport Means Good Loser

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Thanks for being flexible in these negotiations. You're a good sport.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: And by good sport, I mean good loser.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: And by good loser, I mean loser.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Some people call it generous.

characters: Woman negotiator with large curly hair
Man in red shirt and tie
situation: A woman across the table thanks a man for being flexible in negotiations and calls him a good sport. She keeps revising her compliment until it becomes an outright insult, calling him a loser. He responds flatly that some people would call his concessions generous.
punchline: The negotiator's fake praise turns into open mockery of the man who gave in, and his deadpan reply reframes his weakness as generosity.
summary: After winning a negotiation, a woman progressively strips the politeness from her thanks until she is openly calling the other side a loser.

title: Two Trolls Build the Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet the two trolls who create our annual budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do we need two of them?

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: Because it's hard to reach into your own . . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! It's better to keep some mystery.

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting
situation: The Boss introduces two green, horned trolls as the people who create the company's annual budget. Dilbert asks why two are needed, and one troll begins to explain that it is hard to reach into your own... before the Boss cuts him off.
punchline: The troll's answer implies budget figures are pulled out of an orifice, i.e. made up, and the Boss hastily stops him because the mystery is more useful than admitting the numbers are fabricated.
summary: A manager presents a pair of monstrous trolls as the source of the company's yearly budget, and their crude explanation reveals how arbitrary the numbers really are.

title: Boss Emails Choking Tips to Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I traced all of our problems back to your lack of creativity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should be creating ideas that change the course of civilization, but instead, you sit there like a lump.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending you a link that describes fun ways to choke yourself.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and blames the company's problems on Dilbert's lack of creativity. He scolds Dilbert for sitting like a lump instead of changing civilization, then announces he is emailing him a link about fun ways to choke himself. Dilbert sits silently at his computer throughout.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at motivation turns into a callous, darkly absurd suggestion that Dilbert strangle himself, showing how abusive and out of touch he is.
summary: A boss berates his employee for not being world-changingly inventive, then cheerfully offers him self-strangulation tips online.

file: 2013/2013-11-06_computer software_frustration_internet & world wide web_syoe_shut down_quit_drown it.gif
title: Alice Can't Close Skype

transcript.text: Okay, Skype. Let's see if I can figure out how to shut you down.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Close! Quit! Sign out! Minimize! Quit! Yes! Close! Quit! Die! Die! Die!

transcript.text: Click click click click click

transcript.text: Did you close Skype?

transcript.speaker: Alice

situation: Alice sits at her computer calmly trying to shut down Skype, then becomes increasingly furious as it refuses to quit despite repeated clicking. Dilbert walks up with a coffee mug and asks if she closed it, and she says she is carrying her monitor off to drown it in the ocean.
punchline: Alice's rage at software that won't close escalates to the absurd plan of drowning her computer in the ocean, since she has failed to shut it down any normal way.
summary: A woman's battle with a stubborn video-chat program ends with her hauling her monitor away for a watery execution.

title: Avoiding Negative People, Spreading Negativity

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Experts say I should surround myself with people who are positive influences.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm on a call!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I think I absorbed some bad energy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Go away before you bum me out.

situation: Alice announces that experts advise surrounding yourself with positive influences, then angrily shouts at Asok that she is on a phone call. Shaken, Asok wanders over to Wally and says he absorbed some bad energy. Wally, drinking coffee, tells him to go away before he depresses him.
punchline: Everyone claims to want positive influences, yet Alice's hostility is passed along to Asok, who is then rejected by Wally for being a downer, showing that negativity just gets handed down the chain.
summary: A coworker pushes bad vibes onto the next person in line, and nobody is willing to be anyone's positive influence.

file: 2013/2013-08-25_natural disasters_disaster preparedness_famine_keyboard_crumbs_alene invasion_kill a coworker_lizard people_impending collison_asteroid_running in place_earth rotates_planet_hit by asteroid_human flesh_presentation is a disater.gif
title: Disaster Preparedness Presentation Is Itself Disaster

transcript.text: I've been asked to explain our disaster preparedness plan.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the event of famine, turn your keyboard upside down and shake.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If it's anything like mine, you'll find a pound and a half of crumbs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the event of an alien invasion, your best bet is to kill a co-worker to show your allegiance to the lizard-people.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the event of an impending collision with an asteroid, try running in place while the Earth rotates.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you time it right, you'll be on the other side of the planet when the asteroid hits.

transcript.text: To prepare for every other type of disaster, I recommend cultivating a taste for human flesh.

transcript.text: Your presentation is a disaster.

transcript.speaker: Wally

setting: Conference room during a slide presentation
situation: Wally presents the company's disaster preparedness plan to his colleagues, offering absurd and useless advice for famine, alien invasion, and asteroid strikes, ending with a recommendation to eat human flesh. The Boss tells him the presentation was a disaster.
punchline: Wally twists the boss's criticism into a lazy joke that the disaster has now prepared everyone for the next one, turning his useless presentation into an example of his own advice.
summary: A slacker coworker delivers a ridiculous emergency planning talk full of bad advice, then deflects his boss's negative review with a glib quip.

title: Winning Never Feels Like Winning

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got your stupid email with your stupid link to that stupid scientific study.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't care about your so-called "facts." I know I'm right!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Winning an argument never feels like winning.

situation: Dilbert has emailed Alice a link to a scientific study to support his side of an argument. Alice storms up to his cubicle, furious, and declares that she doesn't care about facts because she knows she is right. Dilbert sits quietly and reflects in a thought bubble.
punchline: Dilbert technically wins the argument with evidence, but facing someone who refuses to accept facts means the victory feels hollow and unsatisfying.
summary: A co-worker angrily brushes off the research sent to her, leaving the sender with a victory that brings no satisfaction.

title: Comforting Coworker Catastrophizes Presentation Fears

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm panicked about my presentation tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Relax. What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I could embarrass myself in a career-ending way.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh. I didn't think about that one.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It might be so bad that you can't even get a recommendation for a future job.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then you'd have an emotional meltdown followed by substance abuse, untreated health issues and a lonely death.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And it could all happen because of something as trivial as a typo on one of your slides.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I guess I can add "comforting" to my list of things I'm not good at.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a coffee mug that he is panicked about tomorrow's presentation. The coworker asks what the worst outcome could be, then builds on Dilbert's answer with an escalating chain of disasters ending in a lonely death. By the end Dilbert is visibly shaking and the coworker admits he is bad at comforting people.
punchline: The coworker's attempt to reassure Dilbert instead spirals into an absurdly dire worst-case scenario, and he deadpans that comforting is yet another thing he's not good at.
summary: A well-meaning colleague tries to calm a nervous presenter but only manages to convince him that one small mistake will lead to total ruin.

title: Ignoring Studies Against Brainstorming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wants to go first with the brainstorming?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I suggest we ignore all of the studies that say brainstorming doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I hate you a little extra.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because I agreed with your plan?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by asking who wants to start the brainstorming session. Dilbert raises his hand and suggests the team ignore all the studies showing that brainstorming is ineffective. The Boss responds that he now hates Dilbert a little extra, and Dilbert wryly asks if it's because he agreed with the Boss's plan.
punchline: Dilbert ironically "agrees" with the Boss by ignoring evidence that his plan is flawed, and the Boss resents him anyway, showing that managers dislike even sarcastic compliance that exposes their bad ideas.
summary: A manager's call for group idea generation is met with a deadpan proposal to disregard the research against it, which somehow irritates him even more.

file: 2013/2013-11-25_deception_sales personnel_linux_million dollars_pay for upgrade_away for free.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Free Linux Rights

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It sounds too good to be true.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's not as if I'm giving it away for free.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a salesman, pitches the Pointy-Haired Boss on buying the rights to use Linux for a million dollars, with further payments for every upgrade. The Boss, suspicious, says it sounds too good to be true. Dogbert replies that he is certainly not giving it away for free.
punchline: Linux is actually free, so Dogbert's reassurance that he's not giving it away for free is literally true only because he's scamming the Boss into paying for something that costs nothing.
summary: A scheming salesman dog charges a gullible manager a fortune for software that anyone can download at no cost.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Doesn't matter to me!

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Wally answers a phone call from a headhunter offering a better job, then explains to a coworker that he stages such calls to soften up the room before his performance review. In the boss's office, Wally admits he did nothing all year, and the boss simply doesn't care.
punchline: Wally's elaborate ploy to look in demand is pointless, because the boss is so indifferent that he doesn't care that Wally did nothing all year.
summary: A slacker stages a fake recruiter call to pad his review, only to find his manager is too apathetic to mind his lack of work.

setting: Outdoor grassy lawn that serves as the Elbonian embassy, with a table and chairs
situation: Dilbert is seeking asylum at the Elbonia embassy, which turns out to be a table on a lawn. The Elbonian host explains that their low-tech way of sending a message to the outside world is to carve it on a peanut and hand it to a squirrel. Dilbert points out that the squirrel would simply eat the peanut.
punchline: The Elbonian is amazed that Dilbert, quite reasonably, does not trust squirrels with a peanut, highlighting how absurdly primitive and unreliable Elbonian communication methods are.
summary: A host at a bare-bones embassy proposes a nut-and-rodent mail system, and is astonished that his guest doubts the rodent's honesty.

situation: At a meeting table, Dilbert reads from his phone about a story on the internet detailing the CEO's lavish lifestyle, including a yacht, a New York penthouse, an estate and priceless art. A colleague objects that it isn't the time, and the CEO retorts by pointing out that Dilbert wears a million-dollar watch.
punchline: The CEO deflects criticism of his extravagant wealth by accusing someone of equal extravagance, while the claim that Dilbert has a million-dollar watch implies the exchange is absurd or that Dilbert is being set up as a hypocrite.
summary: A subordinate teasingly reads out the details of a boss's opulent possessions from an online article, only to be shot down with an accusation of his own supposed wealth.

title: Promoting From Within, Repeatedly

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces the company policy is to promote from within. Dilbert asks how the vacated jobs will be backfilled, and the Boss answers 'from within' again. Dilbert sarcastically calls it one of the Boss's better plans.
punchline: The Boss's plan to fill every vacancy by promoting internally is circular and can never actually add staff, and Dilbert's praise of it as 'one of your better plans' is sarcasm that implies the Boss's other plans are even worse.
summary: A manager's staffing strategy turns out to be a loop with no end, which a sarcastic engineer compliments anyway.

summary: A captive engineer's lonely lifestyle turns his interrogation into a treat that unnerves the very agents sent to break him.

punchline: The Boss only wants admiration for his shallow platitudes and cuts off any question that exposes the gaps in his wisdom.
summary: A manager craves an audience for his tidy business maxims, but shuts down his employees the moment one asks a question he can't answer.

punchline: After Dilbert angrily screams at the ignorant salesman, his phone is flung out of the building window and the call still cheerfully offers a customer satisfaction survey.
summary: A salesman guarantees compatibility with a system he knows nothing about, and the argument ends with an absurdly cheerful survey prompt after the phone goes flying out a window.

summary: After slipping back into government computers thanks to unchanged passwords, Dilbert wipes his own record and then rewards a coworker by putting his face on the penny.

summary: A manager replaces his rounds of the office with a homemade hydrogen airship, which predictably meets a fiery end and leaves a coworker holding the remote.

punchline: The boss is so quick to dismiss criticism of the idea that he accepts the peers' judgment as worthless without noticing that Dilbert is also insulting him, and Dilbert's 'Exactly' shows he has cleverly turned the boss's own vanity against the feedback.
summary: Dilbert gets his unpopular idea past the boss by pointing out that the dissenting coworkers also dislike the boss, so their opinion can't be trusted.

title: Passion Advice Triggers Mass Resignation

title: Marketing Outpaces Worsening Products, Raises Follow

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our products are getting worse every day.

transcript.text: But our marketing keeps improving. We're very close to the point where our customers will give us money for no reason.

setting: Executive office or meeting room, seated across a desk
situation: The Boss tells a fellow executive that the company's products keep getting worse while its marketing keeps getting better. He predicts customers will soon pay for nothing, letting the executives award themselves big raises and stop working. The other executive agrees with the plan but objects to being included in it.
punchline: Even the greedy executive wants all the money and none of the sharing, so he approves of the scheme except for splitting it with anyone else.
summary: Two executives gleefully plot to get rich on slick advertising for shoddy goods, until one of them realises he'd rather keep the loot to himself.

title: Napkin Used as Handkerchief

transcript.text: Etiquette training

transcript.text: The napkin goes in your lap.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: HONK

transcript.text: It's not a handkerchief!

transcript.text: It sort of is.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: HONK

setting: A dining table during an etiquette training class
situation: An etiquette instructor tells two trainees that a napkin belongs in the lap. Dilbert immediately blows his nose loudly into his napkin, and the instructor scolds him that it is not a handkerchief. Dilbert replies that it sort of is, while the woman next to him honks into her own napkin too.
punchline: The trainees treat the napkin as a handkerchief right after being told not to, showing the training has no effect on people's habits.
summary: Two students ignore a manners lesson by loudly blowing their noses into their dinner napkins, defending it as practical.

title: Trash Can Helmet Wins Bet

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Our competitors have a technology for reading brain waves at a distance.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: This shielded helmet will prevent them from reading the company secrets in your mind.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You owe me $20.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The bet was that he has to wear the trash can for a week.

situation: A bald coworker warns the Boss that competitors can read brain waves from a distance and hands him a 'shielded helmet' to protect company secrets. The helmet is really a trash can, which the Boss puts on his head. Afterward the coworker collects $20 from Dilbert, because the bet was whether the Boss could be made to wear the trash can for a week.
punchline: The brain-reading threat and shielded helmet were a made-up ruse to trick the gullible Boss into wearing a trash can on his head, all to win a bet.
summary: Two employees con their credulous manager into wearing a garbage can as protective headgear and settle a wager over it.

title: Wally Likes Alice's Grim Weekend

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How was your weekend?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wrapped myself in a blanket and stayed on the couch watching bad TV shows until I smelled like a gym sock with halitosis.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I like how she makes me feel.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks Alice how her weekend went. She bluntly describes spending it in a blanket on the couch watching bad TV until she smelled terrible. In a thought bubble, Wally reveals he is oddly pleased by her answer.
punchline: Wally enjoys Alice's disgusting, self-loathing weekend story because it makes his own lazy, slovenly lifestyle feel normal and acceptable.
summary: A routine weekend-small-talk question gets a gloriously gross answer that secretly makes a co-worker feel better about himself.

title: Apathy Is Awesome, Says Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The government arrested Dilbert for stealing back the data their spy software stole from us.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Whose side are we on?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, I'm not crazy about the government.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But Dilbert can be a pain in the spanx, too.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Have you ever tried apathy? It's awesome.

situation: A bald coworker with glasses, holding a coffee mug, tells Alice that the government arrested Dilbert for retrieving data that government spy software had taken from the company. Alice asks which side they should take, and after weighing both, the coworker recommends simply not caring.
punchline: Faced with a choice between a spying government and an annoying colleague, the coworker dodges the dilemma by recommending apathy as the easiest, most pleasant option.
summary: When a colleague is arrested over a data-spying dispute with the government, two coworkers decide that not caring beats picking a side.

title: Ted's Two-Day Code Was Hard

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to recognize Ted for writing his part of the code in just two days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many days was it supposed to take?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At least a week, I would think.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why would you think that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because it was so hard to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who told you it was hard?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Ted did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All he did was delete some lines from existing code and recompile it.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: It was hard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have any more crazy conspiracy theories?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss praises Ted in a meeting for finishing his portion of the code in two days, and admits he expected it to take a week because it must be hard. Dilbert asks who said it was hard, and the only source turns out to be Ted himself. Dilbert points out Ted merely deleted some lines and recompiled, but Ted insists it was hard and the Boss takes his side.
punchline: The Boss's belief that the task was difficult rests solely on Ted's own claim, so Dilbert's accurate debunking is dismissed and even labeled a conspiracy theory.
summary: A manager lavishes credit on a coworker for a supposedly difficult task whose difficulty is vouched for only by the coworker himself, and brushes off the colleague who exposes how trivial it was.

title: Learning Meetings Are Wasteful In Meeting

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm happy to report that I spent 50% more time in meetings this quarter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not an accomplishment! Meetings are a complete waste of time!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How would I have learned that without this meeting?

situation: An employee sits across the desk from The Boss and proudly reports that he spent 50% more time in meetings this quarter. The Boss scolds him, declaring meetings a complete waste of time. The employee replies that he only learned that fact because of this very meeting.
punchline: The employee's sarcastic reply points out that The Boss is delivering his lecture about wasted time in yet another meeting, which proves the point and exposes the hypocrisy.
summary: A worker brags about attending more meetings, and when his superior condemns them, he drily notes that only the current meeting taught him so.

file: 2013/2013-10-23_engineers_vacations_work ethic_unlimited vacation policy_200 days off_double productivity_no way to measure.gif
title: Unlimited Vacation, Unmeasurable Productivity

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm planning to take advantage of our new unlimited vacation policy. I'll be gone for two hundred days in the coming year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I guarantee I will still double my productivity compared to the prior year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no way to measure productivity for engineers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good to know.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells The Boss he will use the new unlimited vacation policy to take two hundred days off next year. He promises to still double his productivity. The Boss replies that engineer productivity cannot be measured, and Wally takes that as a green light.
punchline: Since the boss admits engineer productivity can't be measured, Wally's promise can never be checked, so he can take nearly the whole year off with no consequences.
summary: A lazy engineer exploits a lenient vacation policy and his manager's own admission that his output can't be tracked.

title: Boss's Own Phone Rings

situation: The Boss opens a meeting by threatening to fire anyone whose phone rings. A phone then rings, and the Boss pointedly stares at Dilbert, who tells him to stop judging him with his eyes. The Boss replies that staring is the only thing keeping his eyes open.
punchline: The Boss's sarcastic reply suggests he is so bored and drowsy in his own meeting that glaring at someone is the only way he stays awake.
summary: A manager's stern warning about ringing phones is undercut when someone's phone goes off and his accusing stare turns out to be mere sleepiness.

title: Flermming the Plootash Obediently

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What makes you this way?

setting: Office, in front of the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he received a nonsensical note left on his desk. He then claims he carried out the gibberish instruction exactly as requested. When the Boss asks why Dilbert is like this, Dilbert replies with a nonsense-based insult.
punchline: Dilbert uses the Boss's meaningless note to mock him by pretending to comply, then insults the Boss's strange behavior by saying his own DNA is 'flermmed'.
summary: A worker responds to a gibberish memo from his manager by feigning perfect compliance and then blaming his genes when questioned.

title: Project Delayed Only for Dumb People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is your project taking longer than expected?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's only taking longer than dumb people expected.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Still, that's a lot of people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What can I say to make this conversation end?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why his project is behind schedule. Dilbert replies that it is only late relative to the expectations of dumb people, and the Boss responds that there are still plenty of such people. Dilbert, stuck at his computer, wonders how to end the conversation.
punchline: Dilbert insults everyone's expectations by implying the schedule was only unrealistic to the foolish, and the Boss's reply that this is still a lot of people shows he gets the dig but misses the point, leaving Dilbert desperate to escape.
summary: Dilbert blames a late project on the unrealistic expectations of fools, and the Boss merely notes that fools are plentiful.

title: Promotion Depends on Your Effectiveness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When the managers meet to talk about promotions, I'll fight for you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you saying my future depends on YOUR effectiveness and not MINE?

transcript.text: This went differently than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why?! Why?! Why?!

situation: The Boss offers to fight for Alice when the managers meet to discuss promotions, expecting her to be grateful. Alice points out that this means her career depends on his effectiveness rather than her own. Realizing the implication, she screams in despair while the Boss remarks that this went differently than he expected.
punchline: The Boss's well-meant promise to advocate for Alice actually highlights that her promotion hinges on his notorious incompetence, which leaves her screaming in horror.
summary: A boss promises to champion his employee for a promotion, and she realizes with dread that her fate now rests in his hopelessly unreliable hands.

title: It Takes Money to Waste Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It takes money to make money.

transcript.text: I'm pretty sure it takes money to waste money, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please stop talking!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss offers the cliche that it takes money to make money. Dilbert asks where the very first money came from, and Wally adds that it also takes money to waste money. The flustered Boss begs them to stop talking.
punchline: The Boss's tired business cliche is picked apart by logic, and Wally's remark implies the company is wasting money, so the Boss shuts down the discussion.
summary: A manager's folksy money maxim gets dismantled by his employees' pointed questions until he pleads for silence.

The coworker confronts him about ignoring his messages for six months, and Dilbert admits it was only a week, then claims he expected the coworker to die from his own incompetence in a workplace accident. The coworker then reveals he was the one trying to avoid the conversation.
punchline: Dilbert insults the coworker's competence by predicting his accidental death, but the coworker turns the tables by revealing he was the one trying to avoid talking to Dilbert.
summary: A man Dilbert has been dodging confronts him, and after an insulting excuse about expecting him to die on the job, the man says he wanted to avoid the chat all along.

title: Peer Coaching Turns Into Insults

punchline: Dilbert's honest question was the genuinely insightful one, and Alice's violent reaction proves his point, while he obliviously treats her abuse as part of the coaching exercise.
summary: A coworker's attempt at a fashionable coaching exercise collapses when her partner's candid observation about her makes her lash out at him.

title: Executive Coaching: Be a Psychopath

situation: Dogbert is acting as an executive coach and tells the Boss that CEOs are disproportionately psychopaths, so the trait must be useful. He then asks the Boss about his grandiose sense of self-worth, and the Boss angrily answers that it's the best and he should kill Dogbert for asking.
punchline: The Boss proves himself a model psychopath by threatening to kill his coach for asking a routine question, showing he has absorbed the coaching advice a little too well.
summary: A canine coach persuades his employer that ruthless, narcissistic psychopathy is a career asset, and the employer immediately demonstrates it with a murderous threat.

punchline: Wally twists a scientific finding into a convenient excuse for his laziness, implying his genes make expertise so unattainable that effort is pointless.
summary: A discussion of how long it takes to master a skill gives the office slacker a perfect excuse for doing nothing.

punchline: Dilbert's claim that an introvert can be literally drained by being near people is exaggerated to the point of physical paralysis, implying her company is both insulting and genuinely debilitating to him.
summary: A coworker's concern for a pale colleague backfires when he blames her very presence for sapping his strength to the point of numbness.

summary: A manager pins the blame for his flopped projects on the person who staffed them and hints that guilt should be punishment enough.
