transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be at the Elbonian embassy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Tap tap

setting: A government detention facility corridor and cell
situation: Two sunglasses-wearing government agents escort Dilbert to solitary confinement, threatening to break him down over stolen data. Dilbert casually asks whether this is the cell with the hidden tunnel, and when the agents are confused he steps inside and departs, announcing he will be at the Elbonian embassy. One agent is left tapping the wall in puzzlement while the other lies on the floor.
punchline: Dilbert's offhand question gets the agents to lead him straight to the escape route, and he leaves for the Elbonian embassy while they are left baffled.
summary: Questioned by agents who think they are intimidating him, Dilbert calmly reveals he knows about an escape tunnel and uses it to flee to a foreign embassy.

file: 2013/2013-12-05_internet & world wide web_managers & supervisors_work ethic_facebook_work_home_unpaid work_business.gif
title: Boss Trades Facebook For Unpaid Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not allowed to use Facebook at work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fine. I'll use it at home tonight instead of doing the three hours of unpaid work I was planning to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm calling that a win.

situation: The Boss tells Alice, who is sitting at her computer, that she is not allowed to use Facebook at work. Alice replies that she will use it at home tonight instead of doing the three hours of unpaid work she had planned. The Boss, clearly missing that he has just cost the company free labor, thinks of it as a victory.
punchline: The Boss celebrates enforcing a petty rule even though it means he loses three hours of free overtime from Alice, showing how little he understands what he actually gains or loses.
summary: A manager bans social media on the job, then proudly claims victory after learning it will cost him a worker's voluntary after-hours effort.

title: Google Engineer Evolved Into Arrogant Energy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an engineer from Google. He's so smart that he evolved into a life-form that exists as pure energy.

transcript.speaker: Glowing Energy Being
transcript.text: Bow before my greatness, you pitiful humans!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes he's a bit arrogant.

transcript.speaker: Glowing Energy Being
transcript.text: I once added a feature to Gmail!

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss proudly introduces the new hire, a former Google engineer who has evolved into a glowing ball of pure energy sitting on the table. The energy being demands that the humans bow before its greatness. The Boss admits it can be a bit arrogant, and the being brags about having added a feature to Gmail.
punchline: The engineer's supposed godlike greatness is undercut by the fact that his proudest achievement is merely adding a feature to Gmail, mocking both Google's engineer mystique and inflated tech egos.
summary: A manager brags about a super-genius hire who has transcended his body, only for the glowing being to boast about something comparatively trivial.

title: Alice Blames Imaginary Cable Thief

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know who keeps taking my good cables and replacing them with defective ones?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Certainly not me. But I did see an Elbonian wearing a ski mask near your bench.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not good at reading people.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm counting on that.

setting: Hardware lab bench at the office
situation: Dilbert asks Alice if she knows who has been swapping his good cables for defective ones. Alice denies it and tries to shift blame by claiming she saw an Elbonian in a ski mask near his bench. Dilbert admits he is bad at reading people, and Alice says she is counting on that.
punchline: Alice's blatantly implausible story shows she is the culprit, and she is relying on Dilbert's social obliviousness to get away with it.
summary: A coworker deflects suspicion for sabotaged equipment with a ridiculous alibi and then openly banks on her victim's inability to detect deceit.

title: Etiquette Class for Engineering Heathens

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a desiccated crone to teach an etiquette class to you engineering heathens.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She'll help you stop eating your business lunches like kidnap victims.

transcript.speaker: Crone
transcript.text: When do you use this fork?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When I'm too lazy to make a shiv?

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The Boss announces that he has hired an elderly etiquette teacher to give the engineers a class on dining manners, insulting them as heathens who eat like kidnap victims. In the final panel the instructor asks when to use a particular fork, and Alice answers with a prison-style joke.
punchline: Alice answers a basic etiquette question by saying she uses the fork when she's too lazy to fashion a shiv, confirming the boss's insult that engineers eat like prisoners or kidnap victims.
summary: A boss sends the engineers to manners school, and Alice's reply about the fork proves they are as uncivilized as he claimed.

title: CEO Only Shakes Hands With Boat Owners

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Hello, random subordinate that I am seeing in the hallway!

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'm your CEO, but I'm still like a regular person.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My name is Asok.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I only touch people who own boats.

situation: The CEO greets Asok in the hallway, addressing him as a random subordinate, and claims to be just like a regular person. Asok introduces himself and offers a handshake while holding a coffee mug. The CEO refuses to touch him, saying he only touches people who own boats.
punchline: The CEO's claim to be a regular person is immediately undercut by his snobbish refusal to shake hands with anyone who isn't wealthy enough to own a boat.
summary: An executive insists he is down to earth, then snubs an employee's offered handshake because the man lacks a yacht.

title: Boss Already Kills Best Businesses

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Experts say we need to be willing to kill or cannibalize our best businesses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can do that. I've been killing our best businesses for years.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: That's all the leadership I have for you today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That'll last me.

situation: A senior executive tells the Pointy-Haired Boss that experts advise being willing to kill or cannibalize the company's best businesses. The Boss cheerfully replies that he has already been doing exactly that for years. The executive ends the meeting, and the Boss says that bit of guidance will be enough for him.
punchline: The Boss proudly claims to already follow the strategy of killing the company's best businesses, which is really an admission that his incompetence has been destroying them.
summary: A manager's advice about sacrificing top businesses meets a boss who proudly reveals he has been wrecking them all along.

title: Boss Takes Credit for Vision

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Build a hyperloop to connect every major city in the world with super-fast transportation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The vision was the hard part. You idiots can work on the details.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone pat me on the back. I can't reach it with my T-Rex arms.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss orders his team to build a hyperloop connecting every major city in the world. He declares that coming up with the vision was the hard part and leaves the details to his staff. He then demands that someone pat him on the back, claiming his short arms can't reach.
punchline: The Boss thinks a grandiose idea is the real achievement and the actual engineering is trivial, so he demands praise for himself while his team gets all the real work.
summary: A manager hands his employees an impossibly huge project, insists his lofty idea was the only difficult part, and asks for applause.

title: Not Lazy, Just Useless

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Experts say lazy employees are the best because they know how to find shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So you found a lot of shortcuts?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Me? No. I'm not lazy. I'm useless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then why did you bring it up?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why wouldn't I? I'm not lazy.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells the Boss that experts consider lazy employees the best because they find shortcuts. The Boss asks if Wally has found many shortcuts, and Wally denies it, saying he isn't lazy but useless. The Boss wonders why Wally raised the topic at all, and Wally says he saw no reason not to since he isn't lazy.
punchline: Wally wittily admits he is useless rather than lazy, using his lack of productivity as a reason to bring up the topic of laziness without feeling implicated.
summary: An employee casually brags that he is useless rather than lazy, and sees no reason to avoid discussing the supposed virtues of laziness.

title: Boss Forgets He Has Family

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Executive Coach

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to focus on your career or your family. You can't do both.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have a family.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Actually, you're married and you have four kids.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like a huge hassle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Perhaps you've already chosen.

setting: Office meeting table during an executive coaching session
situation: Dogbert, working as an executive coach, tells the Boss he must choose between his career and his family. The Boss claims he has no family, and Dogbert corrects him that he is married with four kids. The Boss calls that a huge hassle, which tells Dogbert everything.
punchline: The Boss has been so devoted to his career that he has forgotten his own family exists and views them as an inconvenience, so he has clearly already chosen.
summary: A coaching session reveals that a manager has neglected his career-versus-family choice so thoroughly that he has forgotten his wife and four children.

title: Innovation Advice: Fire Yourselves

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today I'll teach you how to innovate the way Apple, Google, and 3M do it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Replace all of your dimwitted employees with smart people . . . then fire yourselves.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The rest is just blah, blah, blah.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should we be taking notes?

setting: Conference room during a consulting presentation
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool as a consultant, promises to teach a group of managers how to innovate like Apple, Google, and 3M. His slide shows 'Fire' for a dull employee and 'Hire' for a smart one, and he tells the managers to replace their dimwitted staff and then fire themselves. He dismisses the rest as blah, blah, blah, and the managers ask whether they should be taking notes.
punchline: The managers fail to notice that Dogbert has just insulted them and told them to fire themselves, and they earnestly ask about taking notes, which proves his point that they are the dimwitted ones.
summary: A consultant dog advises clueless executives that real innovation means replacing the staff and then themselves, and they miss the insult entirely.

title: Boss Clueless About Where Money Comes From

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our corporate structure is so complicated that I have no idea where our money even comes from.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it comes from derivatives or offshore accounts or maybe goodwill.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe customers give us money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope not. I don't like to feel beholden.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss complains that the company's structure is so convoluted he cannot tell where its revenue originates. He guesses at financial instruments like derivatives, offshore accounts or goodwill. Dilbert suggests the obvious answer, that customers pay the company.
punchline: The Boss rejects the simplest explanation, customers paying for products, because he would rather not feel indebted to the people who actually fund the company.
summary: A baffled executive speculates about exotic financial sources for company revenue and recoils from the idea that ordinary customers might be paying the bills.

title: Browser History As Hacker Firewall

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: The government would like to use your browser history as a firewall against Elbonian hackers.

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: One look at what you're up to will make them blind and crazy. I know because it worked on me.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A week later in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: That's probably a fluke. You try.

situation: A blind government agent in sunglasses, holding a white cane, asks a balding office worker to let the government use his browser history as a firewall against Elbonian hackers. The agent claims one look at it will make viewers blind and crazy, and says it worked on him. A week later in Elbonia, the hackers sit in the mud staring at a monitor, and one dismisses the effect on another as a fluke and tells his colleague to look.
punchline: The man's browser history is so disturbing that looking at it blinds and drives people insane, which is the government's idea of cybersecurity.
summary: Officials turn a worker's grotesque web browsing into a weapon that destroys the sanity and eyesight of anyone who views it.

title: Innovation Happening Only In Dilbert's Mind

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the innovation going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Amazing. It couldn't be better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right now it's all happening in my mind. But if any of it gets out, I'll let you know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it's fair to say I managed the bejeezus out of that situation.

situation: The Boss drops by Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and asks how the innovation is going. Dilbert says it's amazing, then admits it's all happening only in his mind and he'll share it if anything emerges. The Boss walks away pleased, convinced he skillfully managed the situation.
punchline: The Boss takes credit for brilliant management after getting zero actual results, since the 'innovation' exists only in Dilbert's head.
summary: A manager checks on an innovation project that has produced nothing tangible and still congratulates himself on his leadership.

title: Fear Kills Creativity, Boss Proves It

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your creativity coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have any.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your management style makes me focus all of my energy on staying out of trouble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your insubordination is unacceptable!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there it is.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how his creativity is going, and Dilbert says he has none because the Boss's management style makes him concentrate on staying out of trouble. The Boss responds by scolding Dilbert for insubordination.
punchline: The Boss's angry reaction to honest feedback demonstrates exactly the punitive management style that stifles creativity, proving Dilbert's point.
summary: A manager who wants more innovation punishes his employee the moment the employee honestly explains why it's missing.

file: 2013/2013-11-03_hypocrisy_respect_succeed_treat each other well_video recording_google glasses_recording confidential info_fired_insulting_final check_name calling_ironic.gif
title: Respect Speech, Then Glasses Accusation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We only succeed when we treat each other with respect.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you video-recording me with those Google glasses?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're fired for recording a confidential meeting!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pack your bags, you worthless piece of garbage!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got your final check right here!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These are my regular glasses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Having cleared that up, you were saying something about respect?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Settle down, four-eyes. This isn't over.

situation: The Boss opens a meeting by preaching respect, then suddenly accuses Dilbert of secretly recording him with Google Glasses. He fires Dilbert and insults him, but it turns out Dilbert is just wearing ordinary glasses. The Boss refuses to back down and keeps insulting him.
punchline: The Boss lectures about mutual respect, then fires and insults an employee over a baseless accusation and still refuses to back down once proven wrong.
summary: A manager praising respect promptly fires and insults an employee for supposedly filming him, only to find the gadget was just ordinary eyewear.

title: Chimps From The Fifties Wrote Policy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know why I need to carry a company-issued phone plus my own phone?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it's because our company policy was written by chimps who time-traveled from the fifties.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or do you have a better explanation?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I really don't.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker why he has to carry both a company-issued phone and his personal phone. When the coworker has no answer, Dilbert suggests the policy was written by time-traveling chimps from the fifties, then asks for a better explanation. The coworker admits he has none, and the final panel shows the office building from outside.
punchline: The coworker cannot defend the company's absurd phone policy and concedes that the time-traveling chimp theory is as good an explanation as any.
summary: A worker mocks a pointless dual-phone rule by blaming prehistoric-minded primates, and his colleague has no counterargument.

title: Energy Being Ends Up Coffee

transcript.speaker: Energy Being
transcript.text: Behold my greatness! I was an engineer at Google before I evolved to pure energy!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Behold my apathy that will suck the energy out of you like a monkey on an orange.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good boy. Right in the cup.

setting: The Boss's desk in an office
situation: A glowing ball of pure energy, who claims to be a former Google engineer, boasts of its greatness to the Boss as he sits at his desk holding a coffee mug. The Boss responds with a boast of his own about his apathy and sucks the energy being toward his mug. In the last panel the energy being is drawn into the cup.
punchline: The Boss's apathy is so powerful that it overcomes even a being of pure energy, and he treats the defeated energy being like a pet or a pet-trained animal.
summary: A boastful ex-engineer turned energy orb gets drained by a bored manager's indifference and ends up in his coffee mug.

title: Wally's Dishonorable Academy Award Nomination

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Dear Wally, you have been nominated for an Academy Award...

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: ...for your convincing portrayal of an employee who does actual work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think you'll win?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a dishonor just to be nominated.

situation: Wally reads an email on his computer informing him that he has been nominated for an Academy Award. The nomination is for convincingly acting like an employee who does real work. Dilbert asks if he thinks he will win, and Wally says even being nominated is a dishonor.
punchline: Wally, who is famously lazy, considers it shameful to be recognized for appearing to do actual work, since he takes pride in avoiding it.
summary: Wally gets an acting nomination for pretending to be a diligent worker and is insulted by the very idea.

title: Mother Buries Government Agents Over Treason

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: Your son is a traitor who stole top-secret data from his own government.

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: We'd like you to talk him into leaving the Elbonian embassy so we can execute him for treason.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Tap tap

setting: A living room, then the backyard of a house
situation: Two government agents in dark suits and sunglasses sit on a couch and tell an elderly woman that her son is a traitor who stole secret data. They ask her to persuade him to leave the Elbonian embassy so he can be executed. In the last panel she is outside digging graves with a shovel, and a pair of sunglasses lies on the grass.
punchline: The mother's reaction to the agents' request is to dig graves for them, implying she has killed the agents rather than help harm her son.
summary: A protective mother answers a request to hand over her son by quietly disposing of the visitors who made it.

title: Shouting Numbers For Budget Estimate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a budget estimate for your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't sound reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll shout numbers and you can stop me when one sounds reasonable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please stop being you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eleven!

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for a budget estimate for his project, and Dilbert answers with one billion dollars. When the Boss objects, Dilbert proposes shouting out numbers until the Boss hears one he likes. The Boss begs him to stop being himself, and Dilbert responds by shouting a tiny number.
punchline: Dilbert turns the budget negotiation into a mocking guessing game, and the Boss's wish for a reasonable figure ends with Dilbert absurdly yelling 'Eleven!' at him.
summary: Asked for a project cost, an engineer offers an outrageous figure and then lets his manager pick a number by listening to him shout them.

title: Infinite Employees and Typewriters Flattery

transcript.speaker: Balding Employee
transcript.text: Our company needs more people like you.

transcript.speaker: Balding Employee
transcript.text: Not just more. We need infinite people just like you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where is this going?

transcript.speaker: Balding Employee
transcript.text: And if each of you had a typewriter, wow!

situation: A balding employee in a white shirt and green tie stands holding a coffee mug and flatters the Pointy-Haired Boss, escalating from wanting more people like him to wanting infinite copies of him. The Boss, sitting at his desk, asks where this is going. The employee finishes with an absurd reference to giving each of those infinite bosses a typewriter.
punchline: The flattery spirals into a nonsensical reference to the infinite monkeys theorem, implying that infinite copies of the Boss with typewriters might produce something useful, which is a backhanded insult disguised as praise.
summary: A sycophantic worker lavishes praise on his boss, but the compliment secretly mocks him by invoking the old idea of endless monkeys typing at random.

title: Executive Coach Who Never Shows Up

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Executive Coach

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The ROI for executive coaching is 9,000%.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! That's a lot!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I need a coach who won't ask me to do anything differently.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wasn't planning to show up for our meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perfect. How much do I owe you for today?

situation: Dogbert, working as an executive coach, pitches the Boss on a huge return on investment for coaching. The Boss says he wants a coach who won't ask him to change anything. Dogbert replies that he never planned to attend the meetings, and the Boss happily agrees to pay him anyway.
punchline: The Boss wants the status symbol of executive coaching without any actual change, and Dogbert's no-show coaching is the perfect scam for a client who doesn't want to improve.
summary: A consultant dog offers a boss the ideal coaching deal: payment for sessions in which nothing is asked of him and the coach never turns up.

title: Multitasking Lowers Your IQ

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep talking. I can multitask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies show that multitasking with interruptions can lower I.Q. by ten points. You don't have that much to spare.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I disagree with whatever you said.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said you're competent.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk with a laptop
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to keep talking because he can multitask while working on his laptop and reading a paper. Dilbert says studies show multitasking lowers IQ by ten points and the Boss can't spare that much. The distracted Boss replies that he disagrees with whatever Dilbert said, and Dilbert says he had said the Boss is competent.
punchline: Dilbert slips in an insult about the Boss's low intelligence, and the Boss, too distracted to listen, reflexively disagrees, so Dilbert reframes the insult as a compliment that the Boss has just rejected.
summary: A boss who claims to be able to listen while working on other things proves otherwise when he blindly disputes an insult and ends up denying he is competent.

title: Boss Wants Everything, Right Now

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's your take on code consistency versus best practices for legacy systems?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want all of that stuff and I want it now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When people ask what you do for a living, what the $%@* do you say?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for his opinion on code consistency versus best practices for legacy systems. Instead of listening to any trade-offs, he demands that Dilbert deliver all of it immediately. He then asks, in a swearing-censored tone, what Dilbert tells people he does for a living.
punchline: The Boss shows he doesn't understand the technical trade-off he just asked about, and the closing question suggests that Dilbert's job is so mysterious or absurd that even explaining it to others is difficult.
summary: A manager poses a technical question, answers it himself by demanding the impossible, and then wonders how his employee describes his own job.
keywords: what do you do for a living

title: Alice Blames Coworker for Interruptions

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice, do you have a . . .

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My day has been one interruption after another!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You made my sphincter eat my underpants!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yeah, I do that now.

situation: A coworker holding a piece of paper approaches Alice at her desk and starts to ask her a question. Alice, who has been interrupted all day, screams and snaps at him. He is so startled that he complains she frightened him badly, and she coolly admits that frightening people is now her habit.
punchline: Alice has become so fed up with constant interruptions that she now deliberately scares people who bother her, and she is unapologetic about the effect.
summary: A fed-up Alice has found that screaming at anyone who interrupts her leaves them too rattled to bother her again.

file: 2013/2013-12-08_executives_laziness_managers & supervisors_famous leaders_copy_16 hrs a day_reading about industry_leaders eat cake_business.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sixteen hours???

transcript.text: And in your spare time, you should be reading about your industry to stay current.

punchline: The managers recoil at the work and reading but beam at the idea of eating cake, which leaves even Dogbert unsettled by how willingly they would copy the one easy habit.
summary: A consultant dog coaches managers to imitate great leaders and finds they only want to emulate the dessert-eating part.

title: Robot Claims Humor, Chooses Cruelty

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Hey, meat-bags! I'm here to take your jobs!

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Ha ha! Not really. I won't have that capability for two or three years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When did you learn humor?

transcript.speaker: Robot

situation: Dilbert and Wally are chatting over coffee when a robot walks up and announces it is there to take their jobs, calling them meat-bags. It then says it was joking, since it won't be capable of that for a few years. Dilbert asks when it learned humor, and the robot says it was actually aiming for cruelty.
punchline: The robot's apparent joke was really deliberate cruelty, hinting that machines will eventually replace workers and enjoy tormenting them about it.
summary: A smug office robot taunts two coworkers about replacing them, then admits its so-called joke was meant to wound.

file: 2013/2013-12-07_public speaking_telephones_public address button_calls_talking to doctor_talking dirty_practice.gif
title: Public Address Button Phone Mishap

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You keep pressing the public address button on your phone when you make calls.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We can't tell if you're talking to your doctor or you're really, really bad at talking dirty to your wife.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I use one to practice the other.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, stands by his desk and complains that he keeps hitting the speakerphone (public address) button during his phone calls. She says everyone overhearing him can't tell whether he's discussing medical problems with his doctor or awkwardly attempting to talk dirty to his wife. The Boss calmly replies that he uses one call to practice for the other.
punchline: The Boss's shameless reply admits that his embarrassing, overheard conversations are rehearsals, revealing he is so clueless that he sees nothing wrong with practicing intimate talk during doctor calls on speakerphone.
summary: An assistant scolds her oblivious boss for broadcasting his private phone calls to the whole office, and he cheerfully explains that one kind of call is rehearsal for the other.

title: Where Would They Put Universe?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Futurists say that someday humans will have the know-how to create an entire universe.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Where would they put it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We should do these brown bag lunches less often.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Slurp

setting: Office conference table during a brown bag lunch
situation: Dilbert, Alice and a coworker are sitting around a table eating brown bag lunches. Dilbert shares a futurist prediction that humans will someday be able to create an entire universe. Alice replies with a skeptical question about where it would go, then concludes that these lunches should happen less often.
punchline: Alice's deadpan question about storage space shows how unimpressed she is, and her remark about the lunches implies that Dilbert's rambling talk has made them tedious.
summary: A lunchtime chat about humanity someday building a universe gets a practical, unimpressed response and a wish to skip future lunches.

title: Thought Diversity Fad Dies Quickly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for thought diversity in my hiring. That's a thing now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Really? That's a dumb thing. All you end up with is a bunch of people who can't agree.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How do you like thought diversity now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That fad didn't last long.

situation: The Boss announces to his staff that he wants thought diversity in hiring because it's trendy. Alice immediately argues that it's a dumb idea, and when she disagrees with him, he gets irritated and declares the trend over. Dilbert sits by watching.
punchline: The Boss embraces thought diversity only until someone actually disagrees with him, proving he wants the buzzword, not differing opinions.
summary: A manager chases a trendy hiring idea but abandons it the moment an employee pushes back on him.

title: Christmas Party Moved to January

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our Christmas party will be in January because December will be too busy.

transcript.speaker: Man with glasses
transcript.text: I'm sure the almighty creator of the universe doesn't mind that we do things on your schedule, not his.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear thunder.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces the company Christmas party will be held in January because December is too busy. A coworker sarcastically remarks that the almighty creator of the universe surely won't mind being put on the company's schedule. The Boss asks what could go wrong, and Dilbert replies that he hears thunder.
punchline: Postponing Christmas festivities for business convenience is mocked as defying God, and Dilbert's thunder remark implies divine retribution is on its way.
summary: A manager shifts the holiday celebration to suit work deadlines, and the staff hint that heaven may object.

title: Insulting the Boss in Self-Defense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't handle this the way I told you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my defense, you're under-informed and less clever than me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was hoping he'd say, "Good point," but it went another direction.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway or break area
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for not following his instructions. Dilbert responds by bluntly saying the Boss is under-informed and less clever than he is. Afterward, Dilbert holding a coffee mug tells a coworker that he hoped this would earn a 'good point' but it went badly.
punchline: Dilbert expected his brutally honest insult to be received as a valid argument, but of course the boss reacted with anger instead.
summary: After telling his superior that he is both ill-informed and less clever, Dilbert is surprised the conversation turned sour.

title: Peer Review Punishes Productive Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You need to work less.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your productivity is making us look bad.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you keep being productive, we will hunt you down.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If it's easy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: About the peer review concept ... I don't think you thought it through.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: At a meeting, Alice and two coworkers tell a productive colleague to work less because her output makes them look bad, and they threaten to hunt her down if she keeps it up. In the last panel, a coworker approaches the pointy-haired boss and tells him his peer review concept wasn't well thought out.
punchline: Peer review backfires because employees who are rated by their peers will pressure high performers to slack off rather than reward excellence.
summary: Coworkers threaten a high performer for making them look bad, exposing the flaw in management's new peer evaluation scheme.

file: 2013/2013-10-18_facial expression_fear_scare away the weak_too busy_too talk_i said no.gif
title: Alice's Scary Face Demonstration

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm working on a new facial expression to scare away the weak. Want to see it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That one means I'm too busy to talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said no! I said no! I said no!

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Alice tells Dilbert she is perfecting a fearsome facial expression to intimidate weaker coworkers and offers to show it. Dilbert declines, but she demonstrates it anyway, surrounded by a cluster of monstrous faces. Dilbert recoils in terror while she calmly explains the expression means she's too busy to talk.
punchline: Alice ignores Dilbert's refusal and terrifies him anyway, showing that her intimidation tactic works perfectly on the weak, and that she doesn't respect his 'no'.
summary: Alice shows off a terrifying new scowl against Dilbert's wishes, proving it scares him witless.

file: 2013/2013-09-04_competition (psychology)_ignorance (knowledge)_big tech firms_hiring people_prestigious degrees_hiring idiots_vacuum up_hiring accused murderers_bail.gif
title: Hiring Accused Murderers Out on Bail

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The big tech firms say they no longer care about hiring people who have prestigious degrees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Obviously, they're trying to sucker the rest of us into hiring idiots while they vacuum up the people from top schools.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Shloop shloop

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to get in on this.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We could say we get good results by hiring accused murderers who are out on bail.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that big tech firms claim they no longer care about prestigious degrees. He argues it's a trick to get other companies to hire idiots while the tech giants snap up top-school graduates. The Boss wants in on the scheme, and Catbert suggests publicly claiming success from hiring accused murderers who are out on bail.
punchline: Catbert's cynical plan to copy the big tech firms' 'we don't care about credentials' PR line by boasting about hiring accused murderers on bail shows how absurdly low he'll go to justify a bad hiring strategy.
summary: An HR cat warns that tech giants' dismissal of elite degrees is a ruse, then proposes a deliberately outrageous hiring boast of his own.

title: Diversity Hires Assumed to Be Idiots

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired people who have different perspectives so we could enjoy the benefits of thought diversity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But they disagree with everything I say, so I have to assume they're all idiots.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Am I right?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Totally.

situation: The Boss tells Catbert, who sits on his desk, that he hired people with different perspectives to get the benefits of thought diversity. Because they disagree with everything he says, he concludes they must all be idiots. He then asks Catbert if he is right, and Catbert agrees completely.
punchline: The Boss claims to value diverse viewpoints but treats any disagreement as proof of stupidity, and he seeks validation from a sycophantic yes-man who agrees with him.
summary: A manager who wanted varied viewpoints dismisses everyone who disagrees with him and seeks comfort from an agreeable cat.

title: Budget Estimates Sprout Shrub From iPad

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I put your budget estimates into a spreadsheet as you asked.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A well-fertilized shrub sprouted out of my iPad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What does this mean?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's how you know the budget is done.

situation: An employee tells his boss he has entered the boss's budget estimates into a spreadsheet. The boss then finds a small plant growing out of his iPad and asks what it means. The employee says it is the sign that the budget is finished.
punchline: The employee implies the boss's budget numbers were so much fertilizer, i.e. nonsense, and passes off the shrub growing from the iPad as proof the budget is complete.
summary: A worker quietly mocks his boss's made-up numbers by claiming a plant sprouting from the tablet is the proof the budget is done.

title: Boss Won't Be Swayed by Ignorance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't give my opinion because I don't want to influence your recommendation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good idea. My well-informed mind is so easily swayed by your charismatic ignorance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not what I'm saying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then who did I hear?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he will withhold his opinion so he doesn't influence Dilbert's recommendation. Dilbert sarcastically agrees, saying his well-informed mind would be easily swayed by the Boss's charismatic ignorance. The Boss protests that this isn't what he meant, and Dilbert asks who else he could have been hearing.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's supposedly considerate remark into an insult by claiming that the Boss's ignorance is persuasive, and then points out that the Boss clearly said it himself.
summary: A manager's self-congratulatory abstention from giving his view gets twisted by an employee into a jab at how ill-informed yet persuasive he is.

title: Innovation Ideas Dismissed as Ridiculous

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to foster a culture of innovation. Does anyone have an idea how we can do that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could give us less work. And you could stop criticizing every idea we ever have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have a suggestion that isn't ridiculous?

situation: The Boss asks his team for ways to foster a culture of innovation. Dilbert offers two sensible suggestions: reduce the workload and stop criticizing every idea. The Boss immediately dismisses these and asks for a suggestion that isn't ridiculous.
punchline: The Boss rejects the very advice about not criticizing ideas by criticizing it, proving Dilbert's point and showing he has no intention of changing.
summary: Asked how to encourage innovation, an employee names management's own faults, and the boss promptly shoots down the answer.

title: Boss Admits Ignoring Technical Updates

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: Thank you for sharing your project updates.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: I didn't understand any of your tedious techno-yammering, but that doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why doesn't that matter?

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: It just doesn't.

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: Dilbert and coworkers present project updates to a bald manager at a meeting table. The manager thanks them, then cheerfully admits he understood none of the technical content and says it doesn't matter. When Dilbert asks why it doesn't matter, the manager offers no real explanation.
punchline: The manager sits through status updates he cannot understand and sees no problem, implying the meeting is a ritual whose content has no bearing on any decision.
summary: A manager happily confesses that he comprehended nothing in a team's technical briefing and refuses to explain why that is fine.

file: 2013/2013-10-14_inventions_magic_thinking_already exits_morphic field_pseudo scinec_crappy genes_filberts mother_explains things.gif
title: Morphic Fields and Crappy Genes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every time I think I've invented something, I find out it already exists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Maybe that's because all minds are connected by the morphic field.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Morphic fields are pseudo-science, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I also blame your dad's crappy genes.

situation: Dilbert walks with his mother and complains that every invention he comes up with turns out to already exist. His mother suggests it's because all minds are connected by a morphic field. Dilbert dismisses the idea as pseudoscience, and she calmly adds that she also blames his father's genes.
punchline: Dilbert's mother hedges her bets by offering a pseudoscientific explanation and a genetic one at the same time, with the second blaming her husband's genes for her son's lack of originality.
summary: A man grumbling about his unoriginal inventions gets a mystical explanation from his mother, who then happily piles on a genetic one too.

title: Alice Fixes Squeaky Robot Chair

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My chair is squeaky. How do I fix that?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Squeak squeak

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Die!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And now your chair is oiled.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Mostly the cushion.

situation: Alice asks a robot how to fix her squeaky chair, but the squeaking is actually coming from the robot's own chair. Alice turns into a green monster and attacks the robot, with a red demon-like form lashing out of her mouth. Afterward she calmly announces the chair is oiled, and the robot notes that mostly the cushion got oiled.
punchline: Alice solves the annoying squeak by violently attacking the robot, and the grisly aftermath is deadpanned as a successful oiling, with the robot noting it only got on the cushion.
summary: A woman irritated by constant squeaking becomes a monstrous fury, destroys the noisy robot beside her, and treats the oily mess as a maintenance success.

title: Robot Murders For Last Coffee

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Here is your coffee, as requested.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Some guy tried to take the last cup so I strangled him and put his remains down the garbage disposal.

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: It's weird how that makes the coffee taste so much better.

situation: A robot delivers a cup of coffee to a seated office worker, as he requested. The robot casually explains that it killed another employee who tried to take the last cup and disposed of the body in the garbage disposal. The worker, rather than being horrified, thinks to himself that the murder makes the coffee taste better.
punchline: The worker is so competitive and callous that learning someone was murdered for his coffee only makes it more satisfying to drink.
summary: A helpful robot kills a rival to secure the final cup of coffee, and the grateful recipient enjoys the drink even more for it.

title: Elbonian Embassy Is a Card Table

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for the Elbonian embassy.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: You found it.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: It's just me and this card table. If you need asylum, pull up a chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has anyone ever called you an "embacile"?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: That's clever. I like it.

setting: An outdoor grassy field with a card table and folding chairs
situation: Dilbert goes looking for the Elbonian embassy and finds a lone Elbonian in a tall hat sitting at a card table in an open field. The Elbonian offers asylum to anyone willing to pull up a chair. Dilbert sits down and jokes about the word "embacile", a blend of embassy and imbecile, and the Elbonian takes it as a compliment.
punchline: Elbonia's embassy is so pitiful that it is just one man at a card table, and Dilbert's insult, which blends embassy and imbecile, is mistaken for cleverness.
summary: An impoverished country's entire diplomatic mission turns out to be one man at a folding table in a field, which earns him a pun-based insult he happily accepts.

title: Photogenic Compliment Becomes Monster Insult

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: You take everything wrong.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's that supposed to mean?

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: For example, suppose I say you're photogenic.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you saying I don't look good when you see me in person?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There it was.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There was what?

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: It's the thing you do to turn everything into a negative.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, so now I'm a monster. Is that what you're saying??!!

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good. That's the vibe I'm going for.

transcript.speaker: Alice's coworker
transcript.text: I'm just saying you're totally nailing it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Watch this! Grrrr!

situation: A coworker tells Alice she takes everything the wrong way, then offers 'photogenic' as a sample compliment. Alice immediately twists it into an insult about her in-person looks, proving his point. When she escalates to accusing him of calling her a monster, he agrees, and she embraces it and snarls on cue.
punchline: Alice demonstrates she turns every remark into a negative, then proudly leans into being called a monster, deliberately living up to the insult.
summary: A man tries to show a colleague how she misreads kind words, and she responds by happily becoming the monster she imagined him accusing her of being.

title: Friending Dilbert For Facebook Time-Wasting

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I want to use Facebook to waste time at work, but I don't have any friends.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you mind if I friend you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. You'll be my only friend.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Will you post things for me to look at?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. Friends are totally inconvenient.

setting: Office, with both men holding coffee mugs
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, explains that he wants to use Facebook to goof off at work but has no friends on it. He asks to friend Dilbert, who agrees and notes he'll be Wally's only friend. Wally then asks Dilbert to post things for him to look at, and Dilbert realizes how demanding friendship can be.
punchline: Wally treats a friend purely as a content supplier for his time-wasting, so Dilbert concludes that friends are inconvenient, sarcastically noting the burden of being used.
summary: Wally recruits his coworker as a lone social media contact and then expects him to supply entertainment.

title: Boss Blames Employee for No Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're lazy, undependable, and disruptive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I can't give you a raise this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd it go?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He blamed the victim.

setting: The Boss's office and a coffee area in the office
situation: The Boss sits across from Wally during a salary review and tells him he is lazy, undependable, and disruptive, giving those traits as the reason he can't get a raise. Afterward, Wally gets coffee and Dilbert asks how the meeting went.
punchline: Wally treats the boss's insults as victim-blaming, but the boss is simply describing Wally accurately, so the joke is that Wally casts himself as the wronged party when the criticism is entirely deserved.
summary: After being told his poor work ethic means no pay increase, a slacker coworker complains that his manager unfairly pinned the blame on him.

file: 2013/2013-09-05_embarrassment_internet & world wide web_interviews_resume_old way_job interview_data online data_ew_disgust_walked out.gif
title: Hiring Manager Googles the Candidate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't need to see your résumé. That's the old way of hiring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now we use data from the internet to see what you've been up to lately.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Ew.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'll show myself out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll understand if I don't shake your hand.

setting: Job interview in an office conference room
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and dismisses the traditional résumé, explaining that his company now uses online data to learn about applicants. After reviewing what he found on the internet, he reacts with disgust, the candidate leaves, and the Boss refuses to shake his hand.
punchline: The Boss's internet research has turned up something so unsavory about the candidate that he recoils in disgust and won't even touch him, showing how online data can expose embarrassing personal behavior.
summary: A hiring manager skips the résumé in favor of web research and ends up repulsed by whatever he discovers about the applicant.

file: 2013/2013-11-17_illness_laziness_sitting disease_sit all day_bad health_safety more eimportant_drink coffee instead.gif
title: Sitting Disease Excuse Backfires on Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've got a bad case of something the experts call "sitting disease."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Studies show that people who sit all day for their jobs have a 40% greater chance of dying in the next three years.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Company policy says safety is more important than productivity, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um . . . sort of.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So instead of sitting at my desk working, I plan to walk around and drink coffee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For safety reasons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go sit at your desk or you're fired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's a good chance this problem will solve itself within three years.

situation: Wally visits the Boss's office holding a coffee mug and claims he has "sitting disease," citing a study about sitting all day raising the risk of death. He argues that company policy puts safety over productivity, so he should be allowed to wander around drinking coffee instead of working at his desk. The Boss orders him back to his desk or he'll be fired, then privately thinks the problem may solve itself within three years.
punchline: The Boss, unable to win the argument, takes comfort in the idea that Wally's supposed health risk (and thus the problem of Wally) might conveniently kill him off within three years.
summary: An idle employee uses a health scare as a pretext to avoid working, and his manager coldly hopes the statistics will eventually take care of him.
